joel.text: Understanding Reparenting
Welcome, lovey bunnies!
Here’s the idea behind Inner Child Reparenting, in a nutshell:

Growing up, all of us picked up automatic ways of understanding situations we find ourselves in, reacting based on those understandings, and then treating ourselves partly based on how we happened to handle things.
Some of those patterns are still wise in general, although even then, we are always learning from what life throws at us.
Others of those patterns were built for a crisis that’s long over, and some just seem to make every situation worse.
Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding a better Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide.
This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry.
That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding.
At first, it’s deliberate and might feel difficult.
Many struggle to get past the silly, awkward feeling of it.
Over time, instead of shying way from the silly, we can use the silly feeling in the work, to make it more playful.
I call it pl/ork !
With time, the adult/child roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.
If that got to you at all, good.
That was half the idea.
I used to listen to Suzanne Vega’s The Queen and the Soldier every night because it reliably got the tears out.
The crying helped me a lot in terms of not going numb inside.
It didn’t help me develop insight, though.
I could have kept crying forever.
It was Buddhism and then inner child therapy which helped create a new perspective that was more healthy.
But I’m really happy I did do the crying that was needed at the time.
Music can help with feeling love, not just sadness, although sadness is often the first step to open up.
So if you sit down to try any of this and feel nothing, that’s when I’d put a song on.
Céline’s right up there if you don’t have one, and Rosey Grier’s It’s All Right to Cry is a little further down.
My sister used to sing that one to me almost daily in such a silly way.
It was really sweet of her.
Some people, like another ex of mine (X), got so deep into crying that it became traumatizing.
She actually had panic attacks from it.
If you start getting scared of your own crying, turn the song off for tonight.
The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Céline’s song is called On ne change pas—”we don’t change.
I think that’s both fortunately, and unfortunately, true for most of us.
Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding.

Unfortunate in the sense that we often don’t truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren’t made for handling.
This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.
And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to « heal itself, » which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult.

I call that “forced adulthood,” where the child has to deal with situations the evolved inner adult should be handling--we see this in actual children all the time when their parents are not providing care.
People even wear t-shirts saying, “I don’t wanna adult today.
The forced adulting often goes along with a misperception that there is something wrong with the inner child.
Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.
That’s one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in to help with the rent, and each job keeps the others in balance.
Say a party gets to be too much for your little one.
The Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom.
And the Guide helps them think twice about the next weird party they might go to, avoiding another cycle of bathroom vacationing. 🙈

The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most, because a lot of the bad parenting or misdirection we originally received was likely lacking in Protector and Nurturer functions, while over-relying on harsh guidance.

So left it out of the first version of this framework until my friend Key pointed it out as crucial.Without a healed Inner Guide, our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well.
That’s the Guide’s job.
But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves.
And many folks try to find an ideal guide via some kind of guru-led political or religious cult.
If the phrase “inner parent” calls up the wrong archetype for you, pick another one.
Your future self might work, or the captain of a ship, so long as they’d do those three jobs.
But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem.
What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult?
In this case, you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.
Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first.
You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it.
Maybe you copy one small thing you’ve seen them do, or imagine them there when they’re not, and try one piece yourself while they’re still helping with the rest.
That’s what I mean by borrowed adulthood.
You may still need help with almost all of it for a while, but over time there are more and more of those little parts you can do yourself.
Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five progressive stages.
You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):
Forced adulthood : You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together.
At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting: 2.
Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr.
Rogers or Sesame Street?
Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage.
This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby, etc.
Practice being the adult — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and shepherding them.
Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads.
The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone.
This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while.
Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful.
Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!
Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life.
Depending on your maladaptive patterns, improvements could look opposite to each other.
If you’re a workaholic normally, then your little one might start believing in grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore.
Or the opposite, when you stop procrastinating so much and clean your room, then they start beliving in you.
Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, even if you make excellent progress.
You might feel like you’ve mastered the adult/child inner relationship, and then it’s Friday night and your boss asks you to stay late again.
You get up the nerve to tell them no, and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.
My Journey
I used to preach Buddhist enlightenment too much, because that’s what helped me out of a long existential crisis.

From what I’ve seen, most people who chase spiritual freedom, as valid as that is, are, at least at first, trying to get away from something painful in themselves, usually childhood trauma of some kind.
That’s spiritual bypassing.
Plenty of gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example.
The way I think this works is simple.
Imagine you’re broke and starving, and your baby is starving too.
Understandable: there is no food.
Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you’ve got lots of nutritious munchies.
But you’re eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving.
Unforgivable.
Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose.
I just didn’t believe there was a baby.
Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him.
Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I’d already found his way.
Spending your whole life processing your wounded inner child isn’t freedom either.
Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story.
Maybe ordinary life already gives many folks enough love and meaning.
It didn’t for me.
Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.
I was well-loved as a child, but from age 12 to 26, I was depressed, and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world.
Loving-kindness (metta) meditation healed that depression almost instantly for me, so it became my regular practice automatically.
I later found out that many people weren’t able to do a deep metta meditation, because they literally didn’t know what love felt like, as they hadn’t received it as a child.
My 2nd wife told me she didn’t know the word for love in her native language, because her mom never said that word to her.
But it even though my depression was gone, the sending-love-outward metta practice didn’t reach everything in me.
An old childhood wound could still hit, like if someone accused me of being lazy, and then suddenly it’s like I was that same little kid again, even tho the spiritual part of me felt free as a bird.
And a lot of the childhood stuff around my attachment to girls/women was still there.
At some point I guess I heard folks talking about inner child therapy, and being curious about different healing approaches, I thought I’d give it a go even if I wasn’t the prime candidate.
It felt like I was making it up at first, which seems quite common.
That didn’t stop me from occasionally practicing, but I did stop “pushing” it to be a certain way, and I’d stop trying to feel it was realer than it was.
I would go more into listening and waiting mode rather than imagining mode.
At one pivotal point, I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open.
I had a full-on audio-visual communion with my little Joelito and I heard a few things he was still sad about from so long ago.
Things which most people would laugh at, because they’re seemingly so minor.

Like when I hit my neighbor while riding my bicycle, and even after I profusely apologized, her mom said, « Don’t you have any common sense ??? » And I found out why I was always pushing myself to help others.
It was because when I was 5yrs old, at the Zendik community in Texas that we were visiting, they held a meeting with everyone there (like 50 people) and me in the center.
I was critiqued for not offering to help anyone I saw who was working.
Well, sorry !
I never knew I was supposed to.
That’s a pattern that has stuck, although it does help to remember what caused it, so I don’t take it so seriously.
Years later, I found a warm, intuitive inner child therapist, named Daja, randomly (if you believe anything is random), as a friend of a friend, while in Kenya.
I figured I already knew this stuff, but I gave it a shot.
She did actually help me see some things more clearly.
For example, she had me write down how many people I could fully trust as a child (lots), then how many people I could fully trust as an adult (zero).
That was difficult, and it’s actually the opposite of what you might expect from inner-child therapy, since usually that’s for people who had problems trusting as a child.
What it showed me is that I was ignoring a lot of things that were really important to look at, and that was one of them.
I wouldn’t have even thought to ask the question she asked me if I were doing it on my own.
It’s also an example of how therapy can sometimes make you feel worse than before, when you become more aware of problems.
But personally I prefer to see things as they are, so I can figure out how to work with them, rather than just hide in delusions.
It also showed me that I really do need to count more on myself than I assumed.
I need to be much better as an inner adult for my inner child, because my childhood was actually so nice that I kind of just assume I can trust everyone, and that gets me into trouble!
So it got me curious to learn more about inner-child therapy, which is a process I’m still in the midst of as I test this guide with people.
The image below maps out the details as best as I can fit:
Safety and Readiness
Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now?
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Check if you can pause before you act.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Are you following through after making decisions?
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: If you can’t do those things because you’re basically still stuck identifying as the frightened kid still, then let’s leave the deeper conversation until later.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to little you.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: And have someone steady there to support you if possible.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: And if the grown-up you is there, and it’s just how deep you’re going that’s too much, dip your toes in the kiddie pool first.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Like the flight attendants say, it’s good to know where the exits are. 😅 So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room?
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: If you can’t, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I’d come all the way back out first.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Now there’s a grown-up around who can say, “Okay, that’s enough for today,” and try something gentler, like saying hi to them with your eyes open.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: If you need a break from the communion, simply jot down the reason and the progress made so far.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Then come back later, once that reason has changed and you feel comfortable.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I’d call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too.
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Even if you don’t have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this (not hotlines unless it’s an emergency).
path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

joel.text: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, as well as gentle circular or varied directional massage in the solar plexus, neck, head, abdomen, or whatever spot is feeling tense.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: I’d also recommend checking into deeper somatic therapies like Shaking, tapping (EFT), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or some other bottom-up approach.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: When your nervous system is flooded, your protective parts are busy throwing buckets of water out of the boat, so they’re not going to let your little one come out and talk much anyway.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Some people go straight into EMDR to work on desensitizing their worst memory before they can even stay in the room.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Then they get predictably flooded all over again and, running low on buckets, they decide EMDR doesn’t work.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Here’s a map of what to try when:
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: When Therapy Stirs Things Up
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Some somatic work or reparenting therapy can feel pleasant, and some can feel like a raging storm got unleashed.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: It can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes nightmares later on as the memories begin to unwind.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: It’s a bit like going to the gym.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: You want to make gains, and sore muscles the next day can be good, but proper range of (e)motion here is also key to avoid injury.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Keep track of how you feel over the next few days, like how refreshing your sleep is, and how easy it feels to get through your day.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no?
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: If you can’t quite tell yet what feels different, I’d just make the next session simpler, one change at a time, like a science nerd, so you learn what made the difference.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: You can play around with variables like shorter session length, or shallower diving, time of day, keeping eyes open, having a friend around, or holding a teddy bear as a stand-in for your little one.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session?
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: They can show what feels important or frightening right now.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Although sometimes dreams can show you real memories and even predict the future on occasion, we need to be careful not to assume that they are doing that each time.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

joel.text: Notice the Part That Came Here
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: Some people hear all this about loving themself and answer, “No.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: I hate myself.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: Like my friend Malia, who told me, « My inner child is just capricious !
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: What’s to love ? » If that’s what you find, just listen to it, without arguing back.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: But if you opened this article, something in you wanted things to be different, whatever the rest of you was saying.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: The same goes if you came to therapy or asked someone for help.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: It might have been hope, or desperation.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: Maybe you were curious, or scared.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: Some people come here out of duty (my sister kept telling me to see therapists; she says everyone needs therapy).
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: Or it was more like, “I’m not going to keep suffering like this.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: And maybe it was love.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.
path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here

joel.text: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: I’ve been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: For such folks, inner child therapy is clearly not the place to start.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: They need to first deconstruct the adult identity they’ve got.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: When I talk with folks like that, I mostly want to know what the identity gets them and what it costs, and especially what it’s really serving.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Some of them even call themselves « sovereign, » yet somehow there’s an urge they have to obey, which sounds more like slavery to me.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who’s horrified by their own thoughts.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Everybody gets scary thoughts they’d rather not have sometimes, and they don’t make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them?
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you’re calm and actually ready.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: A real parent doesn’t get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to be get a perfect 4.0 GPA on the parent report-card their children bring home . 😛
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: And if somebody actually wonders whether they’re malicious, they’d do better to meditate on it and find out why they’re asking before they bring their inner child anywhere near it.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Are they really feeling malicious, or is it some voice in their head saying so, like the inherited critic?
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: If some of it turns out to be malice they actually want to act on, the inner child can wait.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Ill Will and Loving-Kindness
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up from identity, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Ill will can make you feel powerful.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one getting burnt first.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: The Buddha also told his son, Rahula, that loving-kindness is what gets rid of ill will, and compassion does the same for cruelty.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: I’m biased on loving-kindness, since it got me out of my depression.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: For these folks it starts with the grown-up they are now, though, and their little one stays out of it.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: As for when their little one gets a turn, I’d say once they’ve had some bad days where scaring somebody would’ve felt good, and they didn’t do it.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them for the good they see deep down, and won’t laugh along with the mask persona, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.
path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

joel.text: If You Want to Kill Yourself
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

joel.text: Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

joel.text: Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

joel.text: A crisis line counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

joel.text: As for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who’s doing the noticing (as described in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :).
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

joel.text: The Spiritual Side of the Question
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: I try not to proselytize about spirituality, because I’ve made that mistake before, and I now see that it’s better to let folks find it when they are ready.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: But when someone tells me they want to kill themself, I consider the topic to be brutally opened by default, regardless of whether they meant to do that, because if they actually do kill their body (which they might mistake to be their self), that’s a very powerful spiritual challenge right there, even if they didn’t realize it would be.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Then ask: what is the self you want to kill?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Is that self the same thing as your body?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Why?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Do you have the same body in dreams?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: What exactly do you expect your body’s death to accomplish?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: If the problem is a state of mind, like self-hatred or despair, shame or loneliness, what makes you so sure that destroying the body ends it?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: In Buddhism, death isn’t an off switch, and it isn’t a free new-age get-out-of-jail-free card back to the Divine Source.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Repeated thought and intention shape the mind, and that keeps going through death and rebirth.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Yes, that can include hell realms (and hell can be right here on Earth, also).
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: A human birth is a rare chance to understand suffering and end its causes.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: You don’t have to believe that, but if you’re still thinking of staking your life on the opposite claim, that death is just nothing, might that be a double standard to look into?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Curiosity killed the cat, you might say, so research could be dangerous. 😅 But despite the risk of curiosity, researchers at the University of Virginia have been busy little bees, collecting cases for 60 YEARS now, of young kids who talk about a past life, and there’s a big pile of near-death accounts too.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Even if every case is different, I’d read a few of those cases before betting my life on “nothing.”
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: Right here in this one life, it’s apparent that the more you hate yourself, the better your mind gets at it, and being alone tends to deepen the despair.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: But lucky us, because physical life keeps handing out redirections, like that guy who found me in a random park crying one time, and asked me “What’s wrong?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: If the many traditions and the accumulating scientific evidence are right that the mind’s causal process goes on after the body dies, killing the body may take away some of those redirections and leave the suffering right where it was.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: That sounds like a substantially worse deal to me.
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: My father used to tell suicidal people, “Oh, you want to kill yourself?
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question

joel.text: That’s wonderful!
path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

joel.text: White Knight : this is when problems are created that you need to be saved from, which can then lead back into guilt-tripping, or dependence.
path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult

joel.text: Solve your own challenges rather than letting yourself over-rely on someone as a pattern.
path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult

joel.text: Triangulation is where another person is brought in to the conversation so it becomes 2 vs 1.
path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult

joel.text: Value yourself enough so this doesn’t work.

joel.text: Borrow Someone Else’s Love
When a good friend sits with you while you fall apart it does help you feel better.
You call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while we don’t.
So steal some of it.
Usually what helped was how they just sat there without trying to fix you.
Ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is good enough for a start, so try it before you call next time.
If you don’t have anyone like that right now, try remembering when you did.
Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you.
Think of someone like that you remember fondlly, and imagine how they would sit beside your little one.
Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else
path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else

joel.text: Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, all the conditions you face, and then step outside it and ask what you’d tell them as a friend.
path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else

joel.text: This psychological trick has a rich history around it, and the blind spot behind it even has a name, Solomon’s paradox, after the biblical king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.
path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else

joel.text: Then take a small piece of whatever you’d tell them and do it yourself.
path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else

joel.text: If it’s “get more sleep,” that could be brushing your teeth before midnight instead of at two.
path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else

joel.text: Show Up When Nothing's Wrong
If the only time the Nurturer shows up is when something’s wrong, your little one can start to feel like they’re your job.
Sometimes show up just to say “I’m glad you’re here,” and then enjoy them for a minute, the way you’d enjoy a little kid who wants to show you a rock they found.
Watch how your love lands.
“I care about you” can be patient, or it can be “I care about you, now hurry up and feel better.
Getting close can be too much, too, the way kids squirm away from an aunt they barely know who goes in for the big hug, and then climb all over the uncle who’s just sitting there.
Knowing that love is in you somewhere counts for a lot, and you’re borrowing something you already know how to do.
A Smaller Doorway: Goodwill
Sometimes “I love you” is more than you can honestly say, especially to somebody who’s treated you badly.
Even the usual whittled-down loving-kindness prayer, “May you be happy,” can feel like rewarding them.

That’s why I go with the Buddha’s overall wish (paraphrasing): “May you be loving, peaceful, and free,” since if they were all of those, they wouldn’t have done what they did, and then they actually would be lovable.
This goodwill isn’t just for the target of it, though.
You may find it bounces back and opens up a little warmth in your heart.
And if “I love you” goes flat when you aim it at yourself or your little one, the same wish works there, too. 🫶🏿
Ask God for a Loan
The dog kind of love is real love.
Some people also know a love that’s a whole different size, like God’s, or whatever opened up for them in prayer or on a long retreat, and I don’t want to lump that in with the dog.
If you’ve been there, don’t shrink it down to a thought experiment about a friend.
If you haven’t been there yet (and even if you have), I have good news for you!
Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
One practical door anyone can use to slowly experience divine love is gratitude (even after the Turkey’s done & Thanksgiving is over!).
Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades.
I think it’s essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.
This is a bit tricky to put into words, but let me try anyway…
You may be suffering now, but you could be suffering more.
That’s something to be grateful for (although please don’t fall into the common trap of being grateful that you have what others don’t have, as that’s more like selfishness).
I’m not talking just about changing your “glass half empty” perception to a glass “half full perception.
I’m not pushing “toxic positivity.
Being thankful shouldn’t be pushed on people who just need to grieve for the moment.
On the other hand, I’ve noticed that I can sometimes completely flip a bad psychedelic trip into a good one with gratitude alone.
If you have a moment right now to breathe, and to really feel the beauty of that breath as it goes in and out, that’s something to be grateful for.
I learned this many times the hard way.
For example, when I got tuberculosis from a cave in Mexico at age 20, and coughed for six months straight, eventually having my throat close up, leading to a near death experience.
And then in Senegal, I had a suspected bilharzia infection in 2021, and could only painfully pee blood.
I promised to always be thankful if I could ever pee normally again.
Miraculously, I then found some obscure ethnobotanical research (on Google Scholar, before AI) which led me to drink roselle tea.
Within an hour, I was cured.
I don’t always remember to say “thank you” when I pee now, but I try.
That may sound like a silly, quirky waste of time to some folks.
But what I notice is that saying thank you for every little thing, whenever I remember to, is not about imposing some kind of “spiritual discipline.
It is directly reconnecting me to something pure and sacred.
Mo’ Money, Mo’ Problems
And I’m certainly not preaching “prosperity philosophy,” like the mega churches, even though it can seem to start at that.
We still need to remember that if we can only be thankful for the good things we have, we can fall into the trap of thinking that what we have is happiness itself.
I’m ultimately reaching for something much deeper.
Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn’t lead to being content with less.
When you can see that less is more, at a deeper level, that’s where the real gratitude flourishes.

And even (or especially) when I am suffering, I try to remember to be grateful for that also, because if not for suffering, I would not even think about how much I have enjoyed not suffering as much, and how much this tribulation will help me to develop more humility, compassion, wisdom, and gratitude in future.
Most importantly, it connects me with the plight of the countless other beings suffering at that very moment, authentically bringing up a wellspring of compassion in my heart for all of us.
And I see clearly that it is my inner child who is feeling this pain, and what an honor it is that I can be there for him.
Of course, that’s not to say you should not try to suffer less, or get away from abusers.

The point of life, according to every spiritual tradition and religion, I think, is to suffer less, which first requires us to understand the cause of suffering, and what real suffering and real happiness are.
If you, like Biggie Smalls, have come to understand that having money is not real happiness, that’s a big deal!
That’s something to be grateful for.
If we get a chance to meditate or pray today, while on the toilet, upon waking up, while ChatGPT is “thinking” for us, that’s something to be thankful for, for sure.
Notice how, when you offer thanks (to the universe, to life, to God, whatever you may believe in), a space in your heart opens up.
It might not feel immediately like you suddenly know the real meaning of Divine Love, but it’s a little spark of … something....
There’s a tiny bit of freedom, of peace, stillness, softness.
And as that softness deepens each time, you start to understand what I mean by Divine Love.
Many people have written books on this topic (like A.
Helwa’s book, Secrets of Divine Love, for example). hope you are able to experience this when you try it out for a while, and I’d really love to know how it works for you!
Invite Your Little One In
Once you start to feel that lovely softness of the heart (which can become a very deep field of « perfect freedom »), invite your little one in with you as your spiritual integration practice.
They might go numb, or call BS on that.

If so, they might just need to see if you’re actually humble enough, and grateful enough for them, to listen to their rejection be patient, and be open to the possibility that your Higher View is missing the trees for the forest.
If you instead retreat back into your cozy corner, it’s the food bank feast all over again: You can have an enormous spiritual feast upstairs while the child is still starving downstairs.
A Heart to Child Loop
With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one.
The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso.
One punch there hurts a lot (as I sadly learned while getting beaten up every day at kindergarten recess by a gang organized by my best friend.
Can you believe it?), so it makes sense to look for your little one there.
Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one.
If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop.
That part’s a gift from them, and they don’t owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours.
If you don’t feel the warmth just yet, rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required.
Non-judgement is a place to start.
It can blossom into love over time.
I also enjoy massaging my solar plexus gently.
When the Spiritual Relationship Hurts
If a spiritual teacher you trusted betrayed you, even sitting down to meditate can feel like it belongs to them now.
But if you let an abuser control your appreciation of life, then you’ve given them an unearned win.
Being the grown-up doesn’t mean controlling everything yourself, though.
After a betrayal like that, part of you might want to.
Spiritual support can help you act where it’s yours to act, and let go of outcomes and other people’s choices where it isn’t.
The Serenity Prayer is exactly to remember that.
Make a Simple Vow
If your promises still mean something to your little one, maybe because you’ve kept a few small ones, a quiet vow can help too.
As many real-life parents know, your heart really explodes in such an unexpected and wonderful way when you hold your newborn baby for the first time (happened to me!).
And if you’re not yet a parent, it can really help to imagine holding a baby in your arms to make the vow feel real.
Imagine you just had a baby, how would you feel?
Would you look at him/her with adoration and joy?
Carry that into visualizing yourself with your own inner child:
“I know you’re in there.
I love you.
You don’t have to love me back or trust me yet.
I can’t promise that nothing painful will happen.
Or that I’ll always know what to do, or never react badly.
But I can promise to tell you the truth and listen when you’re angry.
I’ll make our life together safer where I can, and take the next step I can see to protect you.
When I fail, I’ll come back to make it right.
You don’t have to believe these words.
Watch what I do.”
Notice it only promises what you can keep, so your little one can actually watch you keep it.
Whenever your little one shows up looking for their parent, even if they don’t know that’s what they are doing, you go back to being the one they can rely on, and you’re kind to them while you do it.
If they show up to have some innocent fun, don’t “put them in their place” as the adult.
But sometimes they show up as the one who doesn’t want to go to bed.
Now you’re in my mom’s place: you still go to bed, and staying kind about it shows them bedtime isn’t a lack of love.
Remind Yourself
The vow can live somewhere you’ll see it, too, like on a stuffed animal from when you were little, a photo of yourself as a child, or just a sticky note on the bathroom mirror.
Whatever helps you feel connected to the Nurturer and Protector you’ve been practicing.
The Teddy bear note may remind you to think, “When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time.”
A real-life child of yours, or a calm pet, can also act as a companion that brings out the relationship with your own inner child.
My son did that for me, and I think that’s very common for parents.
But those are also their own beings with their own needs as well.
Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.

joel.text: Practicing With Your Little One
Start With Whatever Showed Up
You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you’ve been staring at the rug.
I count that as reparenting, too, even if it feels like it’s in the way.
Before you decide where it’s coming from, ask it what it’s trying to stop, or what it wants.
Maybe it just has something to say.
It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that’s trying to protect you.
Maybe it’s that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.
You can tell that part something like, “I see you.
I’m not going to force my way past you.
What’s going on, boobaloo?
Or however you’d actually say that.
Then wait and listen patiently.

joel.text: Use Childhood Photographs Gently
My friend Cody had trouble imagining his inner child, so he started looking at photos of himself when he was young.
That did the trick !
If you have the same trouble, see if you can find some childhood photos.
While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones.
Use Pema Chödrön’s “feather touch” approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings.
Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand?
Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (”You hated that coat”).
It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream.
Or just nothing comes up.
Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.
We don’t need to ask it leading questions, like “Who abused me & how? » or “What memory is my body hiding?
Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren’t necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important.
Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions.
Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took.
Half of them actually started sorta remembering it.
I’m sure you can relate.
A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed (like O.J.😅)... not necessarily representative.
Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.
If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don’t confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here.
You might be looking at the photo thinking, “That would explain so much.
Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won’t lead you toward an answer.
(If the glove doesn’t fit, you must acquit!)
Put the photo back in its drawer when you’re finished.
If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you’re getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then.
Settle yourself in the present to close out properly.
Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this “Present Time” reminder.
Can be as simple and silly as “Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!”
Journal With Each Hand
Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand.
As titles go, it’s pretty literal.
Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings, as well as some extra creative juice.
The usual hand answers, as the grown-up.
Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with.
A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.

For some people, writing might make them feel more confused, especially at first, or nothing might want to be written.Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.
Which thoughts to talk to
When journaling, you might be surprised sometimes the myriad things that come into your mind seemingly out of nowhere.
Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you’re in.
A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your little one asking.
I wouldn’t spend long deciding what to call each part you meet.
Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included.
A part of you that’s trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn’t have to get any louder.
If no answer comes
That’s fine for now.
No need to answer for that part just because you had set this up as a healing session.
Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

joel.text: If it's anxiety
Anxiety is often a part of you that’s trying to protect you, making a guess about what’s coming, like that people will laugh at you.
Sometimes it’s right, sometimes it’s useful, sometime’s it’s not.
Anxiety is not necessarily bad by itself, but as they say, the fear of fear is worse than the fear itself.
Hearing it out and taking any action that seems legitimately beneficial as a result, often helps it to pass.

joel.text: Gentle Meditation and Mantra
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JQs2watlFws

If the hook is stuck a bit deeper in your mouth and you’re flailing around like a fish out of water, gentle mantra meditation or self-hypnosis (which overlap a lot) are some tools that can really calm your nervous system down.
A lot of people find that a mantra they feel some heart connection to, repeated in their head or out loud, especially with a nice melody, can lower the walls enough for the heart to open up.
It’s not something to lean on all day as a way of coping, but used as therapy it can be super effective.
I personally love this beautiful Om Mane Pemme Hum mantra that I found in the Garchen Rinpoche documentary, For the Benefit of All Beings:

joel.text: Discovering and Healing Old Patterns
How Distrust Reproduces
Say you learned somewhere along the way that if you need someone, they end up leaving you.
You probably never said it to yourself in words, but it steers you before you know why.
But the need for socialization remains a pull, regardless of how unlikely it may be to work.

And so we develop various coping strategies, ranging from distracting ourselves from that natural pull with other things (whether harmless hobbies or bingeing on TastyKakes), to people-pleasing, to insisting we don’t need anybody (sour grapes).
(The TastyKake corporation has asked me to remind you that sometimes a sweet treat is more a celebration than an escape.)
Some people pleasers go along for months as if nothing’s wrong while the pressure builds and then they blow up out of nowhere (one of my old patterns).
Then they feel so bad about it they go right back to going along to get along.
With any of these patterns, I’d ask what it’s protecting you from, because it doesn’t really help to just label it a bad habit.
The most insidious part of these expectations is that we can get stuck in them even when they no longer make valid predictions about the people in our life.
Like my second wife, Bee, who wanted with all her heart to trust me, but set up so many impossible tests that not even Einstein could pass with a perfect score.
I tried to explain to her that she was an unwitting prophet.
Have you ever heard of a self-fulfilling prophecy?
Perhaps nobody ever hears that you’re struggling, since you didn’t think they’d want to.
Then nobody offers to help, and that can look like proof nobody cares.
Keeping quiet might have been the smartest thing you could do as a youngin’ with nobody safe to tell, but now, if there are people who are safely available, it can keep help away.

joel.text: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
Healing does need to get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore.
It can’t be put on a schedule.If someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better.
Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury.
The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person’s conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made.
Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle.
From in there, it was the only move they had.

« Hurt people hurt people, healed people heal people » means that hurt people pass on pain they never worked through, although « externalizers » are the ones who directly hurt others, while « internalizers » try to protect others by holding that « secret burning thread » inside themself, which ends up exploding onto others anyway at times when it gets to be too much to hold, You may have heard this story from somebody telling you to forgive, and it sounded like they must have no clue how deep the betrayal was.
When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.
They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt, even if you see how they got there.
It’s just that punishing them now can’t reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense, the support, or the skills they needed for a respectable response.
What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now.
So a boundary can still be appropriate to enforce with them.
So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it).
Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there.
Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential.
“I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”
Forgiving Yourself
Forgiving yourself works the same way.
Own what you did (only what was really yours), and let yourself feel the remorse.
Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends, and by changing behavior going forward.
Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays.
If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too.

joel.text: Answering the Strict Disciplinarian
A good routine, like yoga in the morning and a proper bedtime, still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s done in a disciplinarian style.
One exercise you can do to handle this is to go back and rewrite your responses to that strict disciplinarian.
First, remember who it was that drove you so hard as a child.
Then start a little rap sheet of their provoking lines.
Comfort your little one before you answer any of it.
Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.
The Critic’s voice can often pile on, to the point where you can’t even understand why or what you’re really feeling anymore.
You feel sad at first, then the Inner Critic calls your inner child pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide.
You could probably have handled the sadness with some simple nurturing instead from the beginning, but now you have to peel back this other nonsense to get to it.

joel.text: When Healing Turns Into Checking
You can get hooked on healing too.
The wound can be completely real while you’re checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you’ve finally grieved it correctly.

Going back to reconnect with your little one is normal parenting/reparenting, but returning to lick the same wound over and over can become a search for certainty in an inherently uncertain existence.
Spending all day asking, “Did I process it properly?
Did I grieve it enough?” is clearly not what we’re after here.
And the checking can take many forms, aside from inner mental checks.
A body scan can turn into one, or a confession.
Even, going on a date, or checking your dating profile matches, can be a version of this if what you’re really after is proof that you’re good and lovable.
It might calm things down for a while, and then the next little wobble matters even more.
If you’re feeling guilty because you didn’t put your seat belt on, just put it on.
If you still want to investigate it later, fine.
Perhaps now and then you feel bad about that time you refused to put it on, broke your collar bone in a crash, and then got blamed for not wearing it.
That’s natural, but doesn’t mean there’s something new to look at.

joel.text: Physical Pain Makes It Harder
Physical pain can bring on the urge to escape too.

Say an attack has you curled up on the bathroom floor, and whatever knocked the pain out last time (say, fent, or ketamine) starts looking real good, though you know it’ll leave you worse if you keep resorting to that quick fix.
By now, you may have already been through a million doctors who shrugged their shoulders, or even alternative treatments that were too costly or hard to grade.
Sometimes it really is so simple that the best doctors and scanners can’t figure it out, like your house is moldy.
It is worth going through all the basic checks first that you can do yourself, and trying the things that make most sense.
For more on that, check my detox guide.

And when the symptoms come and go randomly, the best time to get diagnostics done could be right at the actual time of the crisis, rather than waiting until you feel well enough to make an appointment, and they may be able to treat it while it’s happening.
But what if the attacks come almost every day?
You can’t move into the ER.
And normal test results don’t prove the pain is imaginary, just as a treatment that helps doesn’t explain what’s causing it.

I’d ask for a chronic pain specialist and a written plan for the flare-ups you can see coming, including the new or severe signs that mean you go to the ER right away, but don’t let amelioration of symptoms be the end of the investigation.

joel.text: When Escape Leaves Reality Behind
All kinds of psychoactive drugs can mess with your sense of what’s real, and that’s often the point of them, so you can break free of all your old patterns completely for a bit.
But in general, try to select the healthiest ones and use slow and gentle protocols.
I’d say one of the most abused psychedelics (aside from ketamine, if you call that a psychedelic) is 5-MeO-DMT.
I have a guide on that.
People very often believe you need a huge dose of it for a “full release.
They go through all kinds of screaming and shaking, nearly killing themselves, with absolutely zero inner-child work being done.
Breaking armor down alone is not real healing.

path: If a past trip went badly

joel.text: If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened.
path: If a past trip went badly

joel.text: Don’t try again until you understand what would make it safe.
path: If a past trip went badly

joel.text: I’d look at the drug and the dosage, as well as mindset and setting etc.
path: If a past trip went badly

joel.text: I have a guide on dealing with bad trips and altered states.

path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

joel.text: But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates” has a noticeable dollop of paranoia too, but it’s practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis.
path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

joel.text: “...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!” is leaning psychotic.
path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

joel.text: Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, amphetamines, PCP, dirty LSD, so I’d avoid those.
path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

joel.text: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis
path: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis

joel.text: Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I’d be careful with other drugs that mess with what’s real too.

joel.text: And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it’s family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset.

joel.text: These are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind.
path: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis

joel.text: Who counts as trusted
By trusted, I mean someone you know is trustworthy from a long relationship with them, not someone people on Reddit said was super magical and healing.
That’s called a crapshoot.
It might turn out well, it might not.
It might seem like it did, and then later you realize you were duped, as happened to me with Sidney the iboga shaman.
A new therapist is not as trusted as an old one.
As they say, “new friends are silver, but old friends are gold.”

path: Before you quit a medication or alcohol

joel.text: Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous if you’re physically dependent.
path: Before you quit a medication or alcohol

joel.text: What you mix
Be careful what you mix, too, and not just prescribed medicines.
Even some basic things like cinnamon can be dangerous (and helpful) with ayahuasca, and doctors & AI don’t know about a lot of this.
I also learned that mixing acacia confusa with mimosa hostilis is very destabilizing and challenging, but excellent if you want to know how it feels to be painfully autistic + schizo!
I have a list of things to be cautious about with ayahuasca in particular.

joel.text: Altered States Can Require Reparenting
Have you ever been attacked by a literal demon?
Maybe during sleep paralysis or meditation or on a psychedelic trip?
A lot of modern folk laugh at this, yet it’s really quite a common experience.
I was being psychically attacked by ghosts in my home as a child.
Because I was literally a child, I was an easy target.
And since most people never actually grew up, they are easy targets for every kind of influence, including spirit influence.
It’s like leaving your front door open all night every night in NYC and expecting no thieves to enter.
Those ghosts knew my weakness: dares.
So they would dare me to jump out the window.
I wasn’t suicidal, but I hated to seem like a “wussy.
Luckily, I trusted my parents with this information, and instead of taking me to a psychiatrist and pumping me full of anti-psychotic drugs, they put bars on the windows.
Many kids are not so lucky in modern societies.
They may get pumped full of anti-psychotic drugs for the rest of their life once diagnosed.
That said, it’d make sense to get a professional to weigh in for some situations.
I still played around with half-hanging out the windows, but I wasn’t quite dumb enough to jump out, and I really appreciate that my parents took it seriously without catastrophizing.

Public Service Announcement : If a voice or urge is directing you towards harm, and you feel at risk of acting on it, as with myself and those ghosts at home, move away from that open window and get some outside support.
As a semi-adult, age 26, after my ayahuasca ego deaths, I lost my fear of the dark, death, and ghosts, and I told those ghosts to go into the light.
And they did.
I’m basically a Ghost Buster now.
Then I discovered meditation.
After I began meditating deeply for a while, it seemed like my astral portal opened.
I started getting attacked by spirits during sleep paralysis.
They would sit on me, prevent me from breathing, and instill tremendous fear into the core of my being.
Yep.
Exactly like that.

joel.text: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life
Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist.
But your little one got hurt by people that weren’t either of those, so some of the healing has to happen with real life other people too.
If you’re presently lucky to have some support, it might be mostly one person carrying a lot of it.
Maybe you’re picturing them right now.
Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing.
If it’s more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn’t feel as deep.
Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what they’ve been doing for you, and start doing it yourself.
You’ll find the balance is dynamic between inner & outer reliance, and going too far in either extreme isn’t generally the healthiest.

joel.text: Differentiation: Keeping Your Own Ground
Untangling the Belonging Bargains
Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging.
A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good.
Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about.
But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.
It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.
Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).
Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself.
That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades.
For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems.
It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls.
In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.
Even with good parents, you could have learned unhealthy self-valuation when people repeatedly praised what you did rather than your inherent worth.
That wasn’t your flaw.

joel.text: Practicing Differentiation
Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship.
You’d still belong, but now you come first and belonging second.
As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree.
If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe.
A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance.
It can be the same religion either way.
And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.
As you tell the part you’ve been playing apart from the authentic self that didn’t get much practice, notice whether it makes you more curious about both, and better able to relate to them.
Or does it have you thinking, “That chamelion’s fake, and I’m getting rid of it”?
Keep in mind the chamelion was a skillset that somehow worked to help you fit in.
Even if you’re not planning on playing James Bond anytime soon, you still might need to smooth your edges out sometimes as part of socializing.
You can’t always disagree with everyone on everything and still expect to be enjoyable/enjoy company.
Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:
- Caring about somebody’s feelings without automatically adopting their opinions or sacrificing your own ground.

Their reasons can still change your mind, though. - Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: “Wait, why was I nodding along?” - Noticing when what you thought you knew suddenly feels like water dripping through your hand because of praise or pity, fear or attraction, or something that really resonates with you. - Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places).
That one can take a while. - Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.
Key developed this identity and differentiation portion of the method, drawing on Murray Bowen’s family-systems work and her own self-therapy.

joel.text: 3. Finding People and Building Trust
People? Where Are the People?
I can’t tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I’d bet on more than one place.
Keep the good people you’ve already got.
Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if you find one that fits you.
And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that’s when we ask the Adult Protector to start paying attention.
First Social Connections, Done Right
Then there are people you’re just getting to know.
Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable.
Some people try to make themselves as lovable as possible, hiding their real feelings to do so.
Others have no filter, on purpose, to see if they are still loved and appreciated.

Like my one friend who used to go into churches and tell pastors they were wicked or unfit for their jobs, and then he wondered why he didn’t feel the love those churches promise (which was more proof he was right about them to begin with).

He’s not wrong to speak his mind, but I wonder whether his goal is to reach mutual understanding, to vent, or to re-try dealing with some traumatic childhood pattern of losing himself to fit in with the gang.
Neither of those approaches are the balance we’re seeking, and both are treating the other person like they’re your reassurance machine.
I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests.
Instead, get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present.
Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.
If you find yourself getting strange reactions from people all the time, check what your expectations were about how they’d react.

joel.text: Hearthwork: Taking Turns
The basic premise of Hearthwork, my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time.
Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing.
You speak.
I listen.
Then we switch.
Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality.
It’s kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.
Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too.
When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while.
Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time’s up, lends you the Protector.
If you say no, they don’t push.
But they don’t act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means.
Maybe they’re thinking, “Oh, I know what this is about,” or “Here’s what you should do.
They keep it to themselves.
A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you.
Then you trade places, and it’s your turn to keep “Here’s what you should do” to yourself.
The peer doesn’t become your permanent parent, though.
They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form.
Is that therapy?
Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure.
Professional therapy’s still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.
Dating While You Heal
Maybe you’d rather that your support came from a lover, as well.

Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part.
That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together.
It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know.
I wrote a whole romance guide, mostly due to this.

It’s often in handling conflict that we see the real inner child jump out.

joel.text: Other Folks Also Have Hooks

Once you’re in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don’t go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one “no” or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they’re allowed to say no to you.
Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they’re not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you?
(The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People.
Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?
If it’s the first, it can seem like you haven’t explained yourself well enough yet.
You probably have, and it makes more sense to count on what they keep showing you they can do than on the right words finally getting through to them.
Maybe what they can do is text you something kind the next day and not bring any of it up.
Can They Change?
You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they.
If they promise to change, that’s probably as useful as their prior promises were.
Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy.
Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise?
Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

joel.text: 6. The Love Has to Move
Community can come before the big opening or after it, too.
Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible.
Other times it’s the other way around.
Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn’t have imagined before, and then they start to “manifest” different kinds of people and relationships in their life.
Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.
This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with [building community] (community.u-dont-exist.com).
Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn’t really the point.
The love has to move, and it doesn’t always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop).
From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.
