joel.text: Schema Therapy
Of the scientifically studied clinical approaches I know, Schema Therapy, developed in 1980s-1990s by Jeffrey E.
Young, is the closest to this guide.
Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too.
Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head.
The healthy adult recognizes when a need differs from the strategy you use to meet it, and it helps you set limits..

And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you’ve committed to. all that sounds like my Nurturer, Protector and Guide by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.
Being all scientific and stuff does have its drawbacks also.
Schema Therapy’s name pretty much tells you all you need to know.
What the heck is a Schema anyway ?
(It’s normally described as a « pervasive pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving » (learned in childhood).

Although I find a slightly different definition of it from Cleveland Clinic : « A schema is a long-lasting outlook or assumption that you have about yourself, others or the world. » But yeah, put those together and that’s basically what it’s talking about.

So the schema therapist takes answers from a questionnaire you fill out and maps the your difficulties onto a set list of 18 schemas, which themselves map onto a set of modes, like the Vulnerable Child or the Punitive Parent.
Based on those schemas and modes, the therapist assumes some things about your childhood that would explain them.
Where it really differs is spirituality.

Schema therapy doesn’t build it in, though the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice « an important development. » That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy.
Some people do blend them, though.
Tara Bennett-Goleman’s book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema.
Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that’s the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).
Schema Therapy takes a more combative stance with the inner critic and guards than IFS or my approach, possibly a result of the lack of spirituality in it.
Internal Family Systems (FS)
Richard Schwartz, who developed IFS in the 1980s, called one of his books No Bad Parts.

Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so my section, “meet the protector first,” would fit right in over there, although I focus more on keeping the inner child safe first.
The one exception is that IFS does understand some parts may be entity attachments (« unattached burdens ») which need to be exorcised.
My guide also talks about entity attachments, but I don’t believe that’s reason to start another war.
Rather, I explain the root cause of such attachments as lack of protective love from the inner adult.
My reparenting method diverges from IFS at another important point.
The IFS Institute’s outline of the model says “everyone has a Self,” (a divine True Self, from Advaita) and that the Self “can and should lead,” once your parts stop “blending” with it.
I emphasize the inner adult you borrow, build and practice occupying that has the roles of: Nurturer, Protector, and Guide.
Is a perfect Higher/True Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent?
I’d call that claim [spiritual bypassing] (bypassing.u-dont-exist.com).

I’ve experienced that Higher Self perspective myself, though, in very powerful meditations.For example, one time, while still married to my first wife Ann, who was becoming more violent and crazy as time went on, we got super high on weed and we were both in some higher realm as our higher selves.
My higher self asked her higher self, « Are you going to keep getting more and more crazy ? » Her higher self said, « Yes. » It was like we could see the whole timeline of life from above.
Although, my friends already told me the same thing, quite sober. 😅
So, there is a less subjective way of seeing things as perfectly ordained in reality, despite the ego’s illusions, which matches what others say about it.
As a Buddhist, I no longer see it as « Self », though it can still give the same love, peace, and clarity to whomever accesses it.
Where I part ways with IFS is I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom that can be followed mechanically.
From that higher vantage point, problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.
You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self.
Anthony de Mello is an excellent example.
He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present.
He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods.
He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself.
And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.
I’m also not a fan of the strange and complex cast of characters in IFS.
IFS splits up my « inner child » into an indefinite number of wounded young parts called “exiles.
I find that pathologizing.

I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts...

At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming.
People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before.
I’ve seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
Development of my framework
My inner child reparenting framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice.

Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy.
I borrow particular ideas and practices from each of them, but the mix is mine, so please don’t blame them for it.
Original Teachers and Practice Resources
Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes.
Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it.
She has a book and a free one-hour YouTube training, and she’s on Instagram.
Key helped me think through some of these ideas in a very « embodied » way for a few months, and she added The Guide to make the 3 parental modes.
Lisa Romano brings more neuroscience and CBT, and her video is a good place to start.
She makes the point that remembering the specific details of childhood trauma isn’t necessary, because the felt body knows what needs to come up.
Key developed the Guide’s sense of direction, and the identity and differentiation work from Bowen I mentioned earlier.
She led a guided inner-child meditation in Nairobi in January 2026 for twenty people, and it’s up on YouTube.

base.text: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Céline's song is called On ne change pas—"we don't change.
I think that's both fortunately and unfortunately true for most of us.
Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding.

Unfortunate in the sense that we often don't truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren't made for handling.
This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.
And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to heal itself, which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult.

I call that "forced adulthood," where the child has to deal with situations the evolved inner adult should be handling--we see this in actual children all the time when their parents are not providing care.
People even wear t-shirts saying, "I don't wanna adult today.
The forced adulting often goes along with a misperception that there is something wrong with the inner child.
Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.
That’s one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in to help with the rent, and each job keeps the others in balance.
Say a party gets to be too much for your little one.
The Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom.
And the Guide helps them think twice about the next weird party they might go to, avoiding another cycle of bathroom vacationing. 🙈
The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most.
I left it out of my first version of this guide until my friend Key pointed it out, and without an inner Guide, it’s easy to go looking for one in a cult.
Our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well.
That’s the Guide’s job.
But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves.
If the phrase “inner parent” calls up the wrong archetype for you, pick another one.
Your future self might work, or the captain of a ship, so long as they’d do those three jobs.
But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem.
What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult?
This is much easier when you can already reach one of those adult roles.
But when you can't, it's like you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.
Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first.
You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it.
Maybe you copy one small thing you've seen them do, or imagine them there when they're not, and try one piece yourself while they're still helping with the rest.
That's what I mean by borrowed adulthood.
You may still need help with almost all of it for a while, but over time there are more and more of those little parts you can do yourself.
Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five fairly predictable stages.
You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):
You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together.
At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting: 2.
Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr.
Rogers or Sesame Street?
Those adult role models are what we're looking for at this stage.
This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you'd take care of a baby doll etc.
Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them.
Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads.
The child isn't pushed away, but doesn't have to run the whole life alone.
This can actually feel really weird if you've been stuck in forced adulthood for a while.
Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful.
Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!
Whichever stage you're at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life.
Your little one starts believing the grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you're wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore.
Reparenting isn't an exercise you finish, after all.
Say your boss asks you to stay late again.
You tell them no and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.
The cushion was practice for it.
My Journey
I used to preach Buddhist enlightenment too much, because that's what helped me.

But an old childhood wound could still hit, like if someone accuses me of being lazy, and then suddenly it's like I'm that same little kid again, even tho the spiritual part of me felt free as a bird.

From what I've seen, most people (like me) who chase spiritual freedom, as valid as that is, are, at least at first, trying to get away from something painful in themselves, usually childhood trauma of some kind.
That’s spiritual bypassing.
Plenty of gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example.
The way I think this works is simple.
Imagine you’re broke and starving, and your baby is starving too.
Understandable: there is no food.
Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you’ve got lots of nutritious munchies.
But you’re eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving.
Unforgivable.
Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose.
I just didn’t believe there was a baby.
Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him.
Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I’d already found his way.
Spending your whole life processing your wounded inner child isn’t freedom either.
Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story.
Maybe ordinary life already gives you enough love and meaning.
Great.
It didn’t for me.
Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.
I was well-loved as a child, but from age twelve to twenty-six I was depressed and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world.
Loving-kindness (metta) meditation healed that depression almost instantly for me, so it became my regular practice automatically.
I also found more love in the rest of the Buddhist teachings—which, it turns out, also include inner-child self-love! and later in loveyhuasca.
But it didn’t reach everything.
A lot of the child stuff around my attachment to women was still there.
When I later tried self-directed inner-child therapy, it felt like I was making it up at first.
That didn’t stop me from practicing, but I did stop “pushing” it to be a certain way, and I’d stop trying to feel it was realer than it was.
I would go more into listening and waiting mode rather than imagining mode.
At one pivotal point, I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open.
Years later, I found a warm, intuitive inner child therapist, named Daja, randomly, while in Kenya.
I figured I already knew this stuff, but I gave it a shot.
She did actually help me see some things more clearly.
For example, she had me write down how many people I could fully trust as a child (lots), then how many people I could fully trust as an adult (zero).
That was difficult, and it’s actually the opposite of what you might expect from inner-child therapy, since usually that’s for people who had problems trusting as a child.
What it showed me is that I was ignoring a lot of things that were really important to look at, and that was one of them.
I wouldn’t have even thought to ask the question she asked me if I were doing it on my own.
It’s also an example of how therapy can sometimes make you feel worse than before, when you become more aware of problems.
But personally I prefer to see things as they are, so I can figure out how to work with them, rather than just hide in delusions.
It also showed me that I really do need to count more on myself than I assumed.
I need to be much better as an inner adult for my inner child, because my childhood was actually so nice that I kind of just assume I can trust everyone, and that gets me into trouble.
So it got me curious to learn more about inner-child therapy, which is a process I’m still in the midst of as I test this guide with people.

base.text: Carry that into visualizing yourself with your own inner child:

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

base.text: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming "shenpa," and she says "hooked" is a more descriptive translation than the usual "attachment.
path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

base.text: You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking.
path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

base.text: Or you might notice it embarrassingly late.
path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

base.text: The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you're supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute.
path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

base.text: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh!
path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

base.text: A Heart-to-Child Loop
With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one.
The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso.
One punch there hurts a lot, as I sadly learned while getting beaten up every day at kindergarten recess by a gang organized by my best friend.
Can you believe it?
So it makes sense to look for your little one there.
Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one.
If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop.
That part's a gift from them, and they don't owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours.
No warmth today?
Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required.
Non-judgement is a place to start.
It can blossom into love over time.
Journal With Each Hand
Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand.
As titles go, it's pretty literal.
Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings.
The usual hand answers, as the grown-up.
Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with.
A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it's had its say.
And what if all that writing leaves you more confused than when you started?
Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.
A memory aid doesn't have to explain your life.
It could be a dated note of what happened, or of what helped.
A reminder or a next step works too.
Or you can leave yourself a voice note.
Just Like Me

On a steadier day, when thinking about other people won't pull you out of your own shoes, name the feeling plainly (lonely, say) and think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you.
With that many people feeling the same thing, the theory that you're the defective one gets kind of hard to keep up.
Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.

This is sort of a gentler version of Tibetan Buddhism's tonglen practice (which I learned from Pema Chödrön), where we imagine taking in the suffering of others, transmuting it in our heart, and sending out love and peace to them.

base.text: Use Childhood Photographs Gently
If picturing your little one feels like you’re just making them up, a real photo of you as a child can help, since there’s no face or posture to invent.
While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones.
Use Pema Chödrön's "feather touch" approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings.
Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand?
Some of it you'll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then ("You hated that coat").
It might just be an inference you're guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream.
Or just nothing comes up.
Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.
We don't need to ask it leading questions, like "Who abused me & how?" or "What memory is my body hiding?
Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren't necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important.
Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions.
Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took.
Half of them actually started sorta remembering it.
I'm sure you can relate.
A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed... not necessarily representative.
Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.
If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don't confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here.
You might be looking at the photo thinking, "That would explain so much.
Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won't lead you toward an answer.
Put the photo back in its drawer when you're finished.
If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you're getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then.
Settle yourself in the present to close out properly.
Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this "Present Time" reminder.
Can be as simple and silly as "Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!"

path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Because I was literally a child, I was an easy target.

base.text: And since most people never actually grew up, they are easy targets for every kind of influence, including spirit influence.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Those ghosts knew my weakness: dares.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: So they would dare me to jump out the window.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: I wasn’t suicidal, but I hated to seem like a “wussy.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Luckily, I trusted my parents with this information, and instead of taking me to a psychiatrist and pumping me full of anti-psychotic drugs, they put bars on the windows.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Many kids are not so lucky in modern societies.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: They may get pumped full of anti-psychotic drugs for the rest of their life once diagnosed.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: That said, it'd make sense to get a professional to weigh in for some situations.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: I still played around with half-hanging out the windows, but I wasn’t quite dumb enough to jump out, and I really appreciate that my parents took it seriously without catastrophizing.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: As a semi-adult, age 26, I discovered meditation.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: After I began meditating deeply for a while, it seemed like my astral portal opened.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: I started getting attacked by spirits during sleep paralysis.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: They would sit on me, prevent me from breathing, and instill tremendous fear into the core of my being.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Yep.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Exactly like that.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Sleep paralysis is a trance-like state, and trance can be "more scary" because you're trapped in it, but it's also less actually dangerous.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: You can't ruin your life at all in trance (unless a bad hypnotic suggestion gets deeply implanted, perhaps), while without trance you can "freak out" in a way that might end up getting you committed to a mental hospital, thrown out of your housing, going to jail, possibly even killing yourself.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: You recognize the fear has no real world significance and it's purely just fear, so it's super useful that way.

base.text: We give them the power.

base.text: After multiple episodes of this I decided to stop giving in to the victim mentality, and to start taking it seriously as a part of spiritual practice.

base.text: My inner Guide saw it as a perfect opportunity to demonstrate the power of love over fear.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: The next time it happened, despite how scary it was, I sent unconditional love to this demon on me.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: It took some minutes, but once that love was seen as enduring, the demon left, and it never returned.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: I’ve also trained other people to do this during spiritual attack while on psychedelics.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: It works a lot better if you are already trained in loving-kindness meditation to the point where it’s natural.

base.text: I’d say it works way better than exorcism techniques (like Julian Palmer’s torping, which he also admits doesn’t work as well as love).
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: The astral plane is a bit different from the 3D.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: In the astral realm, unconditional love is a true, ultimately powerful physical force.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Like a river, or a moat.

base.text: There’s no evil that can trespass that moat.

base.text: But don’t assume it will always work like that in the physical plane.
path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: It definitely has worked for me sometimes when facing some thugs, but definitely not with others.

path: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

base.text: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Reparenting assumes there's a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: All this stuff about your little one could have left you wondering who I'm even talking about.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Maybe you started playing that part so early, and it took over so completely, that "What do I believe?" or "What do I want?" has no clear answer of your own.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: They sound like such easy questions, too.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Back then, asking might have gotten you in trouble, or laughed at.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Or there was just no way to ask.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: That can make "love yourself" feel pretty empty (love what, when the part you've been playing doesn't feel real?).
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: From Survival to Experimental Play
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at the part.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: That left much less room for experiments that show you what you like when nobody's grading you.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: People grow into who they are by trying things on and then changing their minds, from what they wear down to the ideas and roles they take up, like a teenager who starts spelling her name with an "i" at the end and later changes it back.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Some of this is developmental pl/ork you get to do late: making it safe enough for your curiosity and experimenting to finally grow, and your preferences too.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: It might feel wrong somehow to like something before you've checked anyone's face.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: You can usually reparent and build who you are at the same time.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: As you tell the part you've been playing apart from the self that didn't get much practice, notice whether it makes you more curious about both, and better able to relate to them.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Or does it have you thinking, "That one's fake, and I'm getting rid of it"?
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: You're after a relationship between them inside you that works better, and that's hard to have if there's a new split between an acceptable self and one that has to disappear.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: When you ask what your little one feels, maybe all you get is a guess, which isn't proof there's no little one in there.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Maybe you hear yourself answer, "Scared?
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: I mean, it would make sense if it was scared."
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: So early on, the practice is finding out who's actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody's around to take your cues from.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Focusing (Eugene Gendlin's method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you've been playing learned to overlook.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Any words you put to them can stay tentative ("I hate cooking... or just for everybody?") while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Untangling the Belonging Bargains
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that's kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Most groups expect some conformity.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: But if going along means betraying yourself, that's the bargain.
path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

base.text: The Inner Guide
As the Guide, you choose what your little one learns and what it gets to experience, and you hold standards, the way a good parent would.
Your parent's harsh tone doesn't come with the job, though.
You ask hard things of it so it can grow, at its own pace.
That's what I was just asking of you, with that new interest.
You also widen its world with art and music, and you point out beautiful things when you see them.
Nature is part of that, and so is the wider world past the end of the street you grew up on.
By the way, this job doesn't have to be called the Guide.
The Wise One works, or your Inner Teacher, and "Guru" does for some people.
Between Spoiling and Clamping Down
Maybe you've let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real.
Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins?
Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling it the same way.
Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting it out of anything hard.
Treats and pampering do better at set times, where they can't get out of hand.
They shouldn't get canceled as a punishment after a bad day, either (ST-CA, section 17.1.4).
After all, sometimes “I want it NOW!” is just that: a rung on the desire treadmill.
No hidden guard or old trauma required, because all creatures have endless desires naturally anyway, especially when immature.
You can hear that want without shame about it.
Hearing it doesn’t require giving into it, especially if getting your way would hurt you or somebody else.
I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together.
It's forced adulthood, and it sounds like "Nope, all good!" from somebody with a fever who's cleaning the whole kitchen anyway.
Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it.
If that's you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it's just more of the same.
I'd try croaking to someone you trust, "Could you pick up some soup?
If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like "Not now, we'll go after lunch."
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it's okay to want a lot of closeness.
So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you've texted "hello??" before they're at the corner.
When they get back, you sulk all night.
Wanting them close is fine!
But they get to go for a walk too.
Ask your little one what it's afraid of.
I think it just wants to know they're coming back.
Then the Guide can come up with something like "See you in an hour?"

base.text: You Belong Everywhere and Nowhere
The Guide also points beyond itself, toward somewhere you belong that doesn’t ask you to give up being yourself.
That might be nature, or existence itself.
It might be whatever your tradition sees as ultimate.
Love can come from any of these places, and you also belong there, which is a little different.
Maybe you’ve felt that outside somewhere, like you didn’t need anybody’s okay to be there.
The way in is time in nature and contemplative practice, like meditation.
With that under you, belonging with people can get a lot less desperate.
Your little one might still think, “If they stop liking me, I won’t belong anywhere,” and the Guide can remind it there’s more to belong to than them.
Timing Is Individual
Most of us need enough Nurturer and Protector first.
Otherwise the Guide just overrules your little one in the name of something higher (spiritual bypassing, dressed up as direction).
Like a shepherd who's beating sheep to make them move.
So warmth and safety come first for a while, and the direction can grow once there's a clear little one in there to guide.
Say you had a spiritual opening years before you had much of a Nurturer or Protector (openings can come that early, and yours may have been completely real).
Has your love grown because of it, and has that love reached your little one yet?
Look at how you are with people, too, whether you’re more compassionate and do more to protect them.
Are you getting better at relationships, including telling the truth when it’s awkward and doing what you said you’d do?

base.text: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist.
But your little one got hurt by people, so some of the healing has to happen with people too.
Often it's mostly one person carrying a lot of it, maybe the one who drives you to your appointments and says it'll be okay.
Maybe you're picturing them right now.
Having someone like that while you're struggling can be an enormous blessing.
If it's more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn't feel as monumental.
Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what they've been doing for you, and start doing it yourself, even that calendar bit.
What you're after is care your little one can count on from more than one place, while the inner relationship stays precious and important.
Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works.
You'll find the balance is dynamic between inner & outer reliance, and going too far in either extreme isn't generally the healthiest.
Dating While You Heal
Maybe you’d rather that your support person were a lover, as well.

Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part.
That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together.
It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know.
I wrote a whole romance guide, mostly due to this.
First Social Connections, Done Right
Then there are people you’re just getting to know.
Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable.
Nobody’s a reassurance machine.
I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests.
Instead, get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present.
Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.
I can’t tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I’d bet on more than one place.
Keep the good people you’ve already got.
Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if you find one that fits you.
And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that’s when we ask the Adult Protector to start paying attention.
The same goes for doctors.
No need to give them a good impression if that means not being your own advocate.
If you don't feel up to it, bring someone you trust to speak up for you (it doesn’t have to be the relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment’s for.

base.text: Other Folks Also Have Hooks

Once you're in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don't go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one "no" or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they're allowed to say no to you.
Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they're not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you?
(The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People.
Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?
If it's the first, it can seem like you haven't explained yourself well enough yet.
You probably have, and it makes more sense to count on what they keep showing you they can do than on the right words finally getting through to them.
Maybe what they can do is text you something kind the next day and not bring any of it up.
Can they change?
You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they.
If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were.
Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy.
Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise?
Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

base.text: Hearthwork: Taking Turns
The basic premise of Hearthwork, my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time.
Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing.
You speak.
I listen.
Then we switch.
Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality.
It's kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.
Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too.
When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while.
Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector.
If you say no, they don't push.
But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means.
Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do.
They keep it to themselves.
A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you.
Then you trade places, and it's your turn to keep "Here's what you should do" to yourself.
The peer doesn't become your permanent parent, though.

They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form (a driving instructor isn't planning to drive you around forever either).
Is that therapy?
Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure.
Professional therapy's still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.
The Love Has to Move
Community can come before the big opening or after it, too.
Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible.
Other times it's the other way around.
Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn't have imagined before, and then they start to "manifest" different kinds of people and relationships in their life.
Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.
This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community.
Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn't really the point.
The love has to move, and it doesn't always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop).
From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.
How to Forgive Without Forgetting
For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore.
It can't be put on a schedule.
And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better.
Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury.
And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person's conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made.
Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn't handle.
From in there, it was the only move they had.
Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through.
You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive.
When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you've held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.
They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt.
Seeing how they got there doesn't make it okay.
It's just that punishing them now can't reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help.
Or the skills.
What's left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now.
So a boundary can still be right.
So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they'd never hear it).
Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there.
Understanding somebody's limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential.
"I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."
Forgiving Yourself
Forgiving yourself works the same way.
Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse.
Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends.
Changing the behavior counts too.
Then you're allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays.
If you're thinking "not me, not after what I did," forgiving other people tends to be harder too.
Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

base.text: How This Relates to IFS
Richard Schwartz, who developed Internal Family Systems (IFS), called one of his books No Bad Parts.
Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so "meet the protector first" would fit right in over there.
That's a lot of the overlap with this method, right there in the title.
My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point.
The IFS Institute's outline of the model says "everyone has a Self," and that the Self "can and should lead," once your parts stop "blending" with it.
I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru.
That's still one grown-up with three jobs, like back in The Chicken-and-Egg Problem.
Can't find a calm, compassionate Self in there?
Then borrow.

One grown-up job at a time, from a friend who'll play Protector for a night, or from something you do, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes (The Parent You Inherited again), until it's yours.
Is a perfect Higher Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent?
I'd call that claim spiritual bypassing.
I've had the Higher Self perspective myself, though.
It's a somewhat less subjective way of seeing things as working perfectly in reality, despite the ego's illusions, which matches what people say about it.
Where I part ways with IFS is the wisdom part.
I don't think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom.

It's a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.
You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self.
Anthony de Mello is an excellent example.
He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego's traps and coming back to the Perfect Present.
He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods.
He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself.
And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as "crazy wisdom" by apologists.
So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely.
The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them.
It can't act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away.
Most reparenting doesn't do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I'm trying to bring together the best of both.
IFS isn't exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here.
It has its own branches and disputes, and that's one more problem I'm trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.
I find that pathologizing.
I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts...

At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming.
People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before.
I've seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
Related Clinical Work
This framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice.

Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy.
I borrow particular ideas and practices from each of them, but the mix is mine, so please don't blame them for it.
Teachers and Practice Resources
Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes.
Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it.
She has a book and a free one-hour YouTube training, and she's on Instagram.
Lisa Romano brings more neuroscience and CBT, and her video is a good place to start.
She makes the point that remembering the specific details of childhood trauma isn't necessary, because the felt body knows what needs to come up.
Key developed the Guide's sense of direction, and the identity and differentiation work from Bowen I mentioned earlier.
She led a guided inner-child meditation in Nairobi in January 2026 for twenty people, and it's up on YouTube.
That just means you start smaller.

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: Welcome, lovey bunnies!

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: Here’s the idea behind Inner Child Reparenting, in a nutshell:

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: Growing up, all of us picked up automatic ways of understanding situations we find ourselves in, reacting based on those understandings, and then treating ourselves partly based on how we happened to handle things. Some of those patterns are still wise in general, although even then, we are always learning from what life throws at us. Others of those patterns were built for a crisis that’s long over, and some just seem to make every situation worse.

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding a better Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding. At first, it’s deliberate and might feel difficult. Many struggle to get past the silly, awkward feeling of it. Over time, instead of shying way from the silly, we can use the silly feeling in the work, to make it more playful. I call it pl/ork ! With time, the adult/child roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: If that got to you at all, good. That was half the idea. I used to listen to Suzanne Vega’s The Queen and the Soldier every night because it reliably got the tears out.

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: The crying helped me a lot in terms of not going numb inside. It didn’t help me develop insight, though. I could have kept crying forever. It was Buddhism and then inner child therapy which helped create a new perspective that was more healthy. But I’m really happy I did do the crying that was needed at the time.

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: Music can help with feeling love, not just sadness, although sadness is often the first step to open up. So if you sit down to try any of this and feel nothing, that’s when I’d put a song on. Céline’s right up there if you don’t have one, and Rosey Grier’s It’s All Right to Cry is a little further down. My sister used to sing that one to me almost daily in such a silly way. It was really sweet of her.

home_path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
paragraphs.text: Some people, like another ex of mine (X), got so deep into crying that it became traumatizing. She actually had panic attacks from it. If you start getting scared of your own crying, turn the song off for tonight.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: Céline’s song is called On ne change pas—”we don’t change.” I think that’s both fortunately, and unfortunately, true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don’t truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren’t made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to « heal  itself, » which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult. I call that “forced adulthood,” where the child has to deal with situations the evolved inner adult should be handling--we see this in actual children all the time when their parents are not providing care. People even wear t-shirts saying, “I don’t wanna adult today.” The forced adulting often goes along with a misperception that there is something wrong with the inner child. Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: That’s one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in to help with the rent, and each job keeps the others in balance. Say a party gets to be too much for your little one. The Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom. And the Guide helps them think twice about the next weird party they might go to, avoiding another cycle of bathroom vacationing. 🙈

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most, because a lot of the bad parenting or misdirection we originally received was likely lacking in Protector and Nurturer functions, while over-relying on harsh guidance. So left it out of the first version of this framework until my friend Key pointed it out as crucial.Without a healed Inner Guide, our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well. That’s the Guide’s job. But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves. And many folks try to find an ideal guide via some kind of guru-led political or religious cult.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: If the phrase “inner parent” calls up the wrong archetype for you, pick another one. Your future self might work, or the captain of a ship, so long as they’d do those three jobs.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? In this case, you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
paragraphs.text: Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first. You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it. Maybe you copy one small thing you’ve seen them do, or imagine them there when they’re not, and try one piece yourself while they’re still helping with the rest. That’s what I mean by borrowed adulthood. You may still need help with almost all of it for a while, but over time there are more and more of those little parts you can do yourself.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Five Stages of Reparenting
paragraphs.text: For now, I think of the whole path in five progressive stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Five Stages of Reparenting
paragraphs.text:
1. Forced adulthood : You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting: 
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby, etc. 
3. Practice being the adult — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step. 
4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and shepherding them. 
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Five Stages of Reparenting
paragraphs.text: Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Depending on your maladaptive patterns, improvements could look opposite to each other. If you’re a workaholic normally, then your little one might start believing in grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore. Or the opposite, when you stop procrastinating so much and clean your room, then they start beliving in you.

home_path: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Five Stages of Reparenting
paragraphs.text: Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, even if you make excellent progress. You might feel like you’ve mastered the adult/child inner relationship, and then it’s Friday night and your boss asks you to stay late again. You get up the nerve to tell them no, and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: I used to preach Buddhist enlightenment too much, because that’s what helped me out of a long existential crisis.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: From what I’ve seen, most people who chase spiritual freedom, as valid as that is, are, at least at first, trying to get away from something painful in themselves, usually childhood trauma of some kind. That’s spiritual bypassing. Plenty of gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: The way I think this works is simple. Imagine you’re broke and starving, and your baby is starving too. Understandable: there is no food. Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you’ve got lots of nutritious munchies. But you’re eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving. Unforgivable.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose. I just didn’t believe there was a baby. Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him. Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I’d already found his way.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: Spending your whole life processing your wounded inner child isn’t freedom either. Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story. Maybe ordinary life already gives many folks enough love and meaning. It didn’t for me. Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: I was well-loved as a child, but from age 12 to 26, I was depressed, and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. Loving-kindness (metta) meditation healed that depression almost instantly for me, so it became my regular practice automatically. I later found out that many people weren’t able to do a deep metta meditation, because they literally didn’t know what love felt like, as they hadn’t received it as a child. My 2nd wife told me she didn’t know the word for love in her native language, because her mom never said that word to her.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: But it even though my depression was gone, the sending-love-outward metta practice didn’t reach everything in me. An old childhood wound could still hit, like if someone accused me of being lazy, and then suddenly it’s like I was that same little kid again, even tho the spiritual part of me felt free as a bird. And a lot of the childhood stuff around my attachment to girls/women was still there.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: At some point I guess I heard folks talking about inner child therapy, and being curious about different healing approaches, I thought I’d give it a go even if I wasn’t the prime candidate. It felt like I was making it up at first, which seems quite common. That didn’t stop me from occasionally practicing, but I did stop “pushing” it to be a certain way, and I’d stop trying to feel it was realer than it was. I would go more into listening and waiting mode rather than imagining mode.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: At one pivotal point, I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open. I had a full-on audio-visual communion with my little Joelito and I heard a few things he was still sad about from so long ago. Things which most people would laugh at, because they’re seemingly so minor. Like when I hit my neighbor while riding my bicycle, and even after I profusely apologized, her mom said, « Don’t you have any common sense ??? » And I found out why I was always pushing myself to help others. It was because when I was 5yrs old, at the Zendik community in Texas that we were visiting, they held a meeting with everyone there (like 50 people) and me in the center. I was critiqued for not offering to help anyone I saw who was working. Well, sorry ! I never knew I was supposed to. That’s a pattern that has stuck, although it does help to remember what caused it, so I don’t take it so seriously.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: Years later, I found a warm, intuitive inner child therapist, named Daja, randomly (if you believe anything is random), as a friend of a friend, while in Kenya. I figured I already knew this stuff, but I gave it a shot. She did actually help me see some things more clearly. For example, she had me write down how many people I could fully trust as a child (lots), then how many people I could fully trust as an adult (zero). That was difficult, and it’s actually the opposite of what you might expect from inner-child therapy, since usually that’s for people who had problems trusting as a child.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: What it showed me is that I was ignoring a lot of things that were really important to look at, and that was one of them. I wouldn’t have even thought to ask the question she asked me if I were doing it on my own. It’s also an example of how therapy can sometimes make you feel worse than before, when you become more aware of problems. But personally I prefer to see things as they are, so I can figure out how to work with them, rather than just hide in delusions.

home_path: My Journey
paragraphs.text: It also showed me that I really do need to count more on myself than I assumed. I need to be much better as an inner adult for my inner child, because my childhood was actually so nice that I kind of just assume I can trust everyone, and that gets me into trouble! So it got me curious to learn more about inner-child therapy, which is a process I’m still in the midst of as I test this guide with people.

paragraphs.text: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Check if you can pause before you act. Are you following through after making decisions? If you can’t do those things because you’re basically still stuck identifying as the frightened kid still, then let’s leave the deeper conversation until later. Do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to little you. And have someone steady there to support you if possible.

path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep

paragraphs.text: And if the grown-up you is there, and it’s just how deep you’re going that’s too much, dip your toes in the kiddie pool first. Like the flight attendants say, it’s good to know where the exits are. 😅 So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room? If you can’t, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I’d come all the way back out first. Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there’s a grown-up around who can say, “Okay, that’s enough for today,” and try something gentler, like saying hi to them with your eyes open.

paragraphs.text: If you need a break from the communion, simply jot down the reason and the progress made so far. Then come back later, once that reason has changed and you feel comfortable.

paragraphs.text: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I’d call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Even if you don’t have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this (not hotlines unless it’s an emergency).

home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep

paragraphs.text: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, as well as gentle circular or varied directional massage in the solar plexus, neck, head, abdomen, or whatever spot is feeling tense.

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

paragraphs.text: I’d also recommend checking into deeper somatic therapies like Shaking, tapping (EFT), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or some other bottom-up approach.

home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
paragraphs.text: When your nervous system is flooded, your protective parts are busy throwing buckets of water out of the boat, so they’re not going to let your little one come out and talk much anyway. Some people go straight into EMDR to work on desensitizing their worst memory before they can even stay in the room. Then they get predictably flooded all over again and, running low on buckets, they decide EMDR doesn’t work. Here’s a map of what to try when:

When Somatic Work Brings Things Up
paragraphs.text: Some somatic work or reparenting therapy can feel pleasant, and some can feel like a raging storm got unleashed. It can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes nightmares later on as the memories begin to unwind. It’s a bit like going to the gym. You want to make gains, and sore muscles the next day can be good, but proper range of (e)motion here is also key to avoid injury.

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
When Somatic Work Brings Things Up
paragraphs.text: Keep track of how you feel over the next few days, like how refreshing your sleep is, and how easy it feels to get through your day. Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? If you can’t quite tell yet what feels different, I’d just make the next session simpler, one change at a time, like a science nerd, so you learn what made the difference. You can play around with variables like shorter session length, or shallower diving, time of day, keeping eyes open, having a friend around, or holding a teddy bear as a stand-in for your little one.

paragraphs.text: And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. Although sometimes dreams can show you real memories and even predict the future on occasion, we need to be careful not to assume that they are doing that each time.

paragraphs.text: Some people hear all this about loving themself and answer, “No. I hate myself.” Like my friend Malia, who told me, « My inner child is just capricious ! What’s to love ? » If that’s what you find, just listen to it, without arguing back. But if you opened this article, something in you wanted things to be different, whatever the rest of you was saying. The same goes if you came to therapy or asked someone for help.

home_path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Notice the Part That Came Here
paragraphs.text: It might have been hope, or desperation. Maybe you were curious, or scared. Some people come here out of duty (my sister kept telling me to see therapists; she says everyone needs therapy). Or it was more like, “I’m not going to keep suffering like this.” And maybe it was love. Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
paragraphs.text: I’ve been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child. Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though. For such folks, inner child therapy is clearly not the place to start. They need to first deconstruct the adult identity they’ve got.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
paragraphs.text: When I talk with folks like that, I mostly want to know what the identity gets them and what it costs, and especially what it’s really serving. Some of them even call themselves « sovereign, » yet somehow there’s an urge they have to obey, which sounds more like slavery to me.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
paragraphs.text: This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who’s horrified by their own thoughts. Everybody gets scary thoughts they’d rather not have sometimes, and they don’t make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them? The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you’re calm and actually ready. A real parent doesn’t get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to be get a perfect 4.0 GPA on the parent report-card their children bring home . 😛

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
paragraphs.text: And if somebody actually wonders whether they’re malicious, they’d do better to meditate on it and find out why they’re asking before they bring their inner child anywhere near it. Are they really feeling malicious, or is it some voice in their head saying so, like the inherited critic? If some of it turns out to be malice they actually want to act on, the inner child can wait.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
Ill Will and Loving-Kindness
paragraphs.text: In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up from identity, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one getting burnt first. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
home_path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
Ill Will and Loving-Kindness
paragraphs.text: The Buddha also told his son, Rahula, that loving-kindness is what gets rid of ill will, and compassion does the same for cruelty. I’m biased on loving-kindness, since it got me out of my depression. For these folks it starts with the grown-up they are now, though, and their little one stays out of it.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

paragraphs.text: As for when their little one gets a turn, I’d say once they’ve had some bad days where scaring somebody would’ve felt good, and they didn’t do it. Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them for the good they see deep down, and won’t laugh along with the mask persona, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.

paragraphs.text: Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
home_path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
paragraphs.text: As for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who’s doing the noticing (as described in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :).

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself

home_path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
paragraphs.text: I try not to proselytize about spirituality, because I’ve made that mistake before, and I now see that it’s better to let folks find it when they are ready. But when someone tells me they want to kill themself, I consider the topic to be brutally opened by default, regardless of whether they meant to do that, because if they actually do kill their body (which they might mistake to be their self), that’s a very powerful spiritual challenge right there, even if they didn’t realize it would be.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
home_path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
paragraphs.text: Then ask: what is the self you want to kill? Is that self the same thing as your body? Why? Do you have the same body in dreams? What exactly do you expect your body’s death to accomplish? If the problem is a state of mind, like self-hatred or despair, shame or loneliness, what makes you so sure that destroying the body ends it?

Those might sound difficult, but they’re actually considerably easier and more likely to help than dying.

paragraphs.text: Some manipulative people are too smart to act perfect. They lead with their wounds, or with how brutally honest they are about their flaws (very disarming, which is sort of the point), and every warning you hear about them just becomes more proof of how profound they are. Your Protector should be called to step in whenever love bombing hides obvious red flags your more skeptical friends would love to point out if you’d listen. After all, “I have honesty issues and I’m working on them” may be a perfectly honest thing to say. It’s also telling you there’s an honesty problem right now, and knowing about a problem isn’t fixing it.
