Other types of manipulation to check for include : 
Gaslighting, when your perception of reality is slowly giving way to someone else’s. Combat this by trusting your perceptions (after documenting or double checking).

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: In abusive relationships, gaslighting often turns into D.A.R.V.O. : Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender. This is how the abuser flips the script on accountability. If you notice this happening, extricate yourself quickly.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: Guilt tripping, where you’re made to feel responsible for things you shouldn’t be. Like someone did something for you and then later makes you seem like a bad person because you haven’t done enough to give back. Check if the guilt is deserved or not.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: White Knight : this is when problems are created that you need to be saved from, which can then lead back into guilt-tripping, or dependence. Solve your own challenges rather than letting yourself over-rely on someone as a pattern.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: Triangulation is where another person is brought in to the conversation so it becomes 2 vs 1. Insist on direct communication with one person if this tactic is employed.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: Silent treatment : when someone cuts back their emotional involvement to punish or control you (can be confused with simply avoiding situations they aren’t able to handle). Don’t chase these people, nor reverse it onto them.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: Breadcrumbing is when silent treatment is reduced just enough to make you hooked on trying to get their attention. Value yourself enough so this doesn’t work.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
paragraphs.text: That’s a lot of manipulation tactics! And those sneaky sneaks are always coming up with new ones, so it’s time we develop our spidey sense. We can also look inward to check if we are using those on ourselves or others.

You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. “What’s an ‘internal attack’?” Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they’re sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back. They don’t trust you yet, and you don’t ask them to. paragraphs.text: I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up. Maybe sometimes that script feels warm, but maybe too often it feels more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound totally reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If your childhood was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed to show up, so they could keep belonging. And if so, do a double check: they might still be doing it!

Then you can feel attacked from both sides: not only are you not good enough, but if you do seem to be good enough, it’s probably fake, so it’s like nothing you do really counts. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” with a background like that, well, of course your little one doesn’t answer.

Remember When You Already Did It
paragraphs.text: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. Getting hit with a stick doesn’t solve the problem, unless you’re a Zen student. 🙃

A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
paragraphs.text: The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
paragraphs.text: Forced adulthood can get into your head too, and it might set the bar too high sometimes. At your grandpa’s funeral, some dumb jingle starts up in your head and you nearly laugh during the eulogy. That doesn’t mean you didn’t love him, or that something’s wrong with you. Minds come up with ugly and embarrassing stuff all the time, some of it the opposite of what you believe, and bodies do their own thing too. The Guide doesn’t need to police your every thought. It notices the jingle and knows you didn’t mean it, and that it isn’t who you are. Then it goes with what you’d stand behind, which here is probably squeezing your mom’s hand and listening, and lets the jingle go.

A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
paragraphs.text: I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about some pattern you have, that might be a signal to give some attention to how you can improve on that pattern. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive, and can be simply let go of.

Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you’re supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. Maybe that’s what happens for some people, but you might not be some people (hehe). If talking into an empty room feels silly, small figures on a table can help (so that you feel even more silly!?), like one for your little one and one for the rest of the gang that shows up. Put whichever one’s running the show on a throne. Both ideas come from sections 12.2 and 13.1 of a book called Schema Therapy for Children and Adolescents, which I’ll call ST-CA.

paragraphs.text: Life is always switching up on us. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first.

My friend Cody had trouble imagining his inner child, so he started looking at photos of himself when he was young. That did the trick ! If you have the same trouble, see if you can find some childhood photos.

home_path: Simple Practices
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
paragraphs.text: While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones. Use Pema Chödrön’s “feather touch” approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (”You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

home_path: Simple Practices
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
paragraphs.text: We don’t need to ask it leading questions, like “Who abused me & how? » or “What memory is my body hiding?” Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren’t necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions. Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I’m sure you can relate.

home_path: Simple Practices
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
paragraphs.text: A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed (like O.J.😅)... not necessarily representative. Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.

home_path: Simple Practices
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
paragraphs.text: If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don’t confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here. You might be looking at the photo thinking, “That would explain so much.” Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won’t lead you toward an answer. (If the glove doesn’t fit, you must acquit!)

home_path: Simple Practices
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
paragraphs.text: Put the photo back in its drawer when you’re finished. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you’re getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present to close out properly. Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this “Present Time” reminder. Can be as simple and silly as “Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!”

home_path: Simple Practices
Journal With Each Hand
paragraphs.text: Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand. As titles go, it’s pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings, as well as some extra creative juice. The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.

home_path: Simple Practices
Journal With Each Hand
paragraphs.text: For some people, writing might make them feel more confused, especially at first, or nothing might want to be written.Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.

Which thoughts to talk to
paragraphs.text: When journaling, you might be surprised sometimes the myriad things that come into your mind seemingly out of nowhere. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you’re in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your little one asking.

home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

Which thoughts to talk to
paragraphs.text: I wouldn’t spend long deciding what to call each part you meet. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that’s trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn’t have to get any louder.

If no answer comes
paragraphs.text: That’s fine for now. No need to answer for that part just because you had set this up as a healing session. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

path: If you do get an answer
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

If you do get an answer
paragraphs.text: An answer could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It’s often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that’s what it wants. How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better.

path: If it tells you to do something
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

If it tells you to do something
paragraphs.text: I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.

If it's anxiety
paragraphs.text: Anxiety is often a part of you that’s trying to protect you, making a guess about what’s coming, like that people will laugh at you. Sometimes it’s right, sometimes it’s useful, sometime’s it’s not. Anxiety is not necessarily bad by itself, but as they say, the fear of fear is worse than the fear itself. Hearing it out and taking any action that seems legitimately beneficial as a result, often helps it to pass.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
home_path: Simple Practices
Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
paragraphs.text: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “shenpa,” and she says “hooked” is a more descriptive translation for that Tibetan concept than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. 💃🏿 Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you’re supposed to be observing yourself. 🤦‍♂️ Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
home_path: Simple Practices
Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
paragraphs.text: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: “Oh! I’m hooked again! That’s awesome I could notice it!” Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Maybe then you’ll find there’s enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you’d regret later. Or enough Guide to redirect attention to where it’s supposed to be.

paragraphs.text: If the hook is stuck a bit deeper in your mouth and you’re flailing around like a fish out of water, gentle mantra meditation or self-hypnosis (which overlap a lot) are some tools that can really calm your nervous system down. A lot of people find that a mantra they feel some heart connection to, repeated in their head or out loud, especially with a nice melody, can lower the walls enough for the heart to open up. It’s not something to lean on all day as a way of coping, but used as therapy it can be super effective. I personally love this beautiful Om Mane Pemme Hum mantra that I found in the Garchen Rinpoche documentary, For the Benefit of All Beings:

paragraphs.text: If what someone did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn’t mean their boundary crossing indicates “They’re evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you’re in your happy place.

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
home_path: Simple Practices

What to Make of a Passing Feeling
paragraphs.text: Feelings about yourself work the same way. “I feel attracted” or “I feel ashamed” is real as a feeling, but it doesn’t settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche’s pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc.

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
home_path: Simple Practices

What to Make of a Passing Feeling
paragraphs.text: You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don’t have to declare your pronouns on social media, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there’s nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see if there’s some avoidance of differentiation. I myself for a long time was accused of « having no opinions » (which I almost prided myself on🙈), and now it’s often the opposite accusation.

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling

What to Make of a Passing Feeling
paragraphs.text: The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later.

paragraphs.text: Then get practical so it doesn’t become another OCD loop: “What small repair or protective act shall I bring in for a proper response to that?”

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

paragraphs.text: And don’t forget to appreciate the good! Moments of warm, beneficial connection (whether internally from child to adult, socially, spiritually, etc) are all to be celebrated. Were you maybe firm like an elephant today, or courageous like a lion? Adopt the entire spirit animal zoo if need be! Turtles are good if you need impulse control.

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
home_path: Simple Practices
One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
paragraphs.text: Count recognition as progress, regardless whether it came up a bit late, as the goal is to bring the awareness closer and closer to the present. All or nothing from the get go would be cool, but we normally have to learn step by step. If/when you interrupted the pattern, pat yourself on the back, or even kiss yourself on the shoulder. You can renew your intention for tomorrow, getting better & better, every day, in every way, as my Dad used to say. And enjoy your well-earned rest tonight.

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
home_path: Simple Practices
Close the Session and Return to Life
paragraphs.text: Without an ending, the processing can just start looping. So when you’re done, look around and say where you are. Feel your feet on the floor, or the chair under you, and remind yourself about something silly and obvious, like what century Pharao Tutankhamun was crowned (1332 BCE in case you forgot!)…

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
home_path: Simple Practices
Close the Session and Return to Life
paragraphs.text: And what’s next for you two? Maybe it’s making food, or just going to bed. Whatever it is, tell your little one, “That’s enough for today. We’re going back to the life we’re building.” Nothing has to be resolved first, and whatever you’re still feeling can come along.

Two Common Guarding Patterns Blocking Reparenting
The Belief Behind the Guards
paragraphs.text: Say you learned somewhere along the way that if you need someone, they end up leaving you. You probably never said it to yourself in words, but it steers you before you know why. But the need for socialization remains a pull, regardless of how unlikely it may be to work. And so we develop various coping strategies, ranging from distracting ourselves from that natural pull with other things (whether harmless hobbies or bingeing on TastyKakes), to people-pleasing, to insisting we don’t need anybody (sour grapes). (The TastyKake corporation has asked me to remind you that sometimes a sweet treat is more a celebration than an escape.)

home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Start With Whatever Showed Up
Two Common Guarding Patterns Blocking Reparenting
The Belief Behind the Guards
paragraphs.text: Some people pleasers go along for months as if nothing’s wrong while the pressure builds and then they blow up out of nowhere (one of my old patterns). Then they feel so bad about it they go right back to going along to get along. With any of these patterns, I’d ask what it’s protecting you from, because it doesn’t really help to just label it a bad habit.

The most insidious part of these expectations is that we can get stuck in them even when they no longer make valid predictions about the people in our life. Like my second wife, Bee, who wanted with all her heart to trust me, but set up so many impossible tests that not even Einstein could pass with a perfect score. I tried to explain to her that she was an unwitting prophet.

home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Start With Whatever Showed Up
Two Common Guarding Patterns Blocking Reparenting
The Belief Behind the Guards
paragraphs.text: Have you ever heard of a self-fulfilling prophecy? Perhaps nobody ever hears that you’re struggling, since you didn’t think they’d want to. Then nobody offers to help, and that can look like proof nobody cares. Keeping quiet might have been the smartest thing you could do as a youngin’ with nobody safe to tell, but now, if there are people who are safely available, it can keep help away.

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
paragraphs.text: Shame comes when you’re holding a dark secret. It might be a secret for someone else who abused you, because it made you feel dirty or worthless. Or it might be due to thoughts in your head that bother you. Or it might be from bad patterns of behavior you have. Whatever the cause, finding someone trusted that you can slowly open up to is a magic cure. You still have to take accountability and repair any damage you caused if you did.

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable

Hear the Guard First
If it all feels like your fault
paragraphs.text: Shame becomes toxic when it gets stuck, and you don’t know what to do with it. Then you can become ashamed of being ashamed, and on and on. Get curious about what makes it so hard to give up. I went through toxic shame for 12 years. I’m sure it will help you to read my full guide on shame. Here’s one trick from that article :

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
home_path: Simple Practices
“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
paragraphs.text: My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. (”Once upon a time…” helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

home_path: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
paragraphs.text: Healing does need to get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule.If someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground. And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury.

home_path: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
paragraphs.text: The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person’s conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle. From in there, it was the only move they had.

home_path: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
paragraphs.text: « Hurt people hurt people, healed people heal people » means that hurt people pass on pain they never worked through, although « externalizers » are the ones who directly hurt others, while « internalizers » try to protect others by holding that « secret burning thread » inside themself, which ends up exploding onto others anyway at times when it gets to be too much to hold, You may have heard this story from somebody telling you to forgive, and it sounded like they must have no clue how deep the betrayal was. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

home_path: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
paragraphs.text: They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt, even if you see how they got there. It’s just that punishing them now can’t reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense, the support, or the skills they needed for a respectable response. What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now.

home_path: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
paragraphs.text: So a boundary can still be appropriate to enforce with them. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”

home_path: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
Forgiving Yourself
paragraphs.text: Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was really yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends, and by changing behavior going forward. Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
paragraphs.text: Now, once you’ve got this cast of perfected future characters in your mind, you can also go back to earlier traumatic memories and relive them in a better way. For example, I’ll take one instance from my own childhood. I was only spanked one time as a child. I hung up the (expensive) phone call my dad was on with a very important official in another country, because I wanted some attention. I don’t think he was exactly furious at me, but he decided this deserved a spanking, even if he didn’t agree with spanking in general. Since he wasn’t furious, the spanking didn’t really hurt, but it hurt me emotionally quite a lot, because I was so extremely shocked that my parents would use physical violence on me. Like I lost my sense of safety with them at that moment. And I may have learned that I was undeserving of attention, that I behaved in ways that made me deserve physical violence, that I was bad, etc.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
paragraphs.text: Many people experienced something like this where the consequences for their little mind were much more severe than anyone would imagine, and in almost every case, the adult themself does not currently understand the extent of the damage until the little one feels safe to tell them. I can’t tell you how many people I’ve worked with have laughed at how brutally they were beaten as kids. Just laughed it off like it was nothing.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
paragraphs.text: Whatever the situation was, we will contrast it with the corrected version.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
paragraphs.text: While often it is obvious how a perfect parent could have responded, in my example, I’m not exactly sure what a perfect father would have done here. But usually what my dad preferred as discipline was a forced « time-in » via a « punishment hug. » (which is called « therapeutic holding » in the literature) and I feel like that worked well for me. I did that with my son, Bear, as well. I would hold him as lovingly as possible, until he started to cry, because he did not seem interested in learning any lessons until that point. After he cried for a bit, we talked about what happened and what was wrong with it. When I felt satisfied he was understanding and aligning his values in a genuine way, the time-in was over, although he might want to continue the time-in sometimes a bit longer also, as it began to feel nice after the ego came down.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
paragraphs.text: My sister disagrees that this was therapeutic for her. She thinks it caused her to feel like hugs in general are punishment. A regular time-out could work, but sometimes it has to be enforced somehow, like locking the kid in their room for a bit (and assuming they can’t just have fun in their room). Recognizing the difficulty in finding a perfect parental response can also help us. Sometimes there was no perfect response that would have been harmless to all parties. But my sister should probably go back to those memories of punishment hugs and ensure that she learns that hugs are loving, even if that particular hug was also designed to teach a lesson about improving her behavior.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
paragraphs.text: I think that what children really need when they are acting narcissistically is some way to break through to real emotional connection. With very stubborn children (most are at times), that may require induced crying. It didn’t always require a punishment hug to do that, either. Just shouting « BEAR ! » could make my son cry at times. It’s crucial here that the caregiver producing the child’s egoic breakdown must have the moral high ground along with compassion, so they aren’t seen as just someone abusing their power. And they should be open themselves to being corrected by the child if the child has a valid counter-argument for who is in the right.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
paragraphs.text: Importantly, there is currently no expert consensus on how children should be disciplined, aside from using the least amount of force possible, in the least traumatizing way, whatever that may happen to be. There isn’t even agreement yet if logical consequences work. And one thing Visakan made me consider is that the parent-child relationship is the only one that’s supposed to change in major ways many times over the years. A parent might be great at a certain phase of child-rearing, and terrible at another (like treating you forever as if you’re 5).

Answering the Strict Disciplinarian
paragraphs.text: A good routine, like yoga in the morning and a proper bedtime, still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s done in a disciplinarian style. One exercise you can do to handle this is to go back and rewrite your responses to that strict disciplinarian. First, remember who it was that drove you so hard as a child. Then start a little rap sheet of their provoking lines. Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.

home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

paragraphs.text: The Critic’s voice can often pile on, to the point where you can’t even understand why or what you’re really feeling anymore. You feel sad at first, then the Inner Critic calls your inner child pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness with some simple nurturing instead from the beginning, but now you have to peel back this other nonsense to get to it.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
paragraphs.text: A lot of people get stuck right at square one. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone or the laundry feels urgent. Or some voice says this is silly, and it’s hard to tell which part of you is saying it.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
paragraphs.text: My friend Scott said:

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
paragraphs.text: “Half the time when I try to connect to baby me, I feel fake and it seems crazy.”

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
paragraphs.text: I used to be all personal trainer and teach persistence on this as the remedy. Keeping at it does help, since a little one who learned to expect being dropped won’t trust you right away. But I don’t think that explains the adult feeling fully. More importantly, I think it could even be like unintentional gaslighting to the little one to ask to connect with them when you don’t believe they’re even real. Like when my mom pretended to listen to me when I was young, but even less excusable (from the inner child’s view) because she was not asking for my time when she did that. So, it’s worth meditating first on why it feels fake.

For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state
home_path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state
paragraphs.text: Like on MDMA or deep in meditation. All of a sudden your little one is right there! Oh my gosh! And the love or grief that sounded like therapy talk is just obvious. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn’t prove they happened. I’d still hang on to that connection you felt, even once it’s gone, and try to bring a little of it into your normal life. You’ve felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn’t just pretending. If you’re « lucky ,» it’s not a question of trying to maintain that connection, but trying to figure out how to deal with the rawness of it after the high wears off. That’s what integration therapy is for. I have more advice on using psychedelics with the therapy in the « Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism » section further on.

path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
home_path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
paragraphs.text: Reparenting assumes there’s a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is. But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form. All this stuff about your little one could have left you wondering who I’m even talking about.

path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
home_path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
paragraphs.text: Maybe you started playing that part so early, and it took over so completely, that “What do I believe?” or “What do I want?” has no clear answer of your own. They sound like such easy questions, too. Back then, asking might have gotten you in trouble, or laughed at. Or there was just no way to ask. That can make “love yourself” feel pretty empty (love what, when the part you’ve been playing doesn’t feel real?), and the authentic self never received the conditions needed to develop. We get deeper into finding and building that self in « Untangling the Belonging Bargains » further on.

path: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow

When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
paragraphs.text: Some people have the opposite problem, where it feels like they’re connecting with their little boo, but then they find out somehow that it was still pretty superficial. Dreams can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in the second half of the night’s sleep, if you wake up in the middle to meditate, as I’ve discovered. That’s a good point to ponder over what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again in the morning (but write it down so you remember!). And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, shorten the practice or do it earlier.

home_path: Building Trust With Your Little One
When Healing Turns Into Checking
paragraphs.text: You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be completely real while you’re checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you’ve finally grieved it correctly.

home_path: Building Trust With Your Little One
When Healing Turns Into Checking
paragraphs.text: Going back to reconnect with your little one is normal parenting/reparenting, but returning to lick the same wound over and over can become a search for certainty in an inherently uncertain existence. Spending all day asking, “Did I process it properly? Did I grieve it enough?” is clearly not what we’re after here.

home_path: Building Trust With Your Little One
When Healing Turns Into Checking
paragraphs.text: And the checking can take many forms, aside from inner mental checks. A body scan can turn into one, or a confession. Even, going on a date, or checking your dating profile matches, can be a version of this if what you’re really after is proof that you’re good and lovable. It might calm things down for a while, and then the next little wobble matters even more.

home_path: Building Trust With Your Little One

Is your paranoia a warning sign?
paragraphs.text: Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn’t automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn’t balanced by practicality. “The CIA is mind-controlling me!” is (mostly) paranoia. “The CIA, marketers, and other forces are conspiring to mind-control me, the way they do to everyone else! But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates” has a noticeable dollop of paranoia too, but it’s practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis. “...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!” is leaning psychotic. Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, amphetamines, PCP, dirty LSD, so I’d avoid those.

These are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can’t, get help from trusted advisors.

paragraphs.text: So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

Untangling the Belonging Bargains
paragraphs.text: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

home_path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

paragraphs.text: Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades. For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.

paragraphs.text: Even with good parents, you could have learned unhealthy self-valuation when people repeatedly praised what you did rather than your inherent worth. That wasn’t your flaw.

Differentiation
paragraphs.text: Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship. You’d still belong, but now you come first and belonging second. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.

Even if you’re not planning on playing James Bond anytime soon, you still might need to smooth your edges out sometimes as part of socializing. paragraphs.text: Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:

home_path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

paragraphs.text:
- Caring about somebody’s feelings without automatically adopting their opinions or sacrificing your own ground. Their reasons can still change your mind, though.
- Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: “Wait, why was I nodding along?”
- Noticing when what you thought you knew suddenly feels like water dripping through your hand because of praise or pity, fear or attraction, or something that really resonates with you.
- Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places). That one can take a while.
- Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.

Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if you find one that fits you. And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that’s when we ask the Adult Protector to start paying attention.

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship

paragraphs.text: Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable.

Some people try to make themselves as lovable as possible, hiding their real feelings to do so. Others have no filter, on purpose, to see if they are still loved and appreciated. Like my one friend who used to go into churches and tell pastors they were wicked or unfit for their jobs, and then he wondered why he didn’t feel the love those churches promise (which was more proof he was right about them to begin with). He’s not wrong to speak his mind, but I wonder whether his goal is to reach mutual understanding, to vent, or to re-try dealing with some traumatic childhood pattern of losing himself to fit in with the gang.

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship

paragraphs.text: Neither of those approaches are the balance we’re seeking, and both are treating the other person like they’re your reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Instead, get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.
If you find yourself getting strange reactions from people all the time, check what your expectations were about how they’d react.

Opening up honestly to the right people at the right pace
paragraphs.text: And reaching out doesn’t mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn’t fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you’re still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I’d either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn’t safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn’t prove you’re meant for each other, or that they’ve earned your trust yet.

But as they say, “assume” makes an “ass” out of “u” and “me.”

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
Hearthwork: Taking Turns
paragraphs.text: The basic premise of Hearthwork, my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It’s kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
Hearthwork: Taking Turns
paragraphs.text: Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time’s up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don’t push. But they don’t act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they’re thinking, “Oh, I know what this is about,” or “Here’s what you should do.” They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places, and it’s your turn to keep “Here’s what you should do” to yourself.

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
Hearthwork: Taking Turns
paragraphs.text: The peer doesn’t become your permanent parent, though. They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form. Is that therapy? Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure. Professional therapy’s still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship
Dating While You Heal
paragraphs.text: Maybe you’d rather that your support came from a lover, as well. Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part. That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know. I wrote a whole romance guide, mostly due to this.
It’s often in handling conflict that we see the real inner child jump out. So if you’ve been wondering where they are in a session, here you, let’s pl/ork !

paragraphs.text: It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent, just like that Pink Elephant. Being totally independent can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!

Differentiation
paragraphs.text: Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. Sometimes you need to take a break from a family, group or relationship, even if they aren’t doing anything to you. Simply being around them may pull you into that programmed space where listening to what you really want becomes harder. Some people come back later on different terms, and sometimes the break has to be long-term because the pattern of losing yourself with them is deeply entrenched. As you differentiate, you learn to tell which of those apply.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
home_path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
paragraphs.text: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one (figurative) life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, or your youngest real child moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
home_path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
paragraphs.text: Your little one might be sure everything’s over. Usually one real thing ended, and the related habits might be held onto like on autopilot. Ask your little one what they’re scared will happen in the bardo between past and future (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
home_path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
paragraphs.text: Something basic can mark the ending, like boxing up the old keys. Nobody needs to know what door will open next. But when the not-knowing feels too heavy, a new identity can sure look tempting. Like a borrowed coat that doesn’t fit but at least it’s warm. But you can’t go far with a borrowed coat anyway, so don’t force the future on. Keep taking care of yourself, and grieve what ended with your little one beside you during the metamorphosis.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
home_path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
Missing Someone
paragraphs.text: When you miss someone, let the ache be a cue for love. It doesn’t have to become one more problem to solve, and pushing it away won’t help. If love’s there, “I miss you” becomes “I love you.” Or there’s the loving-kindness wish: “May you loving, peaceful, and free.” You can picture them. Or don’t, and just feel the care going their way.

home_path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

paragraphs.text: All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it, because the main benefit is for your little one. I have an N of 1 case study that proves this works, also. It’s what rescued me from deep despair when the love of my life, my second wife, Bee, left me.

The Love Has to Move
paragraphs.text: Community can come before the big opening or after it, too. Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible. Other times it’s the other way around. Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn’t have imagined before, and then they start to “manifest” different kinds of people and relationships in their life. Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.

home_path: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship

The Love Has to Move
paragraphs.text: This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with [building community] (community.u-dont-exist.com). Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn’t really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn’t always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
home_path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
paragraphs.text: We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
home_path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
Inner Child Reparenting therapists
paragraphs.text: Inner Child Reparenting therapists do exist, and you can find them, although they often are not licensed, and I don’t know of any central directory, nor of any protocol they’d have in common (aside from Lucia C’s, in the Appendix). There are none which work with my guide yet. I can consult, and if you like the guide, you can ask a therapist to check it out and see what they agree with or disagree with as a great way to vet them.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
If you want a licensed therapist
home_path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
If you want a licensed therapist
paragraphs.text: The best licensed, listed therapists you’ll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I’ll talk more about those in the appendix,. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
home_path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
Before choosing a therapist
paragraphs.text: Get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I’d especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won’t tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I’d also want one who doesn’t put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won’t charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can’t tell you any of that.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
home_path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
AI therapy
paragraphs.text: I’ve tried all the top AI therapy apps, and they’re all pretty bad. I’m trying to make my own based on this guide, but I’m becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn’t mean you can’t get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes, and don’t let it replace real humans who love you and want to think with you Actually, I find one of the best uses for it is to improve my interactions with real people. For example, it can help me formulate more careful replies to people who are too sensitive to take my excessive bluntness or wry humor (although I wouldn’t send them actual AI text).

path: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
home_path: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
paragraphs.text: And the love you’re worthy of is the same love as back in « Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! », the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of relief when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or your subconsciosu, was there before you could earn anything. Love from a person is more conditional than that. Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.

home_path: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
paragraphs.text: Be patient with yourself, and gentle, including with the part of you that thinks you should be over it by now. You are more than your pain and your past. There’s help, and lots of other people are out there learning to look after their own little ones. You can post a comment right here and let us know how it’s goin for you.

path: How This Relates to Similar Therapies
paragraphs.text: My reparenting guide is part of the larger reparenting and inner child therapy category. As far as I can tell, it was first developed in 1976 by Dr. Lucia Capacchione. Although Lucia is no longer with us, [her institute still trains therapists] (https://luciac.com/instructors.php) in her methods (including art therapy and other things). I greatly respect and appreciate what Lucia has given us to work with. While there are many inner child therapy offshoots (often less codified than Lucia’s book, Recovery of Your Inner Child), it would be impossible for me to compare my guide to each inidivdual therapist’s approach. Below are the differences between Lucia’s approach and my guide’s approach :

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to Schema Therapy
paragraphs.text: Of the scientifically studied clinical approaches I know, Schema Therapy, developed in 1980s-1990s by Jeffrey E. Young, is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. The healthy adult recognizes when a need differs from the strategy you use to meet it, and it helps you set limits.. And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you’ve committed to. all that sounds like my Nurturer, Protector and Guide by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.

Being all scientific and stuff does have its drawbacks also. Schema Therapy’s name pretty much tells you all you need to know. What the heck is a Schema anyway ? (It’s normally described as a « pervasive pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving » (learned in childhood). Although I find a slightly different definition of it from Cleveland Clinic : « A schema is a long-lasting outlook or assumption that you have about yourself, others or the world. » But yeah, put those together and that’s basically what it’s talking about. So the schema therapist takes answers from a questionnaire you fill out and maps the your difficulties onto a set list of 18 schemas, which themselves map onto a set of modes, like the Vulnerable Child or the Punitive Parent. Based on those schemas and modes, the therapist assumes some things about your childhood that would explain them.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to Schema Therapy
paragraphs.text: Where it really differs is spirituality. Schema therapy doesn’t build it in, though the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice « an important development. » That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy. Some people do blend them, though.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to Schema Therapy
paragraphs.text: Tara Bennett-Goleman’s book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema. Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that’s the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).
Schema Therapy takes a more combative stance with the inner critic and guards than IFS or my approach, possibly a result of the lack of spirituality in it.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS
paragraphs.text: Richard Schwartz, who developed IFS in the 1980s, called one of his books No Bad Parts. Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so my section, “meet the protector first,” would fit right in over there, although I focus more on keeping the inner child safe first. The one exception is that IFS does understand some parts may be entity attachments (« unattached burdens ») which need to be exorcised. My guide also talks about entity attachments, but I don’t believe that’s reason to start another war. Rather, I explain the root cause of such attachments as lack of protective love from the inner adult.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS
paragraphs.text: My reparenting method diverges from IFS at another important point. The IFS Institute’s outline of the model says “everyone has a Self,” (a divine True Self, from Advaita) and that the Self “can and should lead,” once your parts stop “blending” with it. I emphasize the inner adult you borrow, build and practice occupying that has the roles of: Nurturer, Protector, and Guide.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS
paragraphs.text: Is a perfect Higher/True Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I’d call that claim [spiritual bypassing] (bypassing.u-dont-exist.com). I’ve experienced that Higher Self perspective myself, though, in very powerful meditations.For example, one time, while still married to my first wife Ann, who was becoming more violent and crazy as time went on, we got super high on weed and we were both in some higher realm as our higher selves. My higher self asked her higher self, « Are you going to keep getting more and more crazy ? » Her higher self said, « Yes. » It was like we could see the whole timeline of life from above. Although, my friends already told me the same thing, quite sober. 😅

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS
paragraphs.text: So, there is a less subjective way of seeing things as perfectly ordained in reality, despite the ego’s illusions, which matches what others say about it. As a Buddhist, I no longer see it as « Self », though it can still give the same love, peace, and clarity to whomever accesses it. Where I part ways with IFS is I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom that can be followed mechanically. From that higher vantage point, problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS
paragraphs.text: You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.

home_path: Appendix
How This Relates to IFS
paragraphs.text: I’m also not a fan of the strange and complex cast of characters in IFS. IFS splits up my « inner child » into an indefinite number of wounded young parts called “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming. People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before. I’ve seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.

home_path: Appendix
Related Clinical Work
paragraphs.text: My inner child reparenting framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy. I borrow particular ideas and practices from each of them, but the mix is mine, so please don’t blame them for it.

home_path: Appendix
Teachers and Practice Resources
paragraphs.text: Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes. Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it. She has a book and a free one-hour YouTube training, and she’s on Instagram.
Key helped me think through some of these ideas in a very « embodied » way for a few months, and she added The Guide to make the 3 parental modes.

home_path: Appendix
Teachers and Practice Resources
paragraphs.text: Lisa Romano brings more neuroscience and CBT, and her video is a good place to start. She makes the point that remembering the specific details of childhood trauma isn’t necessary, because the felt body knows what needs to come up. Key developed the Guide’s sense of direction, and the identity and differentiation work from Bowen I mentioned earlier. She led a guided inner-child meditation in Nairobi in January 2026 for twenty people, and it’s up on YouTube.

base_blocks.text: Here's the idea behind Inner Child Reparenting, in a nutshell:

path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
base_blocks.text: Growing up, all of us picked up automatic ways of understanding situations we find ourselves in, reacting based on those understandings, and then treating ourselves partly based on how we happened to handle things. Some of those patterns are wise in general, although even then, we are always learning from what life throws at us. Others of those patterns were built for a crisis that’s long over, and some just seem to make every situation worse.

path: Inner Child Therapy — humanized article so far
base_blocks.text: Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding an Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding. At first, it’s deliberate, even awkward. With time, the roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.

base_blocks.text: Some people, like another ex of mine, got so deep into crying that it became traumatizing. She actually had panic attacks from it. If you start getting scared of your own crying, turn the song off for tonight.
The Chicken-and-Egg Problem

Céline's song is called On ne change pas—"we don't change." I think that's both fortunately and unfortunately true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don't truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren't made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.

And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to heal itself, which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult. I call that "forced adulthood," where the child has to deal with situations the evolved inner adult should be handling--we see this in actual children all the time when their parents are not providing care. People even wear t-shirts saying, "I don't wanna adult today." The forced adulting often goes along with a misperception that there is something wrong with the inner child. Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.

That’s one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in to help with the rent, and each job keeps the others in balance. Say a party gets to be too much for your little one. The Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom. And the Guide helps them think twice about the next weird party they might go to, avoiding another cycle of bathroom vacationing. 🙈

The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most. I left it out of my first version of this guide until my friend Key pointed it out, and without an inner Guide, it’s easy to go looking for one in a cult. Our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well. That’s the Guide’s job. But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves.
If the phrase “inner parent” calls up the wrong archetype for you, pick another one. Your future self might work, or the captain of a ship, so long as they’d do those three jobs.

But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? This is much easier when you can already reach one of those adult roles. But when you can't, it's like you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.

Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first. You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it. Maybe you copy one small thing you've seen them do, or imagine them there when they're not, and try one piece yourself while they're still helping with the rest. That's what I mean by borrowed adulthood. You may still need help with almost all of it for a while, but over time there are more and more of those little parts you can do yourself.
Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five fairly predictable stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):

1. You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting:
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we're looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you'd take care of a baby doll etc. 
3. Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them. 
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn't pushed away, but doesn't have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you've been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!

Whichever stage you're at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Your little one starts believing the grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you're wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore.

Reparenting isn't an exercise you finish, after all. Say your boss asks you to stay late again. You tell them no and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen. The cushion was practice for it.
My Journey

I used to preach Buddhist enlightenment too much, because that's what helped me. But an old childhood wound could still hit, like if someone accuses me of being lazy, and then suddenly it's like I'm that same little kid again, even tho the spiritual part of me felt free as a bird.

From what I've seen, most people (like me) who chase spiritual freedom, as valid as that is, are, at least at first, trying to get away from something painful in themselves, usually childhood trauma of some kind. That’s spiritual bypassing. Plenty of gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example.

The way I think this works is simple. Imagine you’re broke and starving, and your baby is starving too. Understandable: there is no food. Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you’ve got lots of nutritious munchies. But you’re eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving. Unforgivable.

Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose. I just didn’t believe there was a baby. Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him. Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I’d already found his way.

Spending your whole life processing your wounded inner child isn’t freedom either. Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story. Maybe ordinary life already gives you enough love and meaning. Great. It didn’t for me. Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.

I was well-loved as a child, but from age twelve to twenty-six I was depressed and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. Loving-kindness (metta) meditation healed that depression almost instantly for me, so it became my regular practice automatically.
I also found more love in the rest of the Buddhist teachings—which, it turns out, also include inner-child self-love! and later in loveyhuasca.

But it didn’t reach everything. A lot of the child stuff around my attachment to women was still there. When I later tried self-directed inner-child therapy, it felt like I was making it up at first. That didn’t stop me from practicing, but I did stop “pushing” it to be a certain way, and I’d stop trying to feel it was realer than it was. I would go more into listening and waiting mode rather than imagining mode.
At one pivotal point, I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open.

Years later, I found a warm, intuitive inner child therapist, named Daja, randomly, while in Kenya. I figured I already knew this stuff, but I gave it a shot. She did actually help me see some things more clearly. For example, she had me write down how many people I could fully trust as a child (lots), then how many people I could fully trust as an adult (zero). That was difficult, and it’s actually the opposite of what you might expect from inner-child therapy, since usually that’s for people who had problems trusting as a child.

What it showed me is that I was ignoring a lot of things that were really important to look at, and that was one of them. I wouldn’t have even thought to ask the question she asked me if I were doing it on my own. It’s also an example of how therapy can sometimes make you feel worse than before, when you become more aware of problems. But personally I prefer to see things as they are, so I can figure out how to work with them, rather than just hide in delusions.

It also showed me that I really do need to count more on myself than I assumed. I need to be much better as an inner adult for my inner child, because my childhood was actually so nice that I kind of just assume I can trust everyone, and that gets me into trouble. So it got me curious to learn more about inner-child therapy, which is a process I’m still in the midst of as I test this guide with people.
