path: Before You Try to Go Deep
base_blocks.text: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Try looking around the room, pausing before you act, making a choice and following through on it. If you can't do that because you're basically the frightened kid, leave the deeper conversation until later. You may need somebody steady there with you, or to do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to the child.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
base_blocks.text: And if the grown-up you is there, and it's just how deep you're going that's too much, I'd go shallower. Like the flight attendants say, it's good to know where the exits are. 😅 So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room? If you can't, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I'd come all the way back out first. Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there's a grown-up around who can say, "Okay, that's enough for today," and try something gentler, like saying hi to them with your eyes open.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
base_blocks.text: If you need a break from the communion, simply jot down the reason and the progress made so far. Then come back later, once that reason has changed and you feel comfortable.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
base_blocks.text: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I'd call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Even if you don't have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
base_blocks.text: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
base_blocks.text: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, but you can start with some nice circular or spiral massage right on the tense spot.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
base_blocks.text: If that's not enough, there's deeper somatic stuff like Shaking, tapping (EFT), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or some other bottom-up approach.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
base_blocks.text: When your nervous system is flooded, your protective parts are busy throwing buckets of water out of the boat, so they’re not going to let your little one come out and talk much anyway. Some people go straight into EMDR to work on desensitizing their worst memory before they can even stay in the room. Then they get predictably flooded all over again and, running low on buckets, they decide EMDR doesn’t work. Here’s a map of what to try when:

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
When Somatic Work Brings Things Up
base_blocks.text: When Somatic Work Brings Things Up

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
When Somatic Work Brings Things Up
base_blocks.text: Some somatic work can feel pleasant, and some can feel like a raging storm got unleashed. It can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes nightmares later on as the memories begin to unwind. It’s a bit like going to the gym. You want to make gains, and sore muscles the next day can be good, but proper range of (e)motion here is also key to avoid injury.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
When Somatic Work Brings Things Up
base_blocks.text: Keep track of how you feel over the next few days, like how refreshing your sleep is, and how easy it feels to get through your day. Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? If you can’t quite tell yet, I’d just make the next one a bit easier, one change at a time, like a science nerd, so you learn what made the difference. You can play around with variables like shorter session length, or shallower diving, time of day, keeping eyes open, having a friend around, or holding a teddy bear as a stand-in for your little one.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
Your Body Might Need Some Love First
When Somatic Work Brings Things Up
base_blocks.text: And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
base_blocks.text: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
base_blocks.text: If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you’re supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. Maybe that’s what happens for some people, but you might not be some people (hehe). If talking into an empty room feels silly, small figures on a table can help (so that you feel even more silly!?), like one for your little one and one for the rest of the gang that shows up. Put whichever one’s running the show on a throne. Both ideas come from sections 12.2 and 13.1 of a book called Schema Therapy for Children and Adolescents, which I’ll call ST-CA.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
base_blocks.text: You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and yet still be able to think a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, speak or write them. You might feel more comfortable that way than just staying in imagination land.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
base_blocks.text: Then again, maybe what’s actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach. Or perhaps you’re in a place you want to leave. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be nice to do for yourself. And if you don’t know, it’s fine to guess. Maybe it’s some genuine human closeness, or figuring out some way to have more say in your own life.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
base_blocks.text: Life is always switching up on us. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: I've been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child. Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though. For such folks, inner child therapy is clearly not the place to start. They need to first deconstruct the adult identity they've got.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: When I talk with folks like that, I mostly want to know what the identity gets them and what it costs, and especially what it's really serving. Some of them even call themselves sovereign, and then somehow there's an urge they have to obey, which sounds more like slavery to me.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who's horrified by their own thoughts. Everybody gets scary thoughts they'd rather not have sometimes, and they don't make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them? The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you're calm and actually ready. A real parent doesn't get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to be a perfect one.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: And if somebody actually wonders whether they're malicious, they'd do better to meditate on it and find out why they're asking before they bring their inner child anywhere near it. Are they really feeling malicious, or is it some voice in their head saying so, like the inherited critic? If some of it turns out to be malice they actually want to act on, the inner child can wait.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: Ill Will and Loving-Kindness

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: In one of the Buddha's own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it's hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it's not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you're the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you'd be the one burning. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: The Buddha also told his son that loving-kindness is what gets rid of ill will, and compassion does the same for cruelty. I'm biased on loving-kindness, since it got me out of my depression. For these folks it starts with the grown-up they are now, though, and their little one stays out of it.

path: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
base_blocks.text: As for when their little one gets a turn, I'd say once they've had some bad days where scaring somebody would've felt good, and they didn't do it. Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them and won't laugh along, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: Noticing Counts

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: "Huh, somebody in here is really scared." That might be the most adult thing you've got right now, and it's plenty to start with. Whoever's noticing isn't all the way inside the scared one.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: It can help to use your own name. For me, instead of "I'm terrified," that'd be "Little Joel is terrified. What does Little Joel need right now?" You'll sound a bit like Elmo :) In lab studies, though, people who talked to themselves this way reacted less to upsetting pictures and memories, and their brains didn't seem to be working any harder to do it.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: If you can tell your parts apart pretty easily, you've probably got plenty of noticing already. Don't keep drilling it just because the love isn't coming yet. A lot of meditators are great at watching. I was, and baby me was still starving.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: Borrow One Competency at a Time

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it's not just a foolish waste of time. It's actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there's always your future healed self if you can imagine that.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: For warmth

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: Think of someone you remember fondly. How would they sit beside your little one? Just make sure it's someone who liked you the way you were.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: For protecting

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: Ask what a minimally competent adult would do here. Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you're about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you're about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that's ok. "Fake it til you make it" isn't exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, "I did that for us. That was the Protector." If it sounds funny, laugh!

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: For guiding

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
base_blocks.text: The Guide can be you too, just a calmer you. That's a lot easier to imagine than your future healed self. Think back to what (and how) you decided about something like this the last time you were calm. Or ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (like "What would Jesus do?" or "What would Buddha do?") can give some direction, too, until you develop your own internal compass.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
base_blocks.text: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
base_blocks.text: If you weren't loved well as a child, "love your inner child" can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn't close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
base_blocks.text: Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It's scaffolding.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
base_blocks.text: Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. Once a truce is made, we can begin to let down our defenses. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you've never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won't let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it's been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
base_blocks.text: If the love still isn't coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don't expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That's enough to start being the adult, even if it isn't enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn't any yet, borrow some.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
base_blocks.text: Your little one might not take it well at first. 😜 More like "Oh, so NOW you care?" Your first instinct might be "But I'm trying!" Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you'll manage to borrow.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: Borrow Hindsight

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: I sometimes ask: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It's a question borrowed from your future self, and I wouldn't take their answer as gospel. I don't think a perfect Higher Self is waiting in there with the answers, either (more on that in How This Relates to IFS).

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: That future you also knows why you can't pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they'd just make you some food. If you can't picture them, make the food yourself, and don't bother faking a feeling first. A "no" or a pause can count as the food, too.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, as long as you don't assume they'll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Remember When You Already Did It
base_blocks.text: Remember When You Already Did It

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Remember When You Already Did It
base_blocks.text: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you're having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, "The past didn't go anywhere." Your own challenge doesn't need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking "I survived a car crash, so why can't I stop eating when I'm upset?", that's the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you're more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (No example? Try another doorway.)

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Notice the Part That Came Here
base_blocks.text: Notice the Part That Came Here

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Notice the Part That Came Here
base_blocks.text: Some people hear all this about love and answer, "No. I hate myself." If that's what you find, it deserves an honest hearing. Just listen to it, without arguing back. But if you opened this article, something in you wanted things to be different, whatever the rest of you was saying. The same goes if you came to therapy or asked someone for help. Or maybe you'd already decided you were hopeless, and then for some reason you tried again.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Notice the Part That Came Here
base_blocks.text: What was it? It might have been hope, or desperation. Maybe you were curious, or scared. Some people come here out of duty. Or it was more like, "I'm not going to keep suffering like this." And maybe it was love. You don't need to decide which. Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Sometimes it's not that you can't love in general. Your dog can chew up your good shoes and be forgiven before you've found the other one. But maybe you direct that love to your little one and the attempt goes flat, or starts to feel weirdly unsafe. Just feel that love you can feel for others for a minute, in your body, before you try to redirect anything. Then as you relax into that and enjoy it more, imagine it flowing downhill, like an overflowing river of delicious chocolate. Now imagine how happy your inner child is at the bottom of the hill to play in that chocolate love that rolled down!

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Watch how it lands, though. "I care about you" can be patient, or it can be "I care about you, now hurry up and feel better." Getting close can be too much, too, the way kids squirm away from an aunt they barely know who goes in for the big hug, and then climb all over the uncle who's just sitting there. And if nothing moves at all, don't push it. Knowing that love is in you somewhere counts for a lot, and you're borrowing something you already know how to do.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, all the conditions you face, and then step outside it and ask what you’d tell them as a friend. This psychological trick has a rich history around it, and the blind spot behind it even has a name, Solomon’s paradox, after the biblical king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Then take a small piece of whatever you'd tell them and hand it to yourself. If the advice was "get more sleep," then for now just try brushing your teeth before midnight instead of at two. That's how you learn as a kid, and it works now, too. The technical term for this is "scaffolding."

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Show Up When Nothing's Wrong

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: If the only time the Nurturer shows up is when something's wrong, your little one can start to feel like they're your job. Sometimes show up just to say "I'm glad you're here," and then enjoy them for a minute, the way you'd enjoy a little kid who wants to show you a rock they found. Or picture the two of you washing the dishes together, nobody asking anybody how they feel.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: A Smaller Doorway: Goodwill

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Sometimes "I love you" is more than you can honestly say, especially to somebody who's treated you badly. Even the usual whittled-down loving-kindness prayer, "May you be happy," can feel like rewarding them. That's why I go with Buddha's overall wish (paraphrasing): "May you be loving, peaceful, and free," since if they were all of those, they wouldn't have done what they did, and then they actually would be lovable.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: This goodwill isn't just for the target of it, though. You may find it bounces back and opens up a little warmth in your heart. And if "I love you" goes flat when you aim it at yourself or your little one, the same wish works there, too. 🫶🏿

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Ask God for a Loan

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: The dog kind of love is real love. Some people also know a love that's a whole different size, like God's, or whatever opened up for them in prayer or on a long retreat, and I don't want to lump that in with the dog. If you've been there, don't shrink it down to a thought experiment about a friend.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: If you haven’t been there yet (and even if you have), I have good news for you!

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: One practical door anyone can use to slowly experience divine love is gratitude (even after the Turkey’s done & Thanksgiving is over!). Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades. I think it’s essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: This is a bit tricky to put into words, but let me try anyway… You may be suffering now, but you could be suffering more. That’s something to be grateful for (although please don’t fall into the common trap of being grateful that you have what others don’t have, as that’s more like selfishness). I’m not talking just about changing your “glass half empty” perception to a glass “half full perception.” I’m not pushing “toxic positivity.” Being thankful shouldn’t be pushed on people who just need to grieve for the moment. On the other hand, I’ve noticed that I can sometimes completely flip a bad psychedelic trip into a good one with gratitude alone.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: And I’m certainly not preaching “prosperity philosophy,” even though it can seem to start at that. We still need to remember that if we can only be thankful for the good things we have, we can fall into the trap of thinking that what we have is happiness itself. I’m ultimately reaching for something much deeper. Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn't lead to being content with less. When you can see that less is more, at a deeper level, that's where the real gratitude flourishes.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: If you have a moment right now to breathe, that’s something to be grateful for. I learned this many times the hard way. For example, when I got tuberculosis from a cave in Mexico at age 20, and coughed for six months straight, eventually literally unable to breathe, leading to a near death experience. And then in Senegal, I had a suspected bilharzia infection in 2021, and could only painfully pee blood, I promised to always be thankful if I could ever pee normally again. Miraculously, I then found some obscure ethnobotanical research (on Google Scholar, before AI) which led me to drink roselle tea. Within an hour, I was cured. I don’t always remember to say “thank you” when I pee now, but I try.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: That may sound like a silly, quirky waste of time to some folks. But what I notice is that saying thank you for every little thing, whenever I remember to, is not about imposing some kind of “spiritual discipline.” It is directly reconnecting me to something pure and sacred.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: And even (or especially) when I am suffering, I try to remember to be grateful for that also, because if not for suffering, I would not even think about how much I have enjoyed not suffering as much, and how much this tribulation will help me to develop more compassion, wisdom, and gratitude in future. It connects me with the plight of the countless other beings suffering at that very moment, authentically bringing up a wellspring of compassion in my heart for all of us. And I see clearly that it is my inner child who is feeling this pain, and what an honor it is that I can be there for him.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Of course, that’s not to say you should not try to suffer less, or get away from abusers. The point of life, according to every spiritual tradition and religion, I think, is to suffer less, which first requires us to understand the cause of suffering, and what real suffering and real happiness are. If you, like Biggie Smalls, have come to understand that having money is not real happiness, that’s a big deal! That’s something to be grateful for. If we get a chance to meditate or pray today, while on the toilet, upon waking up, while ChatGPT is “thinking” for us, that’s something to be thankful for, for sure.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Notice how, when you offer thanks (to the universe, to life, to God, whatever you may believe in), a space in your heart opens up. It might not feel immediately like you suddenly know the real meaning of Divine Love, but it’s a little spark of … something.... There’s a tiny bit of freedom, of peace, stillness, softness. And as that softness deepens each time, you start to understand what I mean by Divine Love. Many people have written books on this topic (like A. Helwa’s book, Secrets of Divine Love, for example), so I won’t belabor the point further here, but I hope you are able to experience this when you try it out for a while, and I’d really love to know how it works for you!

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Invite Your Little One In

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Once you start to feel that lovely softness of the heart, invite your little one in with you as your spiritual integration practice. They might go numb, or call BS on that. If so, they might just need to see if you're actually humble enough, and grateful enough for them, to listen to their rejection and be patient. If you instead retreat back into your cozy corner, it's the food bank feast all over again: You can have an enormous spiritual feast upstairs while the child is still starving downstairs.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: When the Spiritual Relationship Hurts

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: If a spiritual teacher you trusted betrayed you, even sitting down to meditate can feel like it belongs to them now. Kids quit piano over one bad teacher, and this is way worse. But if you let an abuser control your appreciation of life, then you've given them an unearned win.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
base_blocks.text: Being the grown-up doesn't mean controlling everything yourself, though. After a betrayal like that, part of you might want to. Spiritual support can help you act where it's yours to act, and let go of outcomes and other people's choices where it isn't. The Serenity Prayer is the example I'd give, if prayer still feels like yours.

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: Become the Adult Apprentice

path: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
base_blocks.text: Say a friend sits with you while you fall apart. Most of us feel better and call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while we don't. So steal some of it. Usually what helped was how they just sat there without trying to fix you. Ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is good enough for a start, so try it before you call next time.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Building Trust With Your Little One

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: Not Every Hero Wears A Cape

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: Set one boundary. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! Maybe your little one had grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, and maybe you’ve done it too, so this is how they start to believe you.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. “What’s an ‘internal attack’?” Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they’re sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back. They don’t trust you yet, and you don’t ask them to. They complain about something, and if they’re right, you say so. All of that is evidence they're accepted and you’re safe to be around. Love needs those to start with, but without warmth they can still feel like they’re only being put up with.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: Plenty of people are still at the putting-up-with part. Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector’s plain acts and the warmth can come after, which feels backwards, because you’d think you have to feel it first before you could do anything for them. But yeah, bonding starts somewhere. And this is not to say you’ve never done anything to care for yourself. If not, you’d be dead right now. But we’re making additional acts of care intentional now as a base for love to grow.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: Make It Intentional

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: Intentional, meaning you pick one of those acts and decide when you'll do it, and what the smallest first step is (like with the envelope). If it needs money or somebody's help, sort that out before the day, and if you'll have to tell someone something they won't like, say it out loud to yourself ahead of time. Then put yourself in their shoes to see how it sounds, and go back & forth like that a couple times until both sides feel good about it, or good enough, as long as what you needed to say is still in there.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
base_blocks.text: After the day, look at what actually happened. Say you did the Protector action(s) and you don't feel any better, or you feel worse. Standing up for yourself can do that at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess. But did you know how to do it, and why? Were you worn out? Maybe whoever said they'd help couldn't make it. 🤗

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Sometimes the love is there for your little one and still feels unsafe to them, or safe for a minute and then not. Love and trust don't have to come as a pair, but they got tied together, as if one had to vouch for the other. So your love can sound like you're asking them to trust you. It doesn't need their trust, but it does need you to be honest with them, which isn't the same as perfect.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: The love can go first, though, before their trust is done going over your track record (they've heard what you still call yourself when you mess up, sometimes out loud). Your little one says "I don't trust you." You answer, "I believe you. And I love you."

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: I was about five when my mom told me it was time for bed (or something equally outrageous to a five-year-old). I cried and screamed "I HATE YOU!" 😡 She answered, "But I love you!" 🥰

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: That completely threw me. Fights don't usually go like that. Anger is a way to get more power when you feel a lack of justice or agency. You puff yourself up so you seem frightening or dangerous, or you demand to be heard. My anger was there to get me heard, and her answer showed me I didn't need it for that. Whatever injustice I thought there was wasn't coming from a lack of love, either. So the anger seemed stupid. I saw for myself that it was only hurting me, without helping me see clearly or get what I wanted. Still, what I screamed was true right then, and what she said back was true too, so I could hate somebody who loved me and she'd still be my mom the whole time.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: When it's your little one yelling at you, though, try not to turn "But I love you" into a line you say on cue, because then it can brush the anger off, and what it's really saying is "so stop being angry." I think you can mean it and still be doing that. Does the love stay afterward and take whatever's true in the anger seriously?

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: The love can stay, and your little one might still come back with "Big fuckity whoopty doo. I don't believe you." 🙄 You answer, "Okay. I believe that you don't believe me. I still love you. 🤗 You don't have to love me back. Tell me what feels unsafe."

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Your little one might say it's you. You don't have to accept every conclusion they reach about you, but do listen for the concrete complaint without fighting the yelling and swearing around it. If it's something serious, answer it seriously. The complaint might only be one sentence, once the swearing runs out. Like the anger at bedtime, the swearing is there to get them heard, so once you're listening instead of fighting, they don't need it anymore.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, "I can't imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father." He doesn't collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what's worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest "genuinely tested" him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he's very proud of both his sons. Then he says, "But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn't have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective."

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Also notice what else in you answers your little one, besides what you choose to say. When they say "I don't believe you," something in you might fire back an accusation, and then they can learn your love is only there as long as they take it the right way. The resentment can be purely visceral: being doubted after you've tried feels unfair, but there's nothing unfair in them going over your track record. The part that resents not being believed might be the same one that said "I love you" in the first place, or a different one, or a bit of both. Both talk in your grown-up voice, so to your little one they're the same. Be careful not to take the accusation as proof your love really is conditional, when it could just be another part talking.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Instead of Blame

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Your little one might not be the only one getting accused. When life has gone badly, part of you may try to get some control back by finding someone to blame, like "If you'd gotten it together at fifteen, you could have saved everybody." If it's somebody's fault, it didn't have to happen, and that feels like control. But figuring out which age of you is to blame doesn't give you what it would have taken back then. That part may start picking on a different age.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Whichever age it picks on, saving everybody was never your job. At fifteen you probably didn't even have your own money, or anywhere else to go. And actually, not to beat a dead horse here, but every age of you was stuck with whatever it had then, even the adult you were last year.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: So instead of asking which age of you deserves the blame, I'd ask these:

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text:
1. What was that age of you trying to get, or get away from?
2. What did it understand back then?
3. What options could it actually see? Could it stand to take any of them?
4. What happened because of the choice it made?
5. What was missing? Some ability, or help/protection from someone else?
6. What can you learn or repair now, and how would you act differently in such situations?

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: It can help to sort the guilt, too, since some of it was put on you by people who needed someone to blame, and some is only the critic (ST-CA sorts guilt into four piles, in section 17.1.1). Whatever was missing back then, you can start giving your little one now.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: Your little one has their own version of that last question: "Big fuckity whoopty doo. What are you gonna do for me?" They actually want to know, though I think the first answer may be that you keep loving them, even while they don't believe you. What you do for them takes days to add up, but the moment they doubt you, you can show them right away that the love stays and doesn't turn into an accusation. Then their trust can grow from the stuff back in "Not Every Hero Wears A Cape," like hearing out the sarcasm, or finally opening that envelope.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️
base_blocks.text: If your stomach tightens while your little one waits for an answer, slower exhales may help you stay with them.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Make a Simple Vow

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: If your promises still mean something to your little one, maybe because you've kept a few small ones, a quiet vow can help too. As many real-life parents know, your heart really explodes in such an unexpected and wonderful way when you hold your newborn baby for the first time (happened to me!). And if you're not yet a parent, it can really help to imagine holding a baby in your arms to make the vow feel real. Imagine you just had a baby, how would you feel? Would you look at him/her with adoration and joy? Carry that into visualizing yourself with your own inner child:

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: > "I know you're in there. I love you. You don't have to love me back or trust me yet. I can't promise that nothing painful will happen. Or that I'll always know what to do, or never react badly. But I can promise to tell you the truth and listen when you're angry. I'll make our life together safer where I can, and take the next step I can see to protect you. When I fail, I'll come back to make it right. You don't have to believe these words. Watch what I do."

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Notice it only promises what you can keep, so your little one can actually watch you keep it.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Only say the "I love you" part if you can feel it. If you don't feel the love yet, say you care (with the goodwill prayer: "May you be loving, peaceful, and free"). That's a first step. Or even before that, just promise your little one you won't be cruel to them on purpose. Borrow the Nurturer to improve this.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Whichever you choose, your little one may still answer with "Big fuckity whoopty doo." That's allowed, and one beautiful session wouldn't convince me either. Pick one thing to do that's small enough to repeat. A big gesture you later drop would only prove them right to doubt you, but a small thing you keep doing can change their mind.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Whenever your little one shows up looking for their parent, even if they don't know that's what they are doing, you go back to being the one they can rely on, and you're kind to them while you do it. If they show up to have some innocent fun, don't "put them in their place" as the adult. But sometimes they show up as the one who doesn't want to go to bed. Now you're in my mom's place: you still go to bed, and staying kind about it shows them bedtime isn't a lack of love.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Remind Yourself

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: The vow can live somewhere you'll see it, too, like on a stuffed animal from when you were little, a photo of yourself as a child, or just a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Whatever helps you feel connected to the Nurturer and Protector you've been practicing. The Teddy bear note may remind you to think, "When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time."

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: A real-life child of yours, or a calm pet, can also act as a companion that brings out the relationship with your own inner child. My son did that for me, and I think that's very common for parents. But those are also their own beings with their own needs as well. Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: When Healing Turns Into Checking

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be completely real while you're checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you've finally grieved it correctly.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: Going back can still matter, even when nothing new turns up. But returning to the same wound can also become a search for certainty in an inherently uncertain existence. Spending all day asking, "Did I process it properly? Did I grieve it enough?" is clearly not what we're after here.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: And the checking doesn't always stay in your head. A body scan can turn into one, or a confession. Even, going on a date, or checking your dating profile matches, can be a version of this if what you're really after is proof that you're good and lovable. It might calm things down for a while, and then the next little wobble matters even more.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
base_blocks.text: If you're feeling guilty because you didn't put your seat belt on, just put it on. If you still want to investigate it later, fine. Perhaps now and then you feel bad about that time you refused to put it on, broke your collar bone in a crash, and then got blamed for not wearing it. That's natural, but doesn't mean there's something new to look at. Then the background checker goes, “But are you really listening?” There it is. Seat belt's on. 😇 Where were we?

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
How Would You Know It's Helping?
base_blocks.text: How Would You Know It's Helping?

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
How Would You Know It's Helping?
base_blocks.text: Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
How Would You Know It's Helping?
base_blocks.text: Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
How Would You Know It's Helping?
base_blocks.text: It's like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don't need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
How Would You Know It's Helping?
base_blocks.text: And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

path: Building Trust With Your Little One
How Would You Know It's Helping?
base_blocks.text: If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you're allowed to live, stop there.
Simple Practices

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
base_blocks.text: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
base_blocks.text: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming "shenpa," and she says "hooked" is a more descriptive translation than the usual "attachment." You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you're supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
base_blocks.text: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh! I'm hooked again! That's awesome I could notice it!" Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
What to Make of a Passing Feeling
base_blocks.text: What to Make of a Passing Feeling

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
What to Make of a Passing Feeling
base_blocks.text: Here's where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That's not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though. If what they did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn't mean their boundary crossing indicates “They're evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you're in your happy place.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
What to Make of a Passing Feeling
base_blocks.text: Feelings about yourself work the same way. "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche's pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc. You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don't have to decide what your pronouns are, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there's nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see the pattern.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
What to Make of a Passing Feeling
base_blocks.text: The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with "thought-noting" practice, also isn't healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don't want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later.
A Heart-to-Child Loop

With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso. One punch there hurts a lot, as I sadly learned while getting beaten up every day at kindergarten recess by a gang organized by my best friend. Can you believe it? So it makes sense to look for your little one there.

Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part's a gift from them, and they don't owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. No warmth today? Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required. Non-judgement is a place to start. It can blossom into love over time.
Journal With Each Hand

Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand. As titles go, it's pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings. The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it's had its say.

And what if all that writing leaves you more confused than when you started? Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all. A memory aid doesn't have to explain your life. It could be a dated note of what happened, or of what helped. A reminder or a next step works too. Or you can leave yourself a voice note.
Just Like Me

On a steadier day, when thinking about other people won't pull you out of your own shoes, name the feeling plainly (lonely, say) and think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. With that many people feeling the same thing, the theory that you're the defective one gets kind of hard to keep up. Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.

This is sort of a gentler version of Tibetan Buddhism's tonglen practice (which I learned from Pema Chödrön), where we imagine taking in the suffering of others, transmuting it in our heart, and sending out love and peace to them.

path: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
base_blocks.text: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

path: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
base_blocks.text: My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. ("Once upon a time…" helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

path: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
base_blocks.text: Does saying it make the memory fiction? Well, no, it's still what happened, as far as you remember it, even if some details turn out fuzzy. If the phrase does the trick, leave it at that, no need to narrate the whole thing.

path: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
base_blocks.text: Do keep an ear on who's narrating, though. If the voice starts sneering, like it's making fun of the younger you, stop right there (that's the courtroom creeping back in). Same if you feel more ashamed, or kind of floaty and unreal, since more distance won't help with that. And when it goes well, it's a good time to check in with the younger you in that story. What do they need from you now?

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: In the morning, begin the day intentionally, not just because the sun chose to come up once more, since we can't count on that 🫣. Here's one way you might pl/orkfully start off:

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: “Today I will neither be Peter Pan nor Captain Hook. I will notice a hook or 2 which lead to unconscious behaviors.”

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: Then at night, pay yourself to be your own therapist so as not to break the bank. Equipoisedly look into how the practice went for you today:

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: "Where did I notice the hook?" At dinner with the in-laws? Doom scrolling TikTok nonsense? Watching animé?

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: "Where did it still seem to control me despite noticing it?" (That's the most frustrating part, when you know better, and you still act the same.)

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: Then get practical so it doesn't become another OCD loop: "What small repair or protective act shall I bring in for a proper response to that?"

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: And don't forget to appreciate the good! Moments of warm, beneficial connection (whether internally from child to adult, socially, spiritually, or undefined) are all to be celebrated. Were you maybe firm like an elephant today, or courageous like a lion? Adopt the entire spirit animal zoo if need be! Turtles are good if you need impulse control.

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
base_blocks.text: Count recognition as progress, regardless whether it came up a bit late, as the goal is to bring the awareness closer and closer to the present. All or nothing from the get go would be cool, but we normally have to learn step by step. If/when you interrupted the pattern, pat yourself on the back, or even kiss yourself on the shoulder. You can renew your intention for tomorrow, getting better & better, every day, in every way. And enjoy your well-earned rest tonight.
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
If picturing your little one feels like you’re just making them up, a real photo of you as a child can help, since there’s no face or posture to invent.

While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones. Use Pema Chödrön's "feather touch" approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you'll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then ("You hated that coat"). It might just be an inference you're guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

We don't need to ask it leading questions, like "Who abused me & how?" or "What memory is my body hiding?" Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren't necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions. Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I'm sure you can relate.
A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed... not necessarily representative. Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.

If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don't confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here. You might be looking at the photo thinking, "That would explain so much." Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won't lead you toward an answer.

Put the photo back in its drawer when you're finished. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you're getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present to close out properly. Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this "Present Time" reminder. Can be as simple and silly as "Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!"

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
base_blocks.text: Close the Session and Return to Life

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
base_blocks.text: That "Present Time" ending is worth stealing for every session, photos or no photos. Remember the checking from When Healing Turns Into Checking? Without an ending, the processing can slide right back into that. So when you're done, look around and say where you are. Feel your feet on the floor, or the chair under you, and unclench your jaw and hands, since they've probably been at it this whole time.

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
base_blocks.text: And what's next for you two? Maybe it's making food, or just going to bed. Whatever it is, tell your little one, "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." Nothing has to be resolved first, and whatever you're still feeling can come along.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: A lot of people get stuck right here. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone or the laundry feels urgent. Or some voice says this is silly, and it's hard to tell which part of you is saying it.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: My friend Scott said:

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: > "Half the time when I try to connect to baby me, I feel fake and it seems crazy."

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: I used to be all personal trainer and teach persistence on this as the remedy. Keeping at it does help, since a little one who learned to expect being dropped won't trust you right away. But I don't think that explains the adult feeling fully. More importantly, I think it could even be like unintentional gaslighting to the little one to ask to connect with them when you don't believe they're even real. Like when my mom pretended to listen to me when I was young, but even less excusable (from the inner child's view) because she was not asking for my time when she did that. So, it's worth meditating first on why it feels fake.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Sometimes kindness feels scary more than fake
base_blocks.text: Sometimes kindness feels scary more than fake

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Sometimes kindness feels scary more than fake
base_blocks.text: One study's title has a word for that: "compassion-threat." People in it with anxious or avoidant attachment reacted to compassion imagery like a threat, and a ten-minute exercise in feeling secure helped with the next try. Another found a first try at imagery like that "can be frightening for people who have a tendency to be self-critical." So feeling fake could mean you need a bridge, more than a bigger performance of love.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Picturing one ideal parent seems to help some people
base_blocks.text: Picturing one ideal parent seems to help some people

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Picturing one ideal parent seems to help some people
base_blocks.text: There's a whole method built on it, called the Ideal Parent Figure method. In a small pilot, seventeen adults with complex PTSD from childhood trauma did five weeks of it and were still doing better eight months later. Seventeen people with nobody to compare them to won't prove the whole method, but it's a start.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state
base_blocks.text: For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state
base_blocks.text: Like on MDMA or deep in meditation. All of a sudden your little one is right there! Oh my gosh! And the love or grief that sounded like therapy talk is just obvious. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn't prove they happened. I'd still hang on to what you felt, even once it's gone, and try to bring a little of it into your normal life. You've felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn't just pretending.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: The Parent You Inherited

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up. Maybe sometimes that script feels warm, but maybe too often it feels more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound totally reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If your childhood was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed to show up, so they could keep belonging. And if so, do a double check: they might still be doing it!

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: If the script is mostly critical, it means the parent you inherited is busy measuring whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal. Then you can feel attacked from both sides: not only are you not good enough, but if you do seem to be good enough, it's probably fake, so it's like nothing you do really counts. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” with a background like that, well, of course your little one doesn’t answer.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you just the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little sweetie pie, like letting the phone ring when you know already how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. It may take many such ignored calls before your inner child can start trusting you, and all the while, the parent you inherited calls your efforts fake.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: Answering the Strict Disciplinarian

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: A good routine, like yoga in the morning and a proper bedtime, still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s done in a disciplinarian style. One exercise you can do to handle this is to go back and rewrite your responses to that strict disciplinarian. First, remember who it was that drove you so hard as a child. Then start a little rap sheet of their provoking lines. Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: The Critic's voice can often pile on, to the point where you can't even understand why or what you're really feeling anymore. You feel sad at first, then the Inner Critic calls your inner child pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness with some simple nurturing instead from the beginning, but now you have to peel back this other nonsense to get to it.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Play Is Part of the Work
base_blocks.text: Play Is Part of the Work

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Play Is Part of the Work
base_blocks.text: Your little one wants to play, too, which is why I call the deeper therapy pl/ork, play + work. A lot of the best discoveries come when you're both just messing around, kind of like how kids tell you what's really going on from the back seat, when nobody's looking right at them. Play not only paves the way for therapy, but is a part of how successful therapy should be measured.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
Play Is Part of the Work
base_blocks.text: A lot of what adults tend to lose, your little one still has, like the silliness and the irreverence, the rawness, the creativity, all that, and maybe a connection to the Great Mystery from before any path gave it a name. That's the spark of life they bring, and you get to draw on it and give back, so it's more communion than command. For one example of the spark, there's my post Treasuring the Inner Child's Gift.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: Start With Whatever Showed Up

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you've been staring at the rug. I count that as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it's in the way. Before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants. Maybe it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. Maybe it's that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: You can tell that part something like, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?" Or however you'd actually say that. Then wait and listen patiently.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: If no answer comes

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: That's fine for now. No need to answer for that part just because you'd set this up as a healing session. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
If you do get an answer
base_blocks.text: If you do get an answer

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
If you do get an answer
base_blocks.text: It could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It's often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that's what it wants. How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
If it tells you to do something
base_blocks.text: If it tells you to do something

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
If it tells you to do something
base_blocks.text: I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you're calm and you've checked it against what you actually know.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: Which thoughts to talk to

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: I think a fear that keeps turning up to tell you something is worth talking to as a part of you. If it sounds like your little one, though, hear it out the first time it shows up. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you're in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it's your little one asking.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: I wouldn't spend long deciding what to call each part, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that's trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn't have to get any louder.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: If it's anxiety

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
base_blocks.text: Anxiety is often a part of you that's trying to protect you, making a guess about what's coming, like that people will laugh at you. It can be right! It's probably been wrong before too, and you know some of those times. Unless it might be real danger, or something a doctor should look at, I'd go see.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
If a part hesitates about being touched or about sex, or says no to going deeper in this work or to an altered state
base_blocks.text: If a part hesitates about being touched or about sex, or says no to going deeper in this work or to an altered state
