base_blocks.text: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: If you've got something burning you up that you wanna say, write it out as a reply. There. That got it out. Ahh. Breathing easier. 😌 But don't send it. Take that breather you earned and then come back to it from a cooler place.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: It doesn't mean you need to hide your upset, or apply for a permit to protest, but choose your battles and execute them wisely, so you don't end up regretting how you communicated later. As Lao Tsu might have said (if I could ever have read that whole boring Art of War book), a war with no casualties is the best possible war. When high IQ & EQ communication hits a writer's block, sometimes the best thing is to simply say, "I need some time to think about my response." And if the conflict really requires a response right now, then obviously just do your best rather than wait for the perfect timing.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: And yeah, going back to the writer, which is often my inner child when emotions pop up, is part of the process. It's like I'm holding his hand and showing him a better way, not like I just stole his pencil because he wrote something embarrassing. So what was he actually trying to say? A lot of the time it's just "that hurt."

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: Other times it's "I did this too." My friend Tyler saw a guy smoking in front of a baby and asked him if he thought that was wise. The guy asked if he thought it was wise to mind his own business, and Tyler said, "Well, I believe in Christ, so I thought you might care about life too." Afterward he wasn't sure he'd handled it right, or whether he should have thrown the first stone at all, since he'd smoked in front of a baby himself.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: But Jesus also said to take the log out of your own eye first, and then "you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye." That's exactly what made Tyler the right person to say something. If you actually have the problem they have, and you want to call them out for it, call yourself out for it instead. What we came up with was something like, "Hey man, when I was younger I smoked in front of an infant, not realizing how selfish that was, and I notice you doing the same thing. I'd ask you to please have some compassion for him. I have a young child now, so this really touches me." Tyler's an evangelical Christian who preaches on YouTube, so the fact that he really appreciated this take on Jesus' message is pretty important to me.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: It's also how your voice sounds, though. You can say all the right words, but if the tone is accusatory, it doesn't matter.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
base_blocks.text: Before sending anything, I'd read it once as if I were them, sitting there with my phone. What felt scared when I wrote it can read like a threat from over there.

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
base_blocks.text: Speak Toward What You Are Building

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
base_blocks.text: It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent, just like that Pink Elephant. Being totally independent also isn’t realistic nor ideal, and can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
base_blocks.text: But let’s also make sure we don’t hide from shadow stuff with toxic positivity. Grief is natural, and letting tears flow can be immensely therapeutic, as long as they don’t hijack your perspective with a cemented story of what will always be true. If your little one says “he hurt me,” we honestly label that as harm, even if it was also a learning experience. Same for anger, a "No," who’s responsible, all that. Then once the difficult experience is acknowledged by the Nurturer, the Protector & Guide can lead the way up to more safety and maturity.

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
Ask What Kind of Company They Want
base_blocks.text: Ask What Kind of Company They Want

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
Ask What Kind of Company They Want
base_blocks.text: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: “Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, brainstorm, or...?” Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it’s obvious what they want. But as they say, "assume" makes an "ass" out of "u" and "me."
Hearthwork: Taking Turns

The basic premise of Hearthwork, my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It's kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.

Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places, and it's your turn to keep "Here's what you should do" to yourself.

The peer doesn't become your permanent parent, though. They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form (a driving instructor isn't planning to drive you around forever either). Is that therapy? Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure. Professional therapy's still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.
The Love Has to Move

Community can come before the big opening or after it, too. Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible. Other times it's the other way around. Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn't have imagined before, and then they start to "manifest" different kinds of people and relationships in their life. Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.

This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community. Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn't really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn't always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.
How to Forgive Without Forgetting

For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can't be put on a schedule. And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.

The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person's conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn't handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you've held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn't make it okay. It's just that punishing them now can't reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What's left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now.

So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they'd never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody's limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."
Forgiving Yourself

Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends. Changing the behavior counts too. Then you're allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you're thinking "not me, not after what I did," forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you've left a family or community, maybe you've stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you're doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn't shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo.

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: Your little one might be sure everything's over. Is it? Usually one real thing ended, and there's other stuff you're still trying to keep going, maybe on autopilot. Some of it just isn't known yet, and unknown isn't the same as gone. Ask your little one what they're scared will happen in the meantime (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: Something basic can mark the ending, like boxing up the old keys. Nobody needs to know what door will open next. But when the not-knowing feels too heavy, a new identity can sure look tempting. Like a borrowed coat that doesn't fit but at least it's warm. But you can't go far with a borrowed coat anyway, so don't force the future on. Keep taking care of yourself, and grieve what ended with your little one beside you during the metamorphosis.

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: Missing Someone

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: When you miss someone, let the ache be a cue for love. It doesn't have to become one more problem to solve, and pushing it away won't help. If love's there, "I miss you" becomes "I love you." Or there's the loving-kindness wish: "May you be safe. May you be held in love." You can picture them. Or don't, and just feel the care going their way.

path: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
base_blocks.text: All of this happens in you, so it doesn't matter whether they get any of it. And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can't get back to your life, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." Some of that same care can go to the part of you that's still here.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
base_blocks.text: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood

base_blocks.text: We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide.

base_blocks.text: Inner Child Reparenting therapists do exist, and you can find them, although they often are not licensed, and I don't know of any central directory, nor of any protocol they'd have in common. There are none which work with my guide yet. I can consult, and if you like the guide, you can ask a therapist to check it out and see what they agree with or disagree with as a great way to vet them.

If you want a licensed therapist
base_blocks.text: The best licensed, listed therapists you'll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I'll talk more about those in the appendix, but Schema Therapy comes closest to my approach. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
base_blocks.text: Get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I'd especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won't tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I'd also want one who doesn't put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won't charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can't tell you any of that.

path: How This Relates to Schema Therapy
base_blocks.text: Of the clinical approaches I know, schema therapy is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own "Healthy Adult," who looks after your "Vulnerable Child" and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. It sets limits, too. And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you've committed to. Sound familiar? That's a Nurturer, a Protector and a Guide by other names, and since the therapist's version becomes yours bit by bit, it's borrowed adulthood too.

path: How This Relates to Schema Therapy
base_blocks.text: Where it really differs is spirituality. Schema therapy doesn't build it in, though the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice an important development. That's not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy. Some people do blend them, though. Tara Bennett-Goleman's book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema. Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that's the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).
How This Relates to IFS

Richard Schwartz, who developed Internal Family Systems (IFS), called one of his books No Bad Parts. Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so "meet the protector first" would fit right in over there. That's a lot of the overlap with this method, right there in the title.

My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. The IFS Institute's outline of the model says "everyone has a Self," and that the Self "can and should lead," once your parts stop "blending" with it. I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru. That's still one grown-up with three jobs, like back in The Chicken-and-Egg Problem.

Can't find a calm, compassionate Self in there? Then borrow. One grown-up job at a time, from a friend who'll play Protector for a night, or from something you do, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes (The Parent You Inherited again), until it's yours.

Is a perfect Higher Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I'd call that claim spiritual bypassing. I've had the Higher Self perspective myself, though. It's a somewhat less subjective way of seeing things as working perfectly in reality, despite the ego's illusions, which matches what people say about it. Where I part ways with IFS is the wisdom part. I don't think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom. It's a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.

You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego's traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as "crazy wisdom" by apologists.

So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can't act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn't do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I'm trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn't exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that's one more problem I'm trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.

IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.

And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming. People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before. I've seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
Related Clinical Work

This framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy. I borrow particular ideas and practices from each of them, but the mix is mine, so please don't blame them for it.
Teachers and Practice Resources

Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes. Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it. She has a book and a free one-hour YouTube training, and she's on Instagram.

Lisa Romano brings more neuroscience and CBT, and her video is a good place to start. She makes the point that remembering the specific details of childhood trauma isn't necessary, because the felt body knows what needs to come up. Key developed the Guide's sense of direction, and the identity and differentiation work from Bowen I mentioned earlier. She led a guided inner-child meditation in Nairobi in January 2026 for twenty people, and it's up on YouTube.

joel_blocks.text: Understanding Reparenting
Welcome, lovey bunnies!
Here’s the idea behind Inner Child Reparenting, in a nutshell:

Growing up, all of us picked up automatic ways of understanding situations we find ourselves in, reacting based on those understandings, and then treating ourselves partly based on how we happened to handle things. Some of those patterns are still wise in general, although even then, we are always learning from what life throws at us. Others of those patterns were built for a crisis that’s long over, and some just seem to make every situation worse.

Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding a better Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding. At first, it’s deliberate and might feel difficult. Many struggle to get past the silly, awkward feeling of it. Over time, instead of shying way from the silly, we can use the silly feeling in the work, to make it more playful. I call it pl/ork ! With time, the adult/child roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.
If that got to you at all, good. That was half the idea. I used to listen to Suzanne Vega’s The Queen and the Soldier every night because it reliably got the tears out.

The crying helped me a lot in terms of not going numb inside. It didn’t help me develop insight, though. I could have kept crying forever. It was Buddhism and then inner child therapy which helped create a new perspective that was more healthy. But I’m really happy I did do the crying that was needed at the time.

Music can help with feeling love, not just sadness, although sadness is often the first step to open up. So if you sit down to try any of this and feel nothing, that’s when I’d put a song on. Céline’s right up there if you don’t have one, and Rosey Grier’s It’s All Right to Cry is a little further down. My sister used to sing that one to me almost daily in such a silly way. It was really sweet of her.

Some people, like another ex of mine (X), got so deep into crying that it became traumatizing. She actually had panic attacks from it. If you start getting scared of your own crying, turn the song off for tonight.
The Chicken-and-Egg Problem

Céline’s song is called On ne change pas—”we don’t change.” I think that’s both fortunately, and unfortunately, true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don’t truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren’t made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.

And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to « heal  itself, » which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult. I call that “forced adulthood,” where the child has to deal with situations the evolved inner adult should be handling--we see this in actual children all the time when their parents are not providing care. People even wear t-shirts saying, “I don’t wanna adult today.” The forced adulting often goes along with a misperception that there is something wrong with the inner child. Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.

That’s one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in to help with the rent, and each job keeps the others in balance. Say a party gets to be too much for your little one. The Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom. And the Guide helps them think twice about the next weird party they might go to, avoiding another cycle of bathroom vacationing. 🙈

The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most, because a lot of the bad parenting or misdirection we originally received was likely lacking in Protector and Nurturer functions, while over-relying on harsh guidance. So left it out of the first version of this framework until my friend Key pointed it out as crucial.Without a healed Inner Guide, our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well. That’s the Guide’s job. But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves. And many folks try to find an ideal guide via some kind of guru-led political or religious cult.
If the phrase “inner parent” calls up the wrong archetype for you, pick another one. Your future self might work, or the captain of a ship, so long as they’d do those three jobs.

But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? In this case, you sit there trying to be loving while your mind is becoming controlled again by the inherited critic voice, or you start going numb, throwing a fit, or panicking.

Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first. You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it. Maybe you copy one small thing you’ve seen them do, or imagine them there when they’re not, and try one piece yourself while they’re still helping with the rest. That’s what I mean by borrowed adulthood. You may still need help with almost all of it for a while, but over time there are more and more of those little parts you can do yourself.
Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five progressive stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):

1. Forced adulthood : You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting: 
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby, etc. 
3. Practice being the adult — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step. 
4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and shepherding them. 
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!

Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Depending on your maladaptive patterns, improvements could look opposite to each other. If you’re a workaholic normally, then your little one might start believing in grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore. Or the opposite, when you stop procrastinating so much and clean your room, then they start beliving in you.

Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, even if you make excellent progress. You might feel like you’ve mastered the adult/child inner relationship, and then it’s Friday night and your boss asks you to stay late again. You get up the nerve to tell them no, and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.
My Journey
I used to preach Buddhist enlightenment too much, because that’s what helped me out of a long existential crisis.

From what I’ve seen, most people who chase spiritual freedom, as valid as that is, are, at least at first, trying to get away from something painful in themselves, usually childhood trauma of some kind. That’s spiritual bypassing. Plenty of gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example.

The way I think this works is simple. Imagine you’re broke and starving, and your baby is starving too. Understandable: there is no food. Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you’ve got lots of nutritious munchies. But you’re eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving. Unforgivable.

Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose. I just didn’t believe there was a baby. Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him. Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I’d already found his way.

Spending your whole life processing your wounded inner child isn’t freedom either. Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story. Maybe ordinary life already gives many folks enough love and meaning. It didn’t for me. Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.

I was well-loved as a child, but from age 12 to 26, I was depressed, and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. Loving-kindness (metta) meditation healed that depression almost instantly for me, so it became my regular practice automatically. I later found out that many people weren’t able to do a deep metta meditation, because they literally didn’t know what love felt like, as they hadn’t received it as a child. My 2nd wife told me she didn’t know the word for love in her native language, because her mom never said that word to her.

But it even though my depression was gone, the sending-love-outward metta practice didn’t reach everything in me. An old childhood wound could still hit, like if someone accused me of being lazy, and then suddenly it’s like I was that same little kid again, even tho the spiritual part of me felt free as a bird. And a lot of the childhood stuff around my attachment to girls/women was still there.

At some point I guess I heard folks talking about inner child therapy, and being curious about different healing approaches, I thought I’d give it a go even if I wasn’t the prime candidate. It felt like I was making it up at first, which seems quite common. That didn’t stop me from occasionally practicing, but I did stop “pushing” it to be a certain way, and I’d stop trying to feel it was realer than it was. I would go more into listening and waiting mode rather than imagining mode.

At one pivotal point, I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open. I had a full-on audio-visual communion with my little Joelito and I heard a few things he was still sad about from so long ago. Things which most people would laugh at, because they’re seemingly so minor. Like when I hit my neighbor while riding my bicycle, and even after I profusely apologized, her mom said, « Don’t you have any common sense ??? » And I found out why I was always pushing myself to help others. It was because when I was 5yrs old, at the Zendik community in Texas that we were visiting, they held a meeting with everyone there (like 50 people) and me in the center. I was critiqued for not offering to help anyone I saw who was working. Well, sorry ! I never knew I was supposed to. That’s a pattern that has stuck, although it does help to remember what caused it, so I don’t take it so seriously.

Years later, I found a warm, intuitive inner child therapist, named Daja, randomly (if you believe anything is random), as a friend of a friend, while in Kenya. I figured I already knew this stuff, but I gave it a shot. She did actually help me see some things more clearly. For example, she had me write down how many people I could fully trust as a child (lots), then how many people I could fully trust as an adult (zero). That was difficult, and it’s actually the opposite of what you might expect from inner-child therapy, since usually that’s for people who had problems trusting as a child.

What it showed me is that I was ignoring a lot of things that were really important to look at, and that was one of them. I wouldn’t have even thought to ask the question she asked me if I were doing it on my own. It’s also an example of how therapy can sometimes make you feel worse than before, when you become more aware of problems. But personally I prefer to see things as they are, so I can figure out how to work with them, rather than just hide in delusions.

It also showed me that I really do need to count more on myself than I assumed. I need to be much better as an inner adult for my inner child, because my childhood was actually so nice that I kind of just assume I can trust everyone, and that gets me into trouble! So it got me curious to learn more about inner-child therapy, which is a process I’m still in the midst of as I test this guide with people.

path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
joel_blocks.text: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Check if you can pause before you act. Are you following through after making decisions? If you can’t do those things because you’re basically still stuck identifying as the frightened kid still, then let’s leave the deeper conversation until later. Do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to little you. And have someone steady there to support you if possible.

path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
joel_blocks.text: And if the grown-up you is there, and it’s just how deep you’re going that’s too much, dip your toes in the kiddie pool first. Like the flight attendants say, it’s good to know where the exits are. 😅 So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room? If you can’t, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I’d come all the way back out first. Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there’s a grown-up around who can say, “Okay, that’s enough for today,” and try something gentler, like saying hi to them with your eyes open.

path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
joel_blocks.text: If you need a break from the communion, simply jot down the reason and the progress made so far. Then come back later, once that reason has changed and you feel comfortable.

path: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
joel_blocks.text: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I’d call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Even if you don’t have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this (not hotlines unless it’s an emergency).

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: Your Body Might Need Some Love First

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, as well as gentle circular or varied directional massage in the solar plexus, neck, head, abdomen, or whatever spot is feeling tense.

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: I’d also recommend checking into deeper somatic therapies like Shaking, tapping (EFT), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or some other bottom-up approach.

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: When your nervous system is flooded, your protective parts are busy throwing buckets of water out of the boat, so they’re not going to let your little one come out and talk much anyway. Some people go straight into EMDR to work on desensitizing their worst memory before they can even stay in the room. path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: Some somatic work or reparenting therapy can feel pleasant, and some can feel like a raging storm got unleashed. It can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes nightmares later on as the memories begin to unwind. It’s a bit like going to the gym. You want to make gains, and sore muscles the next day can be good, but proper range of (e)motion here is also key to avoid injury.

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: Keep track of how you feel over the next few days, like how refreshing your sleep is, and how easy it feels to get through your day. Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? If you can’t quite tell yet what feels different, I’d just make the next session simpler, one change at a time, like a science nerd, so you learn what made the difference. You can play around with variables like shorter session length, or shallower diving, time of day, keeping eyes open, having a friend around, or holding a teddy bear as a stand-in for your little one.

path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
joel_blocks.text: And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. Although sometimes dreams can show you real memories and even predict the future on occasion, we need to be careful not to assume that they are doing that each time.

joel_blocks.text: Some people hear all this about loving themself and answer, “No. I hate myself.” Like my friend Malia, who told me, « My inner child is just capricious !
