path: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
Notice the Part That Came Here
joel_blocks.text: It might have been hope, or desperation. Maybe you were curious, or scared. Some people come here out of duty (my sister kept telling me to see therapists; she says everyone needs therapy). Or it was more like, “I’m not going to keep suffering like this.” And maybe it was love. Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: I’ve been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child. Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though. For such folks, inner child therapy is clearly not the place to start. They need to first deconstruct the adult identity they’ve got.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: When I talk with folks like that, I mostly want to know what the identity gets them and what it costs, and especially what it’s really serving. Some of them even call themselves « sovereign, » yet somehow there’s an urge they have to obey, which sounds more like slavery to me.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who’s horrified by their own thoughts. Everybody gets scary thoughts they’d rather not have sometimes, and they don’t make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them? The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you’re calm and actually ready. A real parent doesn’t get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to be get a perfect 4.0 GPA on the parent report-card their children bring home . 😛

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: And if somebody actually wonders whether they’re malicious, they’d do better to meditate on it and find out why they’re asking before they bring their inner child anywhere near it. Are they really feeling malicious, or is it some voice in their head saying so, like the inherited critic? If some of it turns out to be malice they actually want to act on, the inner child can wait.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: Ill Will and Loving-Kindness

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up from identity, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one getting burnt first. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: The Buddha also told his son, Rahula, that loving-kindness is what gets rid of ill will, and compassion does the same for cruelty. I’m biased on loving-kindness, since it got me out of my depression. For these folks it starts with the grown-up they are now, though, and their little one stays out of it.

path: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
joel_blocks.text: As for when their little one gets a turn, I’d say once they’ve had some bad days where scaring somebody would’ve felt good, and they didn’t do it. Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them for the good they see deep down, and won’t laugh along with the mask persona, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
joel_blocks.text: If You Want to Kill Yourself

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
joel_blocks.text: Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
joel_blocks.text: As for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who’s doing the noticing (as described in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :).

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: The Spiritual Side of the Question

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: I try not to proselytize about spirituality, because I’ve made that mistake before, and I now see that it’s better to let folks find it when they are ready. But when someone tells me they want to kill themself, I consider the topic to be brutally opened by default, regardless of whether they meant to do that, because if they actually do kill their body (which they might mistake to be their self), that’s a very powerful spiritual challenge right there, even if they didn’t realize it would be.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: Then ask: what is the self you want to kill? Is that self the same thing as your body? Why? Do you have the same body in dreams? What exactly do you expect your body’s death to accomplish? If the problem is a state of mind, like self-hatred or despair, shame or loneliness, what makes you so sure that destroying the body ends it?

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: In Buddhism, death isn’t an off switch, and it isn’t a free new-age get-out-of-jail-free card back to the Divine Source. Repeated thought and intention shape the mind, and that keeps going through death and rebirth. Yes, that can include hell realms (and hell can be right here on Earth, also). A human birth is a rare chance to understand suffering and end its causes.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: You don’t have to believe that, but if you’re still thinking of staking your life on the opposite claim, that death is just nothing, might that be a double standard to look into? Curiosity killed the cat, you might say, so research could be dangerous. 😅 But despite the risk of curiosity, researchers at the University of Virginia have been busy little bees, collecting cases for 60 YEARS now, of young kids who talk about a past life, and there’s a big pile of near-death accounts too. Even if every case is different, I’d read a few of those cases before betting my life on “nothing.”

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: Right here in this one life, it’s apparent that the more you hate yourself, the better your mind gets at it, and being alone tends to deepen the despair. But lucky us, because physical life keeps handing out redirections, like that guy who found me in a random park crying one time, and asked me “What’s wrong?” If the many traditions and the accumulating scientific evidence are right that the mind’s causal process goes on after the body dies, killing the body may take away some of those redirections and leave the suffering right where it was. That sounds like a substantially worse deal to me.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
The Spiritual Side of the Question
joel_blocks.text: My father used to tell suicidal people, “Oh, you want to kill yourself? That’s wonderful! Now you can change what you’ve always been too afraid to change in your life, and then see if you still want to end it!” So, what would you tell my dad? What’s the change you still can’t bring yourself to make? Leaving a relationship orquitting a job? Telling your family who you really are? Those might sound difficult, but they’re actually considerably easier and more likely to help than dying.

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
This human life is the most precious opportunity
joel_blocks.text: This human life is the most precious opportunity

path: If You Want to Kill Yourself
This human life is the most precious opportunity
joel_blocks.text: As I mentioned in my nibbana article, I’ve had my most profound spiritual peak experiences and realizations when I had the least interest in continued existence. And the Buddha taught in MN 129, attaining a human birth is as rare and precious as it would be for a one-eyed turtle to pop his head up through a hoop on the surface of the vast ocean. You won the cosmic jackpot, so don’t throw away the ticket before you open the envelope to find it!
Building Your Inner Adult

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Now, don’t tell anyone abou tthis ! I’m going to reveal my Magician’s Secret. I call it the « borrowed adulthood trick ».,  The new grown-up you’re moulding can start outside your head, as someone who likes you just the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little sweetie pie, like letting the phone ring when you know already how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. It may take many such ignored calls before your inner child can start trusting you (and all the while, the parent you inherited calls your efforts fake).

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: This is the heart of the reparenting manual. Here’s where you start to come into your power. Try to see the end goal as attainable right at the start here so that you :

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Don’t Sell Your Inner Adult To Buy An Outer Adult
joel_blocks.text: Don’t Sell Your Inner Adult To Buy An Outer Adult

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Don’t Sell Your Inner Adult To Buy An Outer Adult
joel_blocks.text: If you still feel like a kid inside, somebody who seems grown-up can feel like salvation, and letting them do some of the grown-up jobs for you can actually help for a while. But they can know things you don’t and still be wrong for you to follow too much. The test is whether the relationship makes you more grounded, truthful, and free.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Don’t Sell Your Inner Adult To Buy An Outer Adult
joel_blocks.text: How do you check that? I’d keep what you feel around them in mind, and look at their track record too. Do they respect a no, or keep pushing on it, and what happens when you disagree? If something outside of them backs up what they’re telling you, and it all adds up, that’s a good sign.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Don’t Sell Your Inner Adult To Buy An Outer Adult
joel_blocks.text: Even Pema Chödrön(who inspired parts of this guide), who comes from a tradition where devotion to a guru is a big deal, still says a teacher should “wean us from dependency altogether” and help us grow up.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Signs of Manipulation

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Some gurus really do demand surrender, and they’re the opposite of the Guide: they point you at themselves for everything, as if they want to be your God. Others are so professional that they don’t even need to ask anyone to follow them. Someone seems to get your little one like nobody ever has, or treats it like it’s special, and it starts thinking, “They know me better than I know myself ! Can you believe it ?” 🙊 I still remember a Sadhguru video where he said anyone who follows him as an idiot, and his followers were still worshipping him in the comments, proud idiots. 🤪

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Here’s where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That’s not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Some manipulative people are too smart to act perfect. They lead with their wounds, or with how brutally honest they are about their flaws (very disarming, which is sort of the point), and every warning you hear about them just becomes more proof of how profound they are. Your Protector should be called to step in whenever love bombing hides obvious red flags your more skeptical friends would love to point out if you’d listen. After all, “I have honesty issues and I’m working on them” may be a perfectly honest thing to say. It’s also telling you there’s an honesty problem right now, and knowing about a problem isn’t fixing it.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text:
Other types of manipulation to check for include : 
Gaslighting, when your perception of reality is slowly giving way to someone else’s. Combat this by trusting your perceptions (after documenting or double checking).

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: In abusive relationships, gaslighting often turns into D.A.R.V.O. : Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender. This is how the abuser flips the script on accountability. If you notice this happening, extricate yourself quickly.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Guilt tripping, where you’re made to feel responsible for things you shouldn’t be. Like someone did something for you and then later makes you seem like a bad person because you haven’t done enough to give back. Check if the guilt is deserved or not.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: White Knight : this is when problems are created that you need to be saved from, which can then lead back into guilt-tripping, or dependence. Solve your own challenges rather than letting yourself over-rely on someone as a pattern.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Triangulation is where another person is brought in to the conversation so it becomes 2 vs 1. Insist on direct communication with one person if this tactic is employed.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Silent treatment : when someone cuts back their emotional involvement to punish or control you (can be confused with simply avoiding situations they aren’t able to handle). Don’t chase these people, nor reverse it onto them.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Breadcrumbing is when silent treatment is reduced just enough to make you hooked on trying to get their attention. Value yourself enough so this doesn’t work.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: That’s a lot of manipulation tactics! And those sneaky sneaks are always coming up with new ones, so it’s time we develop our spidey sense. We can also look inward to check if we are using those on ourselves or others.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qLfqA2igdUI&list=RDqLfqA2igdUI&start_radio=1

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
joel_blocks.text: Borrow One Competency at a Time

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
joel_blocks.text: A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age (along with spirituality) , but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one capacity at a time from a figure who embodies it well.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
joel_blocks.text: While all of these super powers should be developed alongside each other, the inner child’s receptivity will naturally follow this order : first he/she wants to feel safe (Protector), then, building on that safety, feel loved (Nurterer), and then building on the safety & love, trust allows the little one to be eager to take guidance, and that’s where Guide-building comes.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Noticing Counts

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: Even before you build up any of these capacities, you can start with simply being present with your little one, which does a lot more than you might think to set the stage for the proper division of identity. Just saying, “Huh, somebody in here is really scared.” might be the most adult thing you’ve got right now, but notice that whoever’s noticing isn’t all the way inside the scared one.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: It can help to use your own name. For me, instead of “I’m terrified,” that’d be “Little Joel is terrified. What does Little Joel need right now?” You’ll sound a bit like Elmo :) In lab studies, though, people who talked to themselves this way reacted less to upsetting pictures and memories, and their brains didn’t seem to be working any harder to do it.

path: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
joel_blocks.text: If you can tell your parts apart pretty easily, you’ve probably got plenty of noticing already. Don’t keep drilling it just because the love isn’t coming yet. A lot of meditators are great at watching. I was, and baby me was still starving.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Plenty of people are still at the putting-up-with part of reparenting. Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector’s plain acts and the warmth can come after, which feels backwards, because you’d think you have to feel it first before you could do anything for them. But yeah, bonding starts somewhere. And this is not to say you’ve never done anything to care for yourself. If not, you’d be dead right now. But we’re making additional acts of care intentional now as a base for love to grow.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: As you may have heard, not every hero wears a cape! Maybe an older sibling protected you well at some point, so they were your hero then, even if they weren’t a full adult. So whatever is troubling your inner child right now, start with asking what a minimally competent adult would do in this situation.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Talk to the hand !✋🏿

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Setting boundaries is an obvious first protector move. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, health, or whatever resource). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Maybe it’s something seemingly simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird (that’s one I’m still working on). If you’re about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly how I’d phrase it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh! Laughter is the best medicine.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Keep one small promise to your little one. If you promise to clean your room, then do that. Maybe your little one had grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, and maybe you’ve done it too, so this is how they start to believe you.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Making It Intentional

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Intentional, meaning instead of waiting for crisis to hit to react, you pick one of those protector acts and decide when you’ll do it, and what the first step is. If it needs money or somebody’s help, sort that out before the day, and if you’ll have to tell someone something they won’t like, say it out loud to yourself ahead of time. Then put yourself in their shoes to see how it sounds, and go back & forth like that a couple times until both sides feel good about it, or good enough, as long as what you needed to say is still in there.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: After the day, look at what actually happened. Say you did the Protector action(s) and you don’t feel any better, or you feel worse. Standing up for yourself can do that at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess. But did you know how to do it, and why? Were you worn out? Maybe whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. 🤗

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Protecting them from yourself

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
joel_blocks.text: Even if you mean well, things don’t always come out the way you hoped. You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. “What’s an ‘internal attack’?” Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they’re sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back. They don’t trust you yet, and you don’t ask them to. They complain about something, and if they’re right, you say so. All of that is evidence they’re accepted and you’re safe to be around. Love needs those to start with, but without warmth they can still feel like they’re only being put up with.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
joel_blocks.text: Protecting from the Parent You Inherited

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
joel_blocks.text: I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up. Maybe sometimes that script feels warm, but maybe too often it feels more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound totally reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If your childhood was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed to show up, so they could keep belonging. And if so, do a double check: they might still be doing it!

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
joel_blocks.text: If the script is mostly critical, it means the parent you inherited is busy measuring whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal. Then you can feel attacked from both sides: not only are you not good enough, but if you do seem to be good enough, it’s probably fake, so it’s like nothing you do really counts. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” with a background like that, well, of course your little one doesn’t answer.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
joel_blocks.text: Keep in mind that while a critical voice might be that inherited parent script, or any outside influence with no concern for your welfare, it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
Reframing attacks as unskillful attempts to help
joel_blocks.text: Reframing attacks as unskillful attempts to help

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
Reframing attacks as unskillful attempts to help
joel_blocks.text: One of my favorite teachers, Mr. Rogers, gave us an excellent example of how to extract the sweet nectar of truth from what less advanced souls might recoil at. In the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, “I can’t imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father.” He doesn’t collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what’s worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest “genuinely tested” him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he’s very proud of both his sons. Then he says, “But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn’t have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective.”

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
Reframing attacks as unskillful attempts to help
joel_blocks.text: We want to use the Mr. Rogers reframing trick to stay curious about its motivations, and open to any kernels of truth it points out, without accepting its insults and cruelty. Then we send it on its way with compassion, since that voice surely needs some.

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Earning their trust, day to day
joel_blocks.text: Earning their trust, day to day

path: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
Earning their trust, day to day
joel_blocks.text: A new roommate doesn’t win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up each month. Your Protector earns that guard’s trust about the same way, out there in the real world, day after day. Little things make a big difference, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about, or saying no to the 13th friend today who asked you to Google something for them (I’m still working on that one).
The Nurturer

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: Sometimes the love is there for your little one and still feels unsafe to them, or safe for a minute and then not. Some researchers found a phrase for that: “compassion-threat.” People in their study with anxious or avoidant attachment, or a tendency to be self-critical, reacted to compassion imagery like a threat, especially at first.

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: Love and trust are reciprocal and intertangled, like the Chicken and Egg problem. Without trust, the love seems fake. And without love, the trust is shallow. When you show your love, it can sound like you’re asking them to trust that you love them. But your love doesn’t need their trust. It does need you to be honest with them, which isn’t the same as perfect. They’re still going over your track record (they’ve heard what you still call yourself when you mess up, sometimes out loud).

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: When your little one says “I don’t trust you.” you can answer, “I believe you. And I love you.” I learned this when I was 5. My mom told me it was time for bed (or something equally outrageous to a 5-year-old). I cried and screamed “I HATE YOU! I wish you were dead !” 😡 She answered, “But I love you!” 🥰

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: That completely threw me. Fights don’t usually go like that. Anger is a way to get more power when you feel a lack of justice or agency. You puff yourself up so you seem frightening or dangerous, or you demand to be heard. My anger was there to get me heard, and her answer showed me I didn’t need it for that. Whatever injustice I thought there was wasn’t coming from a lack of love, either. So the anger seemed stupid. I saw for myself that it was only hurting me, without helping me see clearly or get what I wanted. Still, what I screamed was true for a part of me right then, and what she said back was true too, so I could hate somebody who loved me and she’d still be my mom the whole time.

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: When it’s your little one yelling at you, though, try not to turn “But I love you” into a prompted line you say on cue, because then it can feel like a tactical ruse to brush the anger off. You’re little one will be watching to see if the love stays afterward and takes whatever’s true in their anger seriously.

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: But even when the love does stay, your little one might still come back with “Big fuckity whoopty doo. I don’t believe you.” 🙄 You answer, “Okay. I believe that you don’t believe me. I still love you. 🤗 You don’t have to love me back. Tell me what makes the love feel unreal to you.”

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: Your little one might say it’s you, without giving more details at first. Keep practicing your listening, and eventually you’ll get more of a concrete complaint, which you can consider without getting flustered from the meanness they packaged it in. Like my anger at bedtime, their swearing is there to get them heard, so once you’re ears guards are off, they don’t need it anymore.

path: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
joel_blocks.text: And sometimes you might feel the love for them, yet there’s also some other voice at the same time, besides what you choose to say. When they say “I don’t believe you,” something in you might resent that, and maybe even fire back an accusation, and then they can learn your love is only there as long as they take it the right way. The resentment can be purely visceral: being doubted after you’ve tried feels unfair, but there’s nothing unfair in them going over your track record. On the other hand, don’t give in and start believing your love is more conditional than it really is, regardless of the past. Apply the Mr. Rogers reframing trick here as well.

path: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
joel_blocks.text: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet

path: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
joel_blocks.text: If you weren’t loved well as a child, then the suggestion to “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. Yet you still can’t feel the warmth people mean when they say love. One direction to work with is to start smaller.

path: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
joel_blocks.text: Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. This method of finding the most feasible next challenge is calledscaffolding.

path: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
joel_blocks.text: Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. Sometimes the warmth is actually there, with a cold part standing in front of it. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in. But it generally will stand down once it feels its concerns have been heard and addressed . But the guard is still available for dealing with people who haven’t earned your trust.

path: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
joel_blocks.text: If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.

path: If the Love Isn't Coming Yet
joel_blocks.text: Your little one might not take it well at first. More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.
Borrow Someone Else’s Love

When a good friend sits with you while you fall apart it does help you feel better. You call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while we don’t. So steal some of it. Usually what helped was how they just sat there without trying to fix you. Ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is good enough for a start, so try it before you call next time.

If you don’t have anyone like that right now, try remembering when you did. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Think of someone like that you remember fondlly, and imagine how they would sit beside your little one.

path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else
joel_blocks.text: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else

path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else
joel_blocks.text: Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, all the conditions you face, and then step outside it and ask what you’d tell them as a friend. This psychological trick has a rich history around it, and the blind spot behind it even has a name, Solomon’s paradox, after the biblical king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.

path: Borrrow Your Love For Someone Else
joel_blocks.text: Then take a small piece of whatever you’d tell them and do it yourself. If it’s “get more sleep,” that could be brushing your teeth before midnight instead of at two.
Show Up When Nothing's Wrong

If the only time the Nurturer shows up is when something’s wrong, your little one can start to feel like they’re your job. Sometimes show up just to say “I’m glad you’re here,” and then enjoy them for a minute, the way you’d enjoy a little kid who wants to show you a rock they found.

Watch how your love lands. “I care about you” can be patient, or it can be “I care about you, now hurry up and feel better.” Getting close can be too much, too, the way kids squirm away from an aunt they barely know who goes in for the big hug, and then climb all over the uncle who’s just sitting there. Knowing that love is in you somewhere counts for a lot, and you’re borrowing something you already know how to do.
A Smaller Doorway: Goodwill

Sometimes “I love you” is more than you can honestly say, especially to somebody who’s treated you badly. Even the usual whittled-down loving-kindness prayer, “May you be happy,” can feel like rewarding them. That’s why I go with the Buddha’s overall wish (paraphrasing): “May you be loving, peaceful, and free,” since if they were all of those, they wouldn’t have done what they did, and then they actually would be lovable.

This goodwill isn’t just for the target of it, though. You may find it bounces back and opens up a little warmth in your heart. And if “I love you” goes flat when you aim it at yourself or your little one, the same wish works there, too. 🫶🏿
Ask God for a Loan

The dog kind of love is real love. Some people also know a love that’s a whole different size, like God’s, or whatever opened up for them in prayer or on a long retreat, and I don’t want to lump that in with the dog. If you’ve been there, don’t shrink it down to a thought experiment about a friend.
If you haven’t been there yet (and even if you have), I have good news for you!
Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!

One practical door anyone can use to slowly experience divine love is gratitude (even after the Turkey’s done & Thanksgiving is over!). Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades. I think it’s essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.

This is a bit tricky to put into words, but let me try anyway… You may be suffering now, but you could be suffering more. That’s something to be grateful for (although please don’t fall into the common trap of being grateful that you have what others don’t have, as that’s more like selfishness). I’m not talking just about changing your “glass half empty” perception to a glass “half full perception.” I’m not pushing “toxic positivity.” Being thankful shouldn’t be pushed on people who just need to grieve for the moment. On the other hand, I’ve noticed that I can sometimes completely flip a bad psychedelic trip into a good one with gratitude alone.

If you have a moment right now to breathe, and to really feel the beauty of that breath as it goes in and out, that’s something to be grateful for. I learned this many times the hard way. For example, when I got tuberculosis from a cave in Mexico at age 20, and coughed for six months straight, eventually having my throat close up, leading to a near death experience. And then in Senegal, I had a suspected bilharzia infection in 2021, and could only painfully pee blood. I promised to always be thankful if I could ever pee normally again. Miraculously, I then found some obscure ethnobotanical research (on Google Scholar, before AI) which led me to drink roselle tea. Within an hour, I was cured. I don’t always remember to say “thank you” when I pee now, but I try.

That may sound like a silly, quirky waste of time to some folks. But what I notice is that saying thank you for every little thing, whenever I remember to, is not about imposing some kind of “spiritual discipline.” It is directly reconnecting me to something pure and sacred.
Mo’ Money, Mo’ Problems

And I’m certainly not preaching “prosperity philosophy,” like the mega churches, even though it can seem to start at that. We still need to remember that if we can only be thankful for the good things we have, we can fall into the trap of thinking that what we have is happiness itself. I’m ultimately reaching for something much deeper. Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn’t lead to being content with less. When you can see that less is more, at a deeper level, that’s where the real gratitude flourishes.

And even (or especially) when I am suffering, I try to remember to be grateful for that also, because if not for suffering, I would not even think about how much I have enjoyed not suffering as much, and how much this tribulation will help me to develop more humility, compassion, wisdom, and gratitude in future. Most importantly, it connects me with the plight of the countless other beings suffering at that very moment, authentically bringing up a wellspring of compassion in my heart for all of us. And I see clearly that it is my inner child who is feeling this pain, and what an honor it is that I can be there for him.

Of course, that’s not to say you should not try to suffer less, or get away from abusers. The point of life, according to every spiritual tradition and religion, I think, is to suffer less, which first requires us to understand the cause of suffering, and what real suffering and real happiness are. If you, like Biggie Smalls, have come to understand that having money is not real happiness, that’s a big deal! That’s something to be grateful for. If we get a chance to meditate or pray today, while on the toilet, upon waking up, while ChatGPT is “thinking” for us, that’s something to be thankful for, for sure.

Notice how, when you offer thanks (to the universe, to life, to God, whatever you may believe in), a space in your heart opens up. It might not feel immediately like you suddenly know the real meaning of Divine Love, but it’s a little spark of … something.... There’s a tiny bit of freedom, of peace, stillness, softness. And as that softness deepens each time, you start to understand what I mean by Divine Love. Many people have written books on this topic (like A. Helwa’s book, Secrets of Divine Love, for example). hope you are able to experience this when you try it out for a while, and I’d really love to know how it works for you!
Invite Your Little One In

Once you start to feel that lovely softness of the heart (which can become a very deep field of « perfect freedom »), invite your little one in with you as your spiritual integration practice. They might go numb, or call BS on that. If so, they might just need to see if you’re actually humble enough, and grateful enough for them, to listen to their rejection be patient, and be open to the possibility that your Higher View is missing the trees for the forest. If you instead retreat back into your cozy corner, it’s the food bank feast all over again: You can have an enormous spiritual feast upstairs while the child is still starving downstairs.
A Heart to Child Loop

With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso. One punch there hurts a lot (as I sadly learned while getting beaten up every day at kindergarten recess by a gang organized by my best friend. Can you believe it?), so it makes sense to look for your little one there.

Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part’s a gift from them, and they don’t owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. If you don’t feel the warmth just yet, rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required. Non-judgement is a place to start. It can blossom into love over time. I also enjoy massaging my solar plexus gently.
When the Spiritual Relationship Hurts

If a spiritual teacher you trusted betrayed you, even sitting down to meditate can feel like it belongs to them now. But if you let an abuser control your appreciation of life, then you’ve given them an unearned win.

Being the grown-up doesn’t mean controlling everything yourself, though. After a betrayal like that, part of you might want to. Spiritual support can help you act where it’s yours to act, and let go of outcomes and other people’s choices where it isn’t. The Serenity Prayer is exactly to remember that.
Make a Simple Vow

If your promises still mean something to your little one, maybe because you’ve kept a few small ones, a quiet vow can help too. As many real-life parents know, your heart really explodes in such an unexpected and wonderful way when you hold your newborn baby for the first time (happened to me!). And if you’re not yet a parent, it can really help to imagine holding a baby in your arms to make the vow feel real. Imagine you just had a baby, how would you feel? Would you look at him/her with adoration and joy? Carry that into visualizing yourself with your own inner child:

“I know you’re in there. I love you. You don’t have to love me back or trust me yet. I can’t promise that nothing painful will happen. Or that I’ll always know what to do, or never react badly. But I can promise to tell you the truth and listen when you’re angry. I’ll make our life together safer where I can, and take the next step I can see to protect you. When I fail, I’ll come back to make it right. You don’t have to believe these words. Watch what I do.”
Notice it only promises what you can keep, so your little one can actually watch you keep it.

Whenever your little one shows up looking for their parent, even if they don’t know that’s what they are doing, you go back to being the one they can rely on, and you’re kind to them while you do it. If they show up to have some innocent fun, don’t “put them in their place” as the adult. But sometimes they show up as the one who doesn’t want to go to bed. Now you’re in my mom’s place: you still go to bed, and staying kind about it shows them bedtime isn’t a lack of love.
Remind Yourself

The vow can live somewhere you’ll see it, too, like on a stuffed animal from when you were little, a photo of yourself as a child, or just a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Whatever helps you feel connected to the Nurturer and Protector you’ve been practicing. The Teddy bear note may remind you to think, “When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time.”

A real-life child of yours, or a calm pet, can also act as a companion that brings out the relationship with your own inner child. My son did that for me, and I think that’s very common for parents. But those are also their own beings with their own needs as well. Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.

path: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
joel_blocks.text: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

path: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
joel_blocks.text: When you wish someone well, what do you have in mind? Probably something like, “I want them to have enough to eat, a safe place to sleep, some people who like them, etc.” Wanting this for someone is a form of love (this is the kind babies already understand). It’s a good and important thing, this practical love. But the horizon of your wishes may be partly determined by how much happiness/peace/freedom you know to be possible.

path: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
joel_blocks.text: Sometimes your little one already feels cared for in those normal ways, but they need help with deeper existential questions. Maybe your life isn’t meant to be just something to put up with, something to slog through, a hamster wheel, a rat race. Maybe you could live it with a sense of zest and discovery. What would you need for that?

path: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
joel_blocks.text: Maybe you’ve had some big spiritual experiences, and for a while knew a kind of peace/love etc. that you hadn’t known before. Now when you wish someone well, your wishes may be bigger – perhaps much bigger – than they would have been before. You might [« love them in a language they will never learn. »] (<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8o4jvs0s55E&t=3m10s>) This is one reason why loving-kindness meditation can seem kind of silly but actually be very powerful. Saying, “May you be happy,” over and over won’t necessarily zap you into a state of profound love for all beings, but it’s one way people discover that there is such a love and learn to expand it.

path: How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
joel_blocks.text: If you’re curious about this bigger love and happiness, follow that curiosity. You don’t have to pretend to believe anything, but you might read a few people from different traditions (try a Sufi poet or a Zen teacher). If you know anyone who seems consistently happy in this bigger way, check out how they deal with people when things are going badly. And if they still pass that test, consider, “I don’t know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?” That’s what I did, and it was the best move I’ve ever made !
The Joy In Sorrow

path: Jelaluddin Rumi wrote: ‘The most secure place to hide a treasure of gold is some desolate, unnoticed place. Why would anyone hide treasure in plain sight? And so it is said: ‘Joy is hidden in sorrow.’

path: Jelaluddin Rumi wrote: ‘The most secure place to hide a treasure of gold is some desolate, unnoticed place. Why would anyone hide treasure in plain sight? And so it is said: ‘Joy is hidden in sorrow.’
joel_blocks.text: Another Sufi teacher, Hazrat Inayat Khan, wrote,“God breaks the heart again and again and again until it stays open.”

path: Jelaluddin Rumi wrote: ‘The most secure place to hide a treasure of gold is some desolate, unnoticed place. Why would anyone hide treasure in plain sight? And so it is said: ‘Joy is hidden in sorrow.’
joel_blocks.text: Some people find that deep grieving gives way to feeling connected to something much deeper than what was taken away. Being loved can open grief, too. Someone takes care of you, and you think, “Why does this make me sad?” It can be sadness for the care that was missing.

path: Jelaluddin Rumi wrote: ‘The most secure place to hide a treasure of gold is some desolate, unnoticed place. Why would anyone hide treasure in plain sight? And so it is said: ‘Joy is hidden in sorrow.’
joel_blocks.text: As Sister Medhanandi said, « When we are able to come face to face with our own direst fears and vulnerability, when we can step into the unknown with courage and openness, we touch near to the mysteries of this traverse through the human realm to an authentic self-fulfilment. We touch what we fear the most, we transform it, we see the emptiness of it. In that emptiness, all things can abide, all things come to fruition. In this very moment, we can free ourselves. »

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: As the Guide, you choose what your little one learns and what it gets to experience, and you hold standards, the way a good parent would. Your parent’s harsh tone doesn’t come with the job, though.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: By the way, this job doesn’t have to be called the Guide. The Wise One works, or your Inner Teacher, and “Guru” does for some people.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: If you don’t feel like the wisest apple on the tree just yet, that’s perfectly fine, because we can borrow the guiding function to start with, and you can get better at it day by day. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great Guide. Ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (“What would Jesus do?” or “What would Buddha do?”) can give some direction, too, while you develop your own internal compass.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: Borrow Hindsight

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” Some moments of silence then allow incredible wisdom and compassion to pour down in moments of grace. At other times, you might just have a slightly better understanding develop slowly.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: That future you probably also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe instead of a magic solution, they’d remind you of what my mom often reminded me : « Everything always works out in the end, somehow ! ». I thought that was actually pretty funny, but it consoled her. One man’s humor is another’s wisdom.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, although don’t assume they’ll definitely end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, but I’ve definitely felt a lot more patience in arguments when I could imagine the future versions of us saying « that was just a silly misunderstanding ! ».

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
Remember When You Already Did It Well
joel_blocks.text: Remember When You Already Did It Well

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
Remember When You Already Did It Well
joel_blocks.text: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. Getting hit with a stick doesn’t solve the problem, unless you’re a Zen student. 🙃

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
joel_blocks.text: A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
joel_blocks.text: The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
joel_blocks.text: Forced adulthood can get into your head too, and it might set the bar too high sometimes. At your grandpa’s funeral, some dumb jingle starts up in your head and you nearly laugh during the eulogy. That doesn’t mean you didn’t love him, or that something’s wrong with you. Minds come up with ugly and embarrassing stuff all the time, some of it the opposite of what you believe, and bodies do their own thing too. The Guide doesn’t need to police your every thought. It notices the jingle and knows you didn’t mean it, and that it isn’t who you are. Then it goes with what you’d stand behind, which here is probably squeezing your mom’s hand and listening, and lets the jingle go.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
joel_blocks.text: I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about some pattern you have, that might be a signal to give some attention to how you can improve on that pattern. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive, and can be simply let go of.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: You Belong Everywhere and Nowhere

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: The Guide also points beyond itself, toward somewhere you belong that doesn’t ask you to give up being yourself. That might be nature, or existence itself. It might be whatever your tradition sees as ultimate. Love can come from any of these places, and you also belong there. Maybe you’ve felt that randomly while wandering around outside somewhere, like you didn’t need anybody’s permission to be there. The way into « the zone » is time in nature and contemplative practice.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: With that under you, belonging with people can get a lot less desperate. Your little one might still think, “If they stop liking me, I won’t belong anywhere,” and the Guide can remind it there’s more to belong to than them. And then one day you might have the opposite problem, with people wanting to belong too much to you.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: Timing Is Individual

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: Most of us need enough Nurturer and Protector first. Otherwise the Guide just overrules your little one in the name of something higher (spiritual bypassing, dressed up as direction). Like a shepherd who’s beating sheep to make them move. So warmth and safety come first for a while, and the direction can grow once there’s a clear little one in there to guide.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: Say you had a spiritual opening years before you had much of a Nurturer or Protector. Has your love grown because of it, and has that love reached your little one yet? Look at how you are with people, too, whether you’re more compassionate and understanding. Are you getting better at relationships, including telling the truth when it’s awkward and doing what you said you’d do?

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: Between Spoiling and Clamping Down

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: Maybe you’ve let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins? Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling it the same way. Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting it out of anything hard. Treats and pampering do better at set times, where they can’t get out of hand. They shouldn’t get canceled as a punishment after a bad day, either.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: After all, sometimes “I want it NOW!” is just that: a rung on the desire treadmill. No hidden guard or old trauma required, because all creatures have endless desires naturally anyway, especially when immature. You can hear that want without shame about it. Hearing it doesn’t require giving into it, especially if getting your way would hurt you or somebody else.

path: The Inner Guide : Becoming Your Own Shepherd
joel_blocks.text: We also need to remember that many of our desires are covering over deeper desires which we may be afraid to look at. Relationship desires, for example, can be scary because we don’t have unilateral ability to satisfy them. Learning to acknowledge the unmet needs without a definite solution is a deep Guide capacity which takes maturity to appreciate.
Practicing With Your Little One
Start With Whatever Showed Up

You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you’ve been staring at the rug. I count that as reparenting, too, even if it feels like it’s in the way. Before you decide where it’s coming from, ask it what it’s trying to stop, or what it wants. Maybe it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that’s trying to protect you. Maybe it’s that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.
You can tell that part something like, “I see you. I’m not going to force my way past you. What’s going on, boobaloo?” Or however you’d actually say that. Then wait and listen patiently.

path: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
joel_blocks.text: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue

path: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
joel_blocks.text: If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you’re supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. Maybe that’s what happens for some people, but you might not be some people (hehe). If talking into an empty room feels silly, small figures on a table can help (so that you feel even more silly!?), like one for your little one and one for the rest of the gang that shows up. Put whichever one’s running the show on a throne. Both ideas come from sections 12.2 and 13.1 of a book called Schema Therapy for Children and Adolescents, which I’ll call ST-CA.

path: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
joel_blocks.text: You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and yet still be able to think a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, speak or write them. You might feel more comfortable that way than just staying in imagination land.

path: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
joel_blocks.text: Then again, maybe what’s actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach. Or perhaps you’re in a place you want to leave. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be nice to do for yourself. And if you don’t know, it’s fine to guess. Maybe it’s some genuine human closeness, or figuring out some way to have more say in your own life.

path: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
joel_blocks.text: Life is always switching up on us. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first.
Use Childhood Photographs Gently

My friend Cody had trouble imagining his inner child, so he started looking at photos of himself when he was young. That did the trick ! If you have the same trouble, see if you can find some childhood photos.

While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones. Use Pema Chödrön’s “feather touch” approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (”You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

We don’t need to ask it leading questions, like “Who abused me & how? » or “What memory is my body hiding?” Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren’t necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions. Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I’m sure you can relate.
A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed (like O.J.😅)... not necessarily representative. Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.

If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don’t confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here. You might be looking at the photo thinking, “That would explain so much.” Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won’t lead you toward an answer. (If the glove doesn’t fit, you must acquit!)

Put the photo back in its drawer when you’re finished. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you’re getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present to close out properly. Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this “Present Time” reminder. Can be as simple and silly as “Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!”
Journal With Each Hand

Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand. As titles go, it’s pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings, as well as some extra creative juice. The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.

For some people, writing might make them feel more confused, especially at first, or nothing might want to be written.Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.
Which thoughts to talk to

When journaling, you might be surprised sometimes the myriad things that come into your mind seemingly out of nowhere. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you’re in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your little one asking.

I wouldn’t spend long deciding what to call each part you meet. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that’s trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn’t have to get any louder.
If no answer comes

That’s fine for now. No need to answer for that part just because you had set this up as a healing session. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

path: If you do get an answer
joel_blocks.text: If you do get an answer

path: If you do get an answer
joel_blocks.text: An answer could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It’s often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that’s what it wants. How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better.

path: If it tells you to do something
joel_blocks.text: If it tells you to do something

path: If it tells you to do something
joel_blocks.text: I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.
If it's anxiety

Anxiety is often a part of you that’s trying to protect you, making a guess about what’s coming, like that people will laugh at you. Sometimes it’s right, sometimes it’s useful, sometime’s it’s not. Anxiety is not necessarily bad by itself, but as they say, the fear of fear is worse than the fear itself. Hearing it out and taking any action that seems legitimately beneficial as a result, often helps it to pass.
