joel_blocks.text: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
joel_blocks.text: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “shenpa,” and she says “hooked” is a more descriptive translation for that Tibetan concept than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. 💃🏿 Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you’re supposed to be observing yourself. 🤦‍♂️ Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute.

path: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
joel_blocks.text: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: “Oh! I’m hooked again! That’s awesome I could notice it!” Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Maybe then you’ll find there’s enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you’d regret later. Or enough Guide to redirect attention to where it’s supposed to be.
Gentle Meditation and Mantra
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JQs2watlFws

If the hook is stuck a bit deeper in your mouth and you’re flailing around like a fish out of water, gentle mantra meditation or self-hypnosis (which overlap a lot) are some tools that can really calm your nervous system down. A lot of people find that a mantra they feel some heart connection to, repeated in their head or out loud, especially with a nice melody, can lower the walls enough for the heart to open up. It’s not something to lean on all day as a way of coping, but used as therapy it can be super effective. I personally love this beautiful Om Mane Pemme Hum mantra that I found in the Garchen Rinpoche documentary, For the Benefit of All Beings:

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
joel_blocks.text: What to Make of a Passing Feeling

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
joel_blocks.text: If what someone did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn’t mean their boundary crossing indicates “They’re evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you’re in your happy place.

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
joel_blocks.text: Feelings about yourself work the same way. “I feel attracted” or “I feel ashamed” is real as a feeling, but it doesn’t settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche’s pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc.

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
joel_blocks.text: You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don’t have to declare your pronouns on social media, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there’s nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see if there’s some avoidance of differentiation. I myself for a long time was accused of « having no opinions » (which I almost prided myself on🙈), and now it’s often the opposite accusation.

path: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
joel_blocks.text: The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later.

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: In the morning, begin the day intentionally, not just because the sun chose to come up once more, since we can’t count on that. 🫣 Here’s one way you might pl/orkfully start off:

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: “Today I will neither be Peter Pan nor Captain Hook. I will notice a hook or 2 which lead to unconscious behaviors.”

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: Then at night, pay yourself to be your own therapist so as not to break the bank. Equipoisedly look into how the practice went for you today:

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: “Where did I notice the hook?” At dinner with the in-laws? Watching animé?

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: “Where did it still seem to control me despite noticing it?” (That’s the most frustrating part, when you know better, and you still act the same.)

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: Then get practical so it doesn’t become another OCD loop: “What small repair or protective act shall I bring in for a proper response to that?”

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: And don’t forget to appreciate the good! Moments of warm, beneficial connection (whether internally from child to adult, socially, spiritually, etc) are all to be celebrated. Were you maybe firm like an elephant today, or courageous like a lion? Adopt the entire spirit animal zoo if need be! Turtles are good if you need impulse control.

path: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
joel_blocks.text: Count recognition as progress, regardless whether it came up a bit late, as the goal is to bring the awareness closer and closer to the present. All or nothing from the get go would be cool, but we normally have to learn step by step. If/when you interrupted the pattern, pat yourself on the back, or even kiss yourself on the shoulder. You can renew your intention for tomorrow, getting better & better, every day, in every way, as my Dad used to say. And enjoy your well-earned rest tonight.

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
joel_blocks.text: Close the Session and Return to Life

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
joel_blocks.text: Without an ending, the processing can just start looping. So when you’re done, look around and say where you are. Feel your feet on the floor, or the chair under you, and remind yourself about something silly and obvious, like what century Pharao Tutankhamun was crowned (1332 BCE in case you forgot!)…

path: Close the Session and Return to Life
joel_blocks.text: And what’s next for you two? Maybe it’s making food, or just going to bed. Whatever it is, tell your little one, “That’s enough for today. We’re going back to the life we’re building.” Nothing has to be resolved first, and whatever you’re still feeling can come along.
Discovering and Healing Old Patterns
How Distrust Reproduces

Say you learned somewhere along the way that if you need someone, they end up leaving you. You probably never said it to yourself in words, but it steers you before you know why. But the need for socialization remains a pull, regardless of how unlikely it may be to work. And so we develop various coping strategies, ranging from distracting ourselves from that natural pull with other things (whether harmless hobbies or bingeing on TastyKakes), to people-pleasing, to insisting we don’t need anybody (sour grapes). (The TastyKake corporation has asked me to remind you that sometimes a sweet treat is more a celebration than an escape.)

Some people pleasers go along for months as if nothing’s wrong while the pressure builds and then they blow up out of nowhere (one of my old patterns). Then they feel so bad about it they go right back to going along to get along. With any of these patterns, I’d ask what it’s protecting you from, because it doesn’t really help to just label it a bad habit.

The most insidious part of these expectations is that we can get stuck in them even when they no longer make valid predictions about the people in our life. Like my second wife, Bee, who wanted with all her heart to trust me, but set up so many impossible tests that not even Einstein could pass with a perfect score. I tried to explain to her that she was an unwitting prophet.

Have you ever heard of a self-fulfilling prophecy? Perhaps nobody ever hears that you’re struggling, since you didn’t think they’d want to. Then nobody offers to help, and that can look like proof nobody cares. Keeping quiet might have been the smartest thing you could do as a youngin’ with nobody safe to tell, but now, if there are people who are safely available, it can keep help away.

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
joel_blocks.text: Shame can make you feel unlovable

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
joel_blocks.text: Shame comes when you’re holding a dark secret. It might be a secret for someone else who abused you, because it made you feel dirty or worthless. Or it might be due to thoughts in your head that bother you. Or it might be from bad patterns of behavior you have. Whatever the cause, finding someone trusted that you can slowly open up to is a magic cure. You still have to take accountability and repair any damage you caused if you did.

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
joel_blocks.text: Shame becomes toxic when it gets stuck, and you don’t know what to do with it. Then you can become ashamed of being ashamed, and on and on. Get curious about what makes it so hard to give up. I went through toxic shame for 12 years. I’m sure it will help you to read my full guide on shame. Here’s one trick from that article :

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
joel_blocks.text: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

path: Shame can make you feel unlovable
“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
joel_blocks.text: My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. (”Once upon a time…” helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.
How to Forgive Without Forgetting

Healing does need to get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule.If someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground. And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury.

The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person’s conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle. From in there, it was the only move they had.

« Hurt people hurt people, healed people heal people » means that hurt people pass on pain they never worked through, although « externalizers » are the ones who directly hurt others, while « internalizers » try to protect others by holding that « secret burning thread » inside themself, which ends up exploding onto others anyway at times when it gets to be too much to hold, You may have heard this story from somebody telling you to forgive, and it sounded like they must have no clue how deep the betrayal was. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt, even if you see how they got there. It’s just that punishing them now can’t reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense, the support, or the skills they needed for a respectable response. What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now.

So a boundary can still be appropriate to enforce with them. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”
Forgiving Yourself

Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was really yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends, and by changing behavior going forward. Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
joel_blocks.text: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
joel_blocks.text: Now, once you’ve got this cast of perfected future characters in your mind, you can also go back to earlier traumatic memories and relive them in a better way. For example, I’ll take one instance from my own childhood. I was only spanked one time as a child. I hung up the (expensive) phone call my dad was on with a very important official in another country, because I wanted some attention. I don’t think he was exactly furious at me, but he decided this deserved a spanking, even if he didn’t agree with spanking in general. Since he wasn’t furious, the spanking didn’t really hurt, but it hurt me emotionally quite a lot, because I was so extremely shocked that my parents would use physical violence on me. Like I lost my sense of safety with them at that moment. And I may have learned that I was undeserving of attention, that I behaved in ways that made me deserve physical violence, that I was bad, etc.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
joel_blocks.text: Many people experienced something like this where the consequences for their little mind were much more severe than anyone would imagine, and in almost every case, the adult themself does not currently understand the extent of the damage until the little one feels safe to tell them. I can’t tell you how many people I’ve worked with have laughed at how brutally they were beaten as kids. Just laughed it off like it was nothing.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
joel_blocks.text: Whatever the situation was, we will contrast it with the corrected version.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
joel_blocks.text: How should discipline have been done right ?

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
joel_blocks.text: While often it is obvious how a perfect parent could have responded, in my example, I’m not exactly sure what a perfect father would have done here. But usually what my dad preferred as discipline was a forced « time-in » via a « punishment hug. » (which is called « therapeutic holding » in the literature) and I feel like that worked well for me. I did that with my son, Bear, as well. I would hold him as lovingly as possible, until he started to cry, because he did not seem interested in learning any lessons until that point. After he cried for a bit, we talked about what happened and what was wrong with it. When I felt satisfied he was understanding and aligning his values in a genuine way, the time-in was over, although he might want to continue the time-in sometimes a bit longer also, as it began to feel nice after the ego came down.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
joel_blocks.text: My sister disagrees that this was therapeutic for her. She thinks it caused her to feel like hugs in general are punishment. A regular time-out could work, but sometimes it has to be enforced somehow, like locking the kid in their room for a bit (and assuming they can’t just have fun in their room). Recognizing the difficulty in finding a perfect parental response can also help us. Sometimes there was no perfect response that would have been harmless to all parties. But my sister should probably go back to those memories of punishment hugs and ensure that she learns that hugs are loving, even if that particular hug was also designed to teach a lesson about improving her behavior.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
joel_blocks.text: I think that what children really need when they are acting narcissistically is some way to break through to real emotional connection. With very stubborn children (most are at times), that may require induced crying. It didn’t always require a punishment hug to do that, either. Just shouting « BEAR ! » could make my son cry at times. It’s crucial here that the caregiver producing the child’s egoic breakdown must have the moral high ground along with compassion, so they aren’t seen as just someone abusing their power. And they should be open themselves to being corrected by the child if the child has a valid counter-argument for who is in the right.

path: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way
How should discipline have been done right ?
joel_blocks.text: Importantly, there is currently no expert consensus on how children should be disciplined, aside from using the least amount of force possible, in the least traumatizing way, whatever that may happen to be. There isn’t even agreement yet if logical consequences work. And one thing Visakan made me consider is that the parent-child relationship is the only one that’s supposed to change in major ways many times over the years. A parent might be great at a certain phase of child-rearing, and terrible at another (like treating you forever as if you’re 5).
Answering the Strict Disciplinarian

A good routine, like yoga in the morning and a proper bedtime, still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s done in a disciplinarian style. One exercise you can do to handle this is to go back and rewrite your responses to that strict disciplinarian. First, remember who it was that drove you so hard as a child. Then start a little rap sheet of their provoking lines. Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.

The Critic’s voice can often pile on, to the point where you can’t even understand why or what you’re really feeling anymore. You feel sad at first, then the Inner Critic calls your inner child pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness with some simple nurturing instead from the beginning, but now you have to peel back this other nonsense to get to it.
When the Practice Gets Difficult

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
joel_blocks.text: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
joel_blocks.text: A lot of people get stuck right at square one. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone or the laundry feels urgent. Or some voice says this is silly, and it’s hard to tell which part of you is saying it.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
joel_blocks.text: My friend Scott said:

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
joel_blocks.text: “Half the time when I try to connect to baby me, I feel fake and it seems crazy.”

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
joel_blocks.text: I used to be all personal trainer and teach persistence on this as the remedy. Keeping at it does help, since a little one who learned to expect being dropped won’t trust you right away. But I don’t think that explains the adult feeling fully. More importantly, I think it could even be like unintentional gaslighting to the little one to ask to connect with them when you don’t believe they’re even real. Like when my mom pretended to listen to me when I was young, but even less excusable (from the inner child’s view) because she was not asking for my time when she did that. So, it’s worth meditating first on why it feels fake.

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state
joel_blocks.text: For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state

path: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state
joel_blocks.text: Like on MDMA or deep in meditation. All of a sudden your little one is right there! Oh my gosh! And the love or grief that sounded like therapy talk is just obvious. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn’t prove they happened. I’d still hang on to that connection you felt, even once it’s gone, and try to bring a little of it into your normal life. You’ve felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn’t just pretending. If you’re « lucky ,» it’s not a question of trying to maintain that connection, but trying to figure out how to deal with the rawness of it after the high wears off. That’s what integration therapy is for. I have more advice on using psychedelics with the therapy in the « Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism » section further on.

path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
joel_blocks.text: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
joel_blocks.text: Reparenting assumes there’s a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is. But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form. All this stuff about your little one could have left you wondering who I’m even talking about.

path: Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet
joel_blocks.text: Maybe you started playing that part so early, and it took over so completely, that “What do I believe?” or “What do I want?” has no clear answer of your own. They sound like such easy questions, too. Back then, asking might have gotten you in trouble, or laughed at. Or there was just no way to ask. That can make “love yourself” feel pretty empty (love what, when the part you’ve been playing doesn’t feel real?), and the authentic self never received the conditions needed to develop. We get deeper into finding and building that self in « Untangling the Belonging Bargains » further on.

path: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
joel_blocks.text: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow

path: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
joel_blocks.text: Some people have the opposite problem, where it feels like they’re connecting with their little boo, but then they find out somehow that it was still pretty superficial. Dreams can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in the second half of the night’s sleep, if you wake up in the middle to meditate, as I’ve discovered. That’s a good point to ponder over what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again in the morning (but write it down so you remember!). And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, shorten the practice or do it earlier.
When Healing Turns Into Checking
You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be completely real while you’re checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you’ve finally grieved it correctly.

Going back to reconnect with your little one is normal parenting/reparenting, but returning to lick the same wound over and over can become a search for certainty in an inherently uncertain existence. Spending all day asking, “Did I process it properly? Did I grieve it enough?” is clearly not what we’re after here.

And the checking can take many forms, aside from inner mental checks. A body scan can turn into one, or a confession. Even, going on a date, or checking your dating profile matches, can be a version of this if what you’re really after is proof that you’re good and lovable. It might calm things down for a while, and then the next little wobble matters even more.

If you’re feeling guilty because you didn’t put your seat belt on, just put it on. If you still want to investigate it later, fine. Perhaps now and then you feel bad about that time you refused to put it on, broke your collar bone in a crash, and then got blamed for not wearing it. That’s natural, but doesn’t mean there’s something new to look at.

path: How Would You Know It's Helping?
joel_blocks.text: How Would You Know It's Helping?

path: How Would You Know It's Helping?
joel_blocks.text: Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself, “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life.

path: How Would You Know It's Helping?
joel_blocks.text: Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that’s the endgame, it’s just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy.

path: How Would You Know It's Helping?
joel_blocks.text: It’s like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don’t need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate.

path: How Would You Know It's Helping?
joel_blocks.text: And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn’t as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

path: How Would You Know It's Helping?
joel_blocks.text: If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you’re allowed to live, stop there.
When to Change the Strategy

Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I’d want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never have to find out what’s underneath this. Before going with either of those paths, look for what exactly is in the way.

path: How many tries would I give it?
joel_blocks.text: How many tries would I give it?

path: How many tries would I give it?
joel_blocks.text: It’s not like we can just put a number on it. Some things shift in a day. Others take about as long as learning guitar. But do notice if progress is stagnating. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner.

path: If you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results
joel_blocks.text: If you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results

path: If you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results
joel_blocks.text: Consider if you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I’d like to hear about it! Leave a comment here in the article.
If you'd rather stop
Not wanting to do it anymore might be reason enough, but if that “nope” sounds like a part of you that’s trying to protect you, I’d hear it out first to get a better understanding.

path: When the Urge to Escape Arrives
joel_blocks.text: When the Urge to Escape Arrives

path: When the Urge to Escape Arrives
joel_blocks.text: The avoidant guard shows up when you get close to some painful memory or insight. Suddenly you’d rather have a drink, check your phone, or do anything aside from directly feeling it (even a yawn can come with an “I’m so done with this” feeling). Maybe this guard doesn’t believe there’s a grown-up around who could handle what’s coming? That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling , a global movement of peer counseling, counts yawning as productive emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out.

path: When the Urge to Escape Arrives
joel_blocks.text: I’ve found many times that simply staying with the feelings in a meditative way is miraculously transformative. One time, my second wife, Bee, was yelling at me in the kitchen for quite a while, about some kind of accusations that didn’t make much sense to me. I was feeling defensive, but instead of doing or saying something in my defense, on this occasion, I visualized my energetic shield disappearing, and I imagined her negative energy passing right through me. All that clenching relaxed, and it became a peak spiritual experience, where I felt like a conduit for some massive energy flow. My giant smile didn’t seem to help her feel better, though. I can’t say either of us learned how to integrate the lesson from that in a way that made practical sense for our relationship, although I do believe there’s immense freedom there to harness.
Physical Pain Makes It Harder

Physical pain can bring on the urge to escape too. Say an attack has you curled up on the bathroom floor, and whatever knocked the pain out last time (say, fent, or ketamine) starts looking real good, though you know it’ll leave you worse if you keep resorting to that quick fix.

By now, you may have already been through a million doctors who shrugged their shoulders, or even alternative treatments that were too costly or hard to grade. Sometimes it really is so simple that the best doctors and scanners can’t figure it out, like your house is moldy. It is worth going through all the basic checks first that you can do yourself, and trying the things that make most sense. For more on that, check my detox guide.

And when the symptoms come and go randomly, the best time to get diagnostics done could be right at the actual time of the crisis, rather than waiting until you feel well enough to make an appointment, and they may be able to treat it while it’s happening. But what if the attacks come almost every day? You can’t move into the ER. And normal test results don’t prove the pain is imaginary, just as a treatment that helps doesn’t explain what’s causing it.

I’d ask for a chronic pain specialist and a written plan for the flare-ups you can see coming, including the new or severe signs that mean you go to the ER right away, but don’t let amelioration of symptoms be the end of the investigation.

path: Listen To Your Body, Or Else!
joel_blocks.text: Listen To Your Body, Or Else!

path: Listen To Your Body, Or Else!
joel_blocks.text: Sometimes, a physical illness is really partly or wholly an emotional issue, as happened to various friends of mine, including a med student friend who was going to the ER every couple days with undiagnosable phantom issues like paralysis and pain. One doctor finally told him it might be « somatic symptoms », so he tried Somatic Experiencing therapy, which helped more than any medical treatment. The same was true with Lucia Capacchione, PhD., and many of her clients and friends. She wrote one of the first comprehensive inner child therapy guides, Recovery of Your Inner Child, in 1991. While I don’t doubt that many people do recover from mysterious physical illness via meditation, inner child therapy, and somatic therapy, I also don’t want to claim, as some folks do, that all illness is entirely rooted in emotional issues. That is clearly not true. We don’t need to be gaslit to consider all the possibilities. And there have been some studies on this :
Altered States and Intensive Practice

path: Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism
joel_blocks.text: Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism

path: Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism
joel_blocks.text: When the physical or mental pain is intense and impenetrable, the urge usually sits on the fence between escapism and doing hardcore battle with the demons. Why not just blast right past that guard part, with intensive meditation or psychedelics? Sometimes that can help tremendously, but both can get you past the guards before there’s a grown-up big enough to hold whatever comes through, so I’d hold off until there’s enough Nurturer and Protector around. How much is enough depends partly on the medicine and what therapy is done with it. Borrowed is fine, as long as it’s from someone steady who won’t try to run your trip for you.

path: Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism
joel_blocks.text: I’d learn to do inner-child therapy sober first, in your ordinary mindstate, since that’s the one you’ll be living in. Cars don’t start at 60mph, that’s not the way the universe seems to work. First gear leads to second leads to third, etc. Second gear, in this case, may refer to gentle meditation or self-hypnosis. When you’re ready, my self-hypnosis guide and lucid-dreaming guide can take those deeper, into third gear.

path: Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism
joel_blocks.text: Low doses of entheogens can also synergize compatibly with various gears. Like MDMA, female iboga, Loveyhuasca, certain mushrooms, like Orissa India, and San Pedro cactus (esp. with sublingual mapacho + full spectrum CBD tea) are more protective and nurturing than many other medicines, especially at lower doses, so you don’t need as much Nurturer and Protector built up for those, though you still need some. Some people benefit more from solo therapy, while others benefit more from having a trained therapist guide the experience.

path: What to Do With a Peak
joel_blocks.text: What to Do With a Peak

path: What to Do With a Peak
joel_blocks.text: Now, the beautiful stuff. Say one night (on a psychedelic, in a dream, ten days into a meditation retreat, whatever) you felt more love than you knew was possible. Wonderful, and it matters! Keep it as a reference point, and chase it playfully, because it is already a part of you, and you’ll be like a cat chasing its tail, which can be cute and fun, or dizzy and absurd!

path: What to Do With a Peak
joel_blocks.text: Jack Kornfield has a whole book on what comes next, After the Ecstasy, the Laundry. The title kind of says it all. That night can’t be the bar for every morning after, or regular life starts to feel like failing. And gorgeous as it was, it doesn’t mean you’re done healing. The laundry will tell you more, and it’s the same test as in Timing Is Individual.

path: What to Do With a Peak
joel_blocks.text: One reason the peak is so momentary is because we often don’t need to truly give anything up to get it. Say you’re still pretty angry, and you want enlightenment, but it has to come with the money and worldly success in one package. Ketamine can get you to a peak anyway. Then, you might now have some kind of transcendental “understanding” glimpse that seems like it could fix everything, if only you could be more aware of it, which often leads into a cycle of taking more and more medicine over time. I’d prefer to ask if any of the discontent has been let go, or the anger? If not, that peak was less the love we’re after here than “I’ll be grateful once I’ve got it all,” the gratitude with conditions from Ask God for a Loan.

path: What to Do With a Peak
joel_blocks.text: And if your little one still can’t take the love in? Hold off on going for bigger, crazier breakthroughs, however tempting it is, or at least know that they are a double-edged sword. Something’s in the way, and getting to know it is your next job. Often it’s a protective part that’s seen love come with strings before. Hear it out first.
When Escape Leaves Reality Behind

All kinds of psychoactive drugs can mess with your sense of what’s real, and that’s often the point of them, so you can break free of all your old patterns completely for a bit. But in general, try to select the healthiest ones and use slow and gentle protocols. I’d say one of the most abused psychedelics (aside from ketamine, if you call that a psychedelic) is 5-MeO-DMT. I have a guide on that. People very often believe you need a huge dose of it for a “full release.” They go through all kinds of screaming and shaking, nearly killing themselves, with absolutely zero inner-child work being done. Breaking armor down alone is not real healing.

path: If a past trip went badly
joel_blocks.text: If a past trip went badly

path: If a past trip went badly
joel_blocks.text: If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don’t try again until you understand what would make it safe. I’d look at the drug and the dosage, as well as mindset and setting etc. I have a guide on dealing with bad trips and altered states.

path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?
joel_blocks.text: Is your paranoia a warning sign?

path: Is your paranoia a warning sign?
joel_blocks.text: Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn’t automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn’t balanced by practicality. “The CIA is mind-controlling me!” is (mostly) paranoia. “The CIA, marketers, and other forces are conspiring to mind-control me, the way they do to everyone else! But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates” has a noticeable dollop of paranoia too, but it’s practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis. “...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!” is leaning psychotic. Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, amphetamines, PCP, dirty LSD, so I’d avoid those.

path: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis
joel_blocks.text: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis

path: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis
joel_blocks.text: Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I’d be careful with other drugs that mess with what’s real too. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it’s family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset. These are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can’t, get help from trusted advisors.
Who counts as trusted

By trusted, I mean someone you know is trustworthy from a long relationship with them, not someone people on Reddit said was super magical and healing. That’s called a crapshoot. It might turn out well, it might not. It might seem like it did, and then later you realize you were duped, as happened to me with Sidney the iboga shaman. A new therapist is not as trusted as an old one. As they say, “new friends are silver, but old friends are gold.”

path: If you keep coming back from trips confused or spaced out
joel_blocks.text: If you keep coming back from trips confused or spaced out

path: If you keep coming back from trips confused or spaced out
joel_blocks.text: Maybe nothing worse happens, but after several trips like that I’d be concerned. If you’re having episodes when you’re sober, or any of them are severe, see a psychiatrist.

path: Before you quit a medication or alcohol
joel_blocks.text: Before you quit a medication or alcohol

path: Before you quit a medication or alcohol
joel_blocks.text: Don’t suddenly stop a medication just because you suspect it’s involved. Talk to the doctor who prescribed it. Benzos can be dangerous to quit cold turkey. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous if you’re physically dependent.
What you mix

Be careful what you mix, too, and not just prescribed medicines. Even some basic things like cinnamon can be dangerous (and helpful) with ayahuasca, and doctors & AI don’t know about a lot of this. I also learned that mixing acacia confusa with mimosa hostilis is very destabilizing and challenging, but excellent if you want to know how it feels to be painfully autistic + schizo! I have a list of things to be cautious about with ayahuasca in particular.

path: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
joel_blocks.text: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon

path: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
joel_blocks.text: The first time I took San Pedro cactus, at a medium-low dose, it made me super emotional, and I cried a lot. It was very therapeutic, actually. But I still squandered that opportunity: with a better understanding of reparenting, it could have been much more therapeutic.

path: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
joel_blocks.text: Ayahuasca was often much more challenging, because at first I was taking huge doses for ego death. It gave me a connection to divinity, and inner-child reparenting does work best with a little of that. But then I squandered the opportunity to bring that love down from the heavens to my inner child, which led me to be more like a preacher than a fully well-rounded individual who could lead by example.

path: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
joel_blocks.text: At first, I thought I was just naturally very capable of handling powerful mind-shattering experiences. Like Psychedelic Superman. Then later I learned it was the ayahuasca harmala trance helping me. When you’re deeply entranced, you can’t freak out: no matter how scary something is, it’s just like, “Oh, this is scary, OK, oh well.” That’s not a good excuse to take crazy doses tho.

path: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
joel_blocks.text: How did I learn the trance was what helped ? Because I went psychotic once on ayahuasca made with pure THH (an alkaloid from the ayahuasca vine) and Mimosa hostilis bark, which has DMT in it. THH alone isn’t hypnotic (trance-like) enough to keep people safe with higher doses of DMT. I was very lucky that my landlord, a Quaker family friend, was super understanding and talked me down gently. Otherwise the cops might have been called, and I could still be in jail, perhaps, since ayahuasca was illegal there at the time, not to mention I had a lifetime stockpile of mimosa bark in the house that they might have claimed was for distributing. In general, don’t call the cops and expect it to go well. That’s a real last resort.

path: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
joel_blocks.text: Out of hundreds of times I’ve taken iboga, there was one time just a small amount of male iboga root bark got me a bit hypomanic, to the point where a thought came: “Everyone should listen to me!” Luckily, I was trained in Buddhist meditation, so I immediately challenged it with “Why should anyone listen if they have no interest?” I stopped using iboga for a while after that, and I warn people about that potential issue with male iboga specifically, although it can show up with any psychedelic, but usually with higher doses.
Altered States Can Require Reparenting

Have you ever been attacked by a literal demon? Maybe during sleep paralysis or meditation or on a psychedelic trip? A lot of modern folk laugh at this, yet it’s really quite a common experience. I was being psychically attacked by ghosts in my home as a child. Because I was literally a child, I was an easy target. And since most people never actually grew up, they are easy targets for every kind of influence, including spirit influence. It’s like leaving your front door open all night every night in NYC and expecting no thieves to enter.

Those ghosts knew my weakness: dares. So they would dare me to jump out the window. I wasn’t suicidal, but I hated to seem like a “wussy.” Luckily, I trusted my parents with this information, and instead of taking me to a psychiatrist and pumping me full of anti-psychotic drugs, they put bars on the windows. Many kids are not so lucky in modern societies. They may get pumped full of anti-psychotic drugs for the rest of their life once diagnosed. That said, it’d make sense to get a professional to weigh in for some situations. I still played around with half-hanging out the windows, but I wasn’t quite dumb enough to jump out, and I really appreciate that my parents took it seriously without catastrophizing.

Public Service Announcement : If a voice or urge is directing you towards harm, and you feel at risk of acting on it, as with myself and those ghosts at home, move away from that open window and get some outside support.
As a semi-adult, age 26, after my ayahuasca ego deaths, I lost my fear of the dark, death, and ghosts, and I told those ghosts to go into the light. And they did. I’m basically a Ghost Buster now.

Then I discovered meditation. After I began meditating deeply for a while, it seemed like my astral portal opened. I started getting attacked by spirits during sleep paralysis. They would sit on me, prevent me from breathing, and instill tremendous fear into the core of my being.
Yep. Exactly like that.

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: Sleep paralysis is a trance-like state, and trance can be “more scary” because you’re trapped in it, but it’s also less actually dangerous. You can’t ruin your life at all in trance (unless a bad hypnotic suggestion gets deeply implanted, perhaps), while without trance you can “freak out” in a way that might end up getting you committed to a mental hospital, thrown out of your housing, going to jail, possibly even killing yourself. In trance you can basically work with the fear. You hopefully, eventually, recognize the fear has no real-world significance and it’s purely just fear, so it’s super useful that way. The thing to fear is fear itself, since it actually opens us up to being manipulated by demons, which feed on it directly. So it’s not really that they have no power. We give them the power.

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: After multiple episodes of this I decided to stop giving in to the victim mentality, and to start taking it seriously as a part of spiritual practice. My inner Guide saw it as a perfect opportunity to demonstrate the power of love over fear. The next time it happened, despite how scary it was, I sent unconditional love to this demon on me. It took some minutes, but once that love was seen as enduring, the demon left, and it never returned.

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: I’ve also trained other people to do this during spiritual attack while on psychedelics. It works a lot better if you are already trained in loving-kindness meditation to the point where it’s natural. I’d say it works way better than exorcism techniques (like Julian Palmer’s torping, which he also admits doesn’t work as well as love).

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: The astral plane is a bit different from the 3D. In the astral realm, unconditional love is a true, ultimately powerful physical force. Like a river, or a moat. There’s no evil that can trespass that moat. But don’t assume it will always work like that in the physical plane. It has worked for me sometimes when facing some thugs, but definitely not with others. Loving someone does not mean you leave the front door unlocked with a sign saying “take whatever you want,” unless you’re a non-Shaolin Buddhist monastic like Ajahn Brahm.

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: If you’re not able yet (or in the moment) to summon real love for an enemy, you can first send love to your frightened little one from your adult Nurturer. Many people also find they can borrow support from God, Jesus, angels, devas, or whatever loving spiritual presence fits their tradition. If I were to do that, I would still be framing it as “Please help this situation with love” rather than “Strike down the enemy!”

path: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
joel_blocks.text: Borrowing support like that is basically borrowed adulthood. At first you may need to feel protected or loved by something bigger than you, before that love starts to feel like yours, and then bit by bit it starts to become your own. Send some of it down to your frightened little one, and when that’s possible, toward whatever you’re afraid of. Continuing to relate to benevolent spiritual powers/beings is still perfectly fine, but they would surely be happy if they rubbed off on you! If you’re Christian, remember that In John 14:12, Jesus told his disciples whoever believed in him would do greater works than he did.

path: Non-altered states can feel like this too
joel_blocks.text: Non-altered states can feel like this too

path: Non-altered states can feel like this too
joel_blocks.text: Even social media algorithms will turn your life into hell if you don’t have the loving, protective inner parent developed. When you do, social media actually becomes useful and feels nice to interact with now and then. I can’t tell you how many people I’ve talked to who said they love life once they turn off their phone for a few days.

path: Non-altered states can feel like this too
joel_blocks.text: Many people think reparenting sounds silly, or like the kind of ridiculous therapy people do when they have too much time or money. But you know what’s even sillier? Wandering the world aimlessly and getting manipulated by all kinds of evil forces. 💀
Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life

Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt by people that weren’t either of those, so some of the healing has to happen with real life other people too. If you’re presently lucky to have some support, it might be mostly one person carrying a lot of it. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing. If it’s more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn’t feel as deep.

Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what they’ve been doing for you, and start doing it yourself. You’ll find the balance is dynamic between inner & outer reliance, and going too far in either extreme isn’t generally the healthiest.

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
Play Is Part of the Work
joel_blocks.text: Your little one wants to play, too, which is why I call the deeper therapy pl/ork, play + work. Many times we adults see things as work that a child would see as play, like yoga, for example. So if it feels like you’re enforcing everything as a discipline, see if you can change that discipline into a game. Personally, I can really get a lot of enjoyment when I feel those lovely stretches without thinking it’s another task. A lot of the best discoveries come when you’re both just messing around, kind of like how kids tell you what’s really going on from the back seat, when nobody’s looking right at them. Play not only paves the way for therapy, but is a part of how successful therapy should be measured.

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
Play Is Part of the Work
joel_blocks.text: A lot of what adults tend to lose, your little one still has, like the silliness and the irreverence, the rawness, the creativity, all that, and maybe a connection to the Great Mystery from before your karma ran over my dogma 🤪. That’s the spark of life they bring, and you get to draw on it and give back, so it’s more communion than command. For one example of the spark, there’s my post Treasuring the Inner Child’s Gift

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences

joel_blocks.text: But that spark of life might have been suppressed as you grew up..

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
joel_blocks.text: If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at playing the « chamelion ».

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
joel_blocks.text: So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
Let the Child Be Bad at Things
joel_blocks.text: Reflection can show you what got sMothered/suppressed. For identity you also need some experiments out in real life, so go try something new just for you. Maybe a foraging group, or a painting class. Stargazing can be awe-inspiring, and you might even see a UFO! Notice what holds your attention when nobody is impressed.

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
Let the Child Be Bad at Things
joel_blocks.text: The old parent in your head may demand immediate talent, though, and then the first time you’re awkward at it, that’s “evidence” that you’re stupid or clumsy. Or you hear, “Come on, you’re not really the type.” I think your little one is listening to see if anybody’s going to stick up for them. The grown-up you’re building has to be the one who does: “It’s okay if we’re bad at this, nobody’s on trial. We’re just seeing if we like it. And it’s ok to be great at it also !”

path: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
Let the Child Be Bad at Things
joel_blocks.text: Give a new interest enough tries to get past the humiliation of being a beginner, when you keep telling people, “Sorry, I’m new.” Maybe after that you still genuinely dislike it, and then you may quit. You may also discover a part of yourself that never had permission to exist.
Differentiation: Keeping Your Own Ground
Untangling the Belonging Bargains

Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades. For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.
Even with good parents, you could have learned unhealthy self-valuation when people repeatedly praised what you did rather than your inherent worth. That wasn’t your flaw.

path: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
joel_blocks.text: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child

path: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
joel_blocks.text: Pema Chödrön has a quick map for finding the bargain. Your little one can panic when something hurts, and also when something good might disappear, like praise, romance, money, status, belonging or a spiritual high. You might still be enjoying one of those when your little one starts asking how long this is going to last.

path: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
joel_blocks.text: When that happens, you can ask yourself these, once you’ve caught your breath:

path: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
joel_blocks.text:
- What do I think I’m about to get, or lose?
- Whose approval suddenly feels like I can’t live without it? It isn’t always who you’d guess.
- Is this a value I’m standing up for, or a high I’m trying to keep?
- Would this still be something I’d feel is worth doing if at the end of the day, I didn’t get praise from anyone for it?

path: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
joel_blocks.text: You don’t have to stop enjoying pleasure, praise, gain or belonging, as long as they don’t define you.
Practicing Differentiation

Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship. You’d still belong, but now you come first and belonging second. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.

As you tell the part you’ve been playing apart from the authentic self that didn’t get much practice, notice whether it makes you more curious about both, and better able to relate to them. Or does it have you thinking, “That chamelion’s fake, and I’m getting rid of it”? Keep in mind the chamelion was a skillset that somehow worked to help you fit in. Even if you’re not planning on playing James Bond anytime soon, you still might need to smooth your edges out sometimes as part of socializing. You can’t always disagree with everyone on everything and still expect to be enjoyable/enjoy company.
Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:

- Caring about somebody’s feelings without automatically adopting their opinions or sacrificing your own ground. Their reasons can still change your mind, though.
- Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: “Wait, why was I nodding along?”
- Noticing when what you thought you knew suddenly feels like water dripping through your hand because of praise or pity, fear or attraction, or something that really resonates with you.
- Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places). That one can take a while.
- Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.
Key developed this identity and differentiation portion of the method, drawing on Murray Bowen’s family-systems work and her own self-therapy.

path: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
joel_blocks.text: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone

path: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
joel_blocks.text: Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”

path: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
joel_blocks.text: That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!

path: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
joel_blocks.text: What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. Do your part for people who are suffering, and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.

path: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
joel_blocks.text: Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.

path: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
joel_blocks.text: I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.
3. Finding People and Building Trust
People? Where Are the People?

I can’t tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I’d bet on more than one place. Keep the good people you’ve already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if you find one that fits you. And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that’s when we ask the Adult Protector to start paying attention.
First Social Connections, Done Right

Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable.

Some people try to make themselves as lovable as possible, hiding their real feelings to do so. Others have no filter, on purpose, to see if they are still loved and appreciated. Like my one friend who used to go into churches and tell pastors they were wicked or unfit for their jobs, and then he wondered why he didn’t feel the love those churches promise (which was more proof he was right about them to begin with). He’s not wrong to speak his mind, but I wonder whether his goal is to reach mutual understanding, to vent, or to re-try dealing with some traumatic childhood pattern of losing himself to fit in with the gang.

Neither of those approaches are the balance we’re seeking, and both are treating the other person like they’re your reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Instead, get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.
If you find yourself getting strange reactions from people all the time, check what your expectations were about how they’d react.

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
joel_blocks.text: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
joel_blocks.text: And reaching out doesn’t mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn’t fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you’re still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I’d either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn’t safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn’t prove you’re meant for each other, or that they’ve earned your trust yet.

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
joel_blocks.text: Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
joel_blocks.text: Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, and of course that’s exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. I’d assume that what you tell won’t be completely confidential, especially if it sounds like something dangerous.

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
joel_blocks.text: You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. Just because Mr. Boopaloopa was your name on WhatsApp doesn’t guarantee you’re anonymous, by the way.

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
joel_blocks.text: And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
joel_blocks.text: So I’d ask this person, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That’s a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn’t even bother with that, because whatever they tell you today, the law can change tomorrow.

path: Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
joel_blocks.text: You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

path: Ask What Kind of Company They Want
joel_blocks.text: Ask What Kind of Company They Want

path: Ask What Kind of Company They Want
joel_blocks.text: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: “Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, brainstorm, or...?” Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it’s obvious what they want. But as they say, “assume” makes an “ass” out of “u” and “me.”
Hearthwork: Taking Turns

The basic premise of Hearthwork, my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It’s kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.

Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time’s up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don’t push. But they don’t act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they’re thinking, “Oh, I know what this is about,” or “Here’s what you should do.” They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places, and it’s your turn to keep “Here’s what you should do” to yourself.

The peer doesn’t become your permanent parent, though. They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form. Is that therapy? Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure. Professional therapy’s still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.
Dating While You Heal

Maybe you’d rather that your support came from a lover, as well. Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part. That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know. I wrote a whole romance guide, mostly due to this.
Speaking Up and Handling Conflict
It’s often in handling conflict that we see the real inner child jump out. So if you’ve been wondering where they are in a session, here you, let’s pl/ork !
