joel_blocks.text: If Someone Has Actually Hurt or Threatened You

path: If Someone Has Actually Hurt or Threatened You
joel_blocks.text: Even once, whether or not it brings up old stuff, get safe first, which is not a small thing at all, I know.

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
joel_blocks.text: Speak Toward What You Are Building

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
joel_blocks.text: It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent, just like that Pink Elephant. Being totally independent can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!

path: Speak Toward What You Are Building
joel_blocks.text: But let’s also make sure we don’t hide from shadow stuff with toxic positivity. Grief is natural, and letting tears flow can be immensely therapeutic, as long as they don’t hijack your perspective with a cemented story of what will always be true. If your little one says “he hurt me,” we honestly label that as harm, even if it was also a learning experience. Same for anger, a “No,” who’s responsible, all that. Then once the difficult experience is acknowledged by the Nurturer, the Protector & Guide can lead the way up to more safety and maturity.

path: Being Your Own Advocate With Doctors
joel_blocks.text: Being Your Own Advocate With Doctors

path: Being Your Own Advocate With Doctors
joel_blocks.text: No need to give them a good impression if that means not being your own advocate. If you don’t feel up to it, bring someone you trust to speak up for you (like, not that relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment’s for.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: If you’ve got something burning you up that you wanna say, write it out as a reply. There. That got it out. Ahh. Breathing easier. 😌 But don’t send it. Take that breather you earned and then come back to it from a cooler place.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: It doesn’t mean you need to hide your upset, or apply for a permit to protest, but choose your battles and execute them wisely, so you don’t end up regretting how you communicated later. As Lao Tsu might have said (if I could ever have read that whole boring Art of War book), a war with no casualties is the best possible war. When high IQ & EQ communication hits a writer’s block, sometimes the best thing is to simply say, “I need some time to think about my response.” And if the conflict really requires a response right now, then obviously just do your best rather than wait for the perfect timing.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: Be honest with yourself about what your goal is for this communication. Do you want to break someone mighty down ? To show that you or your views matter ? Or do you want them to listen and hear you without getting defensive ? Sometimes folks are shocked at the response they get (why does everyone always reject me?), without even considering whether that response was easily predictable based on the energy they gave out to spark it.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: This is where I turn inward and talk to my writer, which is often my inner child when emotions pop up. It’s like I’m holding his hand and showing him a better way, not like I just stole his pencil because he wrote something embarrassing. So what was he actually trying to say? A lot of the time it’s just “that hurt.”

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: Other times it’s “I did this too.” My friend Tyler saw a guy smoking in front of a baby and asked him if he thought that was wise. The guy asked if he thought it was wise to mind his own business, and Tyler said, “Well, I believe in Christ, so I thought you might care about life too.” Afterward he wasn’t sure he’d handled it right, or whether he should have thrown the first stone at all, since he’d smoked in front of a baby himself.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: But Jesus also said to take the log out of your own eye first, and then “you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.” That’s exactly what made Tyler the right person to say something. If you actually have the problem they have, and you want to call them out for it, call yourself out for it instead. What we came up with was something like, “Hey man, when I was younger I smoked in front of an infant, not realizing how selfish that was, and I notice you doing the same thing. I’d ask you to please have some compassion for him. I have a young child now, so this really touches me.” Tyler’s an evangelical Christian who preaches on YouTube, so the fact that he really appreciated this take on Jesus’ message is pretty salient to me.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: It’s also how your voice sounds, though. You can say all the right words, but if the tone is accusatory, it doesn’t matter.

path: Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
joel_blocks.text: Before sending anything, I’d read it once as if I were them, sitting there with my phone. Stuff I wrote while I was scared can sound like a threat to them.

path: If You Really Did Hurt Them
joel_blocks.text: If You Really Did Hurt Them

path: If You Really Did Hurt Them
joel_blocks.text: Repair it. Easier said than done...

path: If You Really Did Hurt Them
joel_blocks.text: Are you sorry for what you did, or are you starting to take back the complaint too because they’re still upset? Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. 😅 And if it fails again, and you’ve said what you mean, well, you can’t guarantee they’ll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn’t tell you the whole conflict was your fault, nor does it prove they’re manipulating you.
Other Folks Also Have Hooks

Once you’re in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don’t go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one “no” or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they’re allowed to say no to you. Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they’re not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you? (The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People.) Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?

If it’s the first, it can seem like you haven’t explained yourself well enough yet. You probably have, and it makes more sense to count on what they keep showing you they can do than on the right words finally getting through to them. Maybe what they can do is text you something kind the next day and not bring any of it up.
Can They Change?

You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that’s probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

path: If a Relationship Keeps Making You Feel Less Safe
joel_blocks.text: If a Relationship Keeps Making You Feel Less Safe

path: If a Relationship Keeps Making You Feel Less Safe
joel_blocks.text: Meditate on why it makes you feel unsafe, and what keeps you in it. Might it be due to a lack of the healed inner child/inner adult relationship? (If so, you’re reading the right guide!)

path: Taking a Break From a Family, Group, or Relationship
joel_blocks.text: Taking a Break From a Family, Group, or Relationship

path: Taking a Break From a Family, Group, or Relationship
joel_blocks.text: Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. Sometimes you need to take a break from a family, group or relationship, even if they aren’t doing anything to you. Simply being around them may pull you into that programmed space where listening to what you really want becomes harder. Some people come back later on different terms, and sometimes the break has to be long-term because the pattern of losing yourself with them is deeply entrenched. As you differentiate, you learn to tell which of those apply.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one (figurative) life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, or your youngest real child moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: Your little one might be sure everything’s over. Usually one real thing ended, and the related habits might be held onto like on autopilot. Ask your little one what they’re scared will happen in the bardo between past and future (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: Something basic can mark the ending, like boxing up the old keys. Nobody needs to know what door will open next. But when the not-knowing feels too heavy, a new identity can sure look tempting. Like a borrowed coat that doesn’t fit but at least it’s warm. But you can’t go far with a borrowed coat anyway, so don’t force the future on. Keep taking care of yourself, and grieve what ended with your little one beside you during the metamorphosis.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: Missing Someone

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: When you miss someone, let the ache be a cue for love. It doesn’t have to become one more problem to solve, and pushing it away won’t help. If love’s there, “I miss you” becomes “I love you.” Or there’s the loving-kindness wish: “May you loving, peaceful, and free.” You can picture them. Or don’t, and just feel the care going their way.

path: 5. When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun
joel_blocks.text: All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it, because the main benefit is for your little one. I have an N of 1 case study that proves this works, also. It’s what rescued me from deep despair when the love of my life, my second wife, Bee, left me.
6. The Love Has to Move

Community can come before the big opening or after it, too. Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible. Other times it’s the other way around. Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn’t have imagined before, and then they start to “manifest” different kinds of people and relationships in their life. Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.

This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with [building community] (community.u-dont-exist.com). Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn’t really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn’t always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into your relationship with the grown-up you, then out to other people, and back again.

joel_blocks.text: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
joel_blocks.text: We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide.

joel_blocks.text: Inner Child Reparenting therapists

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
joel_blocks.text: Inner Child Reparenting therapists do exist, and you can find them, although they often are not licensed, and I don’t know of any central directory, nor of any protocol they’d have in common (aside from Lucia C’s, in the Appendix). There are none which work with my guide yet. I can consult, and if you like the guide, you can ask a therapist to check it out and see what they agree with or disagree with as a great way to vet them.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
If you want a licensed therapist
joel_blocks.text: If you want a licensed therapist

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
If you want a licensed therapist
joel_blocks.text: The best licensed, listed therapists you’ll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I’ll talk more about those in the appendix,. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
joel_blocks.text: Before choosing a therapist

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
joel_blocks.text: Get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I’d especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won’t tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I’d also want one who doesn’t put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won’t charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can’t tell you any of that.

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
joel_blocks.text: AI therapy

path: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
joel_blocks.text: I’ve tried all the top AI therapy apps, and they’re all pretty bad. I’m trying to make my own based on this guide, but I’m becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn’t mean you can’t get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes, and don’t let it replace real humans who love you and want to think with you Actually, I find one of the best uses for it is to improve my interactions with real people. For example, it can help me formulate more careful replies to people who are too sensitive to take my excessive bluntness or wry humor (although I wouldn’t send them actual AI text).
Conclusion and Appendix

path: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
joel_blocks.text: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.

path: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
joel_blocks.text: And the love you’re worthy of is the same love as back in « Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! », the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of relief when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or your subconsciosu, was there before you could earn anything. Love from a person is more conditional than that. Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.

path: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
joel_blocks.text: Be patient with yourself, and gentle, including with the part of you that thinks you should be over it by now. You are more than your pain and your past. There’s help, and lots of other people are out there learning to look after their own little ones. You can post a comment right here and let us know how it’s goin for you.
Appendix

path: How This Relates to Similar Therapies
joel_blocks.text: How This Relates to Similar Therapies

path: How This Relates to Similar Therapies
joel_blocks.text: My reparenting guide is part of the larger reparenting and inner child therapy category. As far as I can tell, it was first developed in 1976 by Dr. Lucia Capacchione. Although Lucia is no longer with us, [her institute still trains therapists] (https://luciac.com/instructors.php) in her methods (including art therapy and other things). I greatly respect and appreciate what Lucia has given us to work with. While there are many inner child therapy offshoots (often less codified than Lucia’s book, Recovery of Your Inner Child), it would be impossible for me to compare my guide to each inidivdual therapist’s approach. Below are the differences between Lucia’s approach and my guide’s approach :
Schema Therapy

Of the scientifically studied clinical approaches I know, Schema Therapy, developed in 1980s-1990s by Jeffrey E. Young, is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. The healthy adult recognizes when a need differs from the strategy you use to meet it, and it helps you set limits.. And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you’ve committed to. all that sounds like my Nurturer, Protector and Guide by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.

Being all scientific and stuff does have its drawbacks also. Schema Therapy’s name pretty much tells you all you need to know. What the heck is a Schema anyway ? (It’s normally described as a « pervasive pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving » (learned in childhood). Although I find a slightly different definition of it from Cleveland Clinic : « A schema is a long-lasting outlook or assumption that you have about yourself, others or the world. » But yeah, put those together and that’s basically what it’s talking about. So the schema therapist takes answers from a questionnaire you fill out and maps the your difficulties onto a set list of 18 schemas, which themselves map onto a set of modes, like the Vulnerable Child or the Punitive Parent. Based on those schemas and modes, the therapist assumes some things about your childhood that would explain them.

Where it really differs is spirituality. Schema therapy doesn’t build it in, though the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice « an important development. » That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy. Some people do blend them, though.

Tara Bennett-Goleman’s book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema. Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that’s the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).
Schema Therapy takes a more combative stance with the inner critic and guards than IFS or my approach, possibly a result of the lack of spirituality in it.
Internal Family Systems (FS)

Richard Schwartz, who developed IFS in the 1980s, called one of his books No Bad Parts. Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so my section, “meet the protector first,” would fit right in over there, although I focus more on keeping the inner child safe first. The one exception is that IFS does understand some parts may be entity attachments (« unattached burdens ») which need to be exorcised. My guide also talks about entity attachments, but I don’t believe that’s reason to start another war. Rather, I explain the root cause of such attachments as lack of protective love from the inner adult.

My reparenting method diverges from IFS at another important point. The IFS Institute’s outline of the model says “everyone has a Self,” (a divine True Self, from Advaita) and that the Self “can and should lead,” once your parts stop “blending” with it. I emphasize the inner adult you borrow, build and practice occupying that has the roles of: Nurturer, Protector, and Guide.

Is a perfect Higher/True Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I’d call that claim [spiritual bypassing] (bypassing.u-dont-exist.com). I’ve experienced that Higher Self perspective myself, though, in very powerful meditations.For example, one time, while still married to my first wife Ann, who was becoming more violent and crazy as time went on, we got super high on weed and we were both in some higher realm as our higher selves. My higher self asked her higher self, « Are you going to keep getting more and more crazy ? » Her higher self said, « Yes. » It was like we could see the whole timeline of life from above. Although, my friends already told me the same thing, quite sober. 😅

So, there is a less subjective way of seeing things as perfectly ordained in reality, despite the ego’s illusions, which matches what others say about it. As a Buddhist, I no longer see it as « Self », though it can still give the same love, peace, and clarity to whomever accesses it. Where I part ways with IFS is I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom that can be followed mechanically. From that higher vantage point, problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.

You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.

I’m also not a fan of the strange and complex cast of characters in IFS. IFS splits up my « inner child » into an indefinite number of wounded young parts called “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming. People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before. I’ve seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
Development of my framework

My inner child reparenting framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy. I borrow particular ideas and practices from each of them, but the mix is mine, so please don’t blame them for it.
Original Teachers and Practice Resources

Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes. Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it. She has a book and a free one-hour YouTube training, and she’s on Instagram.
Key helped me think through some of these ideas in a very « embodied » way for a few months, and she added The Guide to make the 3 parental modes.

Lisa Romano brings more neuroscience and CBT, and her video is a good place to start. She makes the point that remembering the specific details of childhood trauma isn’t necessary, because the felt body knows what needs to come up. Key developed the Guide’s sense of direction, and the identity and differentiation work from Bowen I mentioned earlier. She led a guided inner-child meditation in Nairobi in January 2026 for twenty people, and it’s up on YouTube.
